20.  The Secretary informed the Committee that the major investment in the port development would be c oming from the 
private sector because the development was on the P PP mode. During the year 2010-11, the proposal is t o award about 25 
projects which will have a total estimated outlay of Rs.18,228 crore, an envisaged capacity addition of 236.9 million tonnes. 
21.  Ministry of Shipping informed that for port se ctor an amount of Rs.920 crore including plan/non-plan was allocated at BE 
2009-10 which was reduce to Rs.700.03 crore at RE stage. Upto January, 2010 a total of Rs.279.11 crore was utilized. 
22.   The Committee finds that the total allocation for p orts sector during 2009-10 under both plan and non- plan was 
Rs.700.03 crore. Out of this amount Rs. 279.11 cror e only the Ministry was able to utilize up to Febru ary, 2010 which is 
close to 40 % of the total allocation. This slow pa ce of programme implementation is a matter of serio us concern. 
Already our port carriage is negligible compared to  the global capacity. Time bound completion of proj ects not only 
controls cost escalations but also the revenue earn ings directly and indirectly as a result of increas ed imports and 
exports. The Committee therefore recommends that th e Ministry should have a clear picture of the progr ammes to be 
implemented during the financial year with the allocated grants.  
PORTS-MAJOR AND MINOR  
23.  It was brought to the notice of the Committee that in 1999 Major Ports accounted for almost 95% o f the country’s total 
cargo handling while the share of minor ports stood at only 5%. However, in 2009, share of the major ports plummeted to 65%, 
whereas that of minor ports increased to 35%. Minor  ports offer much better facilities as compared to the major ones. Cargo 
clearance and other formalities are undertaken in a hassle-free manner, which lure shipping firms to avail their services. 
24.  Another advantage enjoyed by minor ports is th at since they are listed under the concurrent list of the Indian Constitution, 
most of the decisions regarding their developmental activities are undertaken by the respective State Governments. In fact many 
States have undertaken several measures to expand t heir port capacity. Minor port projects worth Rs 5, 163 crore to be 
undertaken under the National Maritime Development Programme (NMDP) are expected to further bolster bu siness of minor 
ports in the country. 
25.  On a query the Secretary informed the Committe e that “the cargo handling at Colombo is cheaper as  compared to Indian 
Ports. Indian ports charges are notified by Tariff Authority for Major Ports (TAMP), an independent re gulatory authority, on 
cost plus basis. The cost of the port operations is  higher because of multiple handling of cargo, poor  infrastructure and high 
levels of manual handling of work. 
26.  The Ministry further informed that Port of Sin gapore Authority is the biggest Port in Singapore, handling primarily 
containers. They handled 2,99,20,000 TEUs in the year 2008. Indian Ports, except JNPT, are handling multiple cargo liquid and 
solid bulk as well as containers. So, the traffic handled by them cannot be compared. However, the containers handled by JNPT 
are 39,53,000 TEUs in 2008-09. Chennai had handled 11,44,000 TEU and Visakhapatnam handled 88,000 TEUs  in the year 
2008-09. All the Indian Ports together handled only 65,88,000 TEUs. . 
27.  The Committee is of the view that the ports play a major role in the economic development of the count ry. The 
Committee, however, notes that the. major ports of the country are already facing stiff competition fr om the ports of 
neighbouring countries particularly from Sri Lanka and Singapore. Now, development of private and mino r ports are 
taking away the business of Major Ports. This according to the Committee is clear reflection on the manner in which the 

Government are handling the affairs of the Major Po rts, wherein the crore of rupees of tax payers have  been invested. 
The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure level playing field for the Major Ports so that they can 
perform and compete with private and minor ports. I n this connection the Committee would like to reite rate its earlier 
recommendations contained in its 134th report which is reproduced as below :– 
“The Committee notes that the Department of Shippin g is in the process of formulating a Maritime Polic y for the 
maritime sector which seeks to ensure a coordinated  development of Ports, Shipping, Inland Water Trans port, 
Ship building and Ship repairing with the objective  to upgrade and modernize the port infrastructure i n India to 
benchmark its performance against global standards.  The Committee also gathered from the replies that the 
regulatory authority will be set up at an appropria te time. The Committee observes that since much of the 
activities in the port sector are taking place with  private participation, there is need to establish regulatory 
authority well in time and that too before coming a cross any problem for better control, coordination and 
monitoring for achieving excellence in the port and  shipping sector besides addressing serious securit y 
implications. The Committee, therefore, recommends,  the Department to take steps for setting up of a r egulatory 
authority on the pattern of Telecom Regulatory Auth ority of India (TRAI) and Insurance Regulatory and 
Development Authority (IRDA) for creating a level p laying field and foster healthy competition and to encourage 
investments for the shipping and port sector beside s monitoring performance standards and adjudication  of 
disputes and disposal of appeal thereof.”  
28.  The Committee appreciates the performance of minor ports, whose cargo handling has grown up from mere 5 per 
cent in 1999 to 35 per cent of total cargo handling  in 2009. This only that implies that Government’s policy has not 
allowed major ports to grow and therefore, is losin g business. The Government themselves admitted that  minor ports 
offer better facilities, cargo clearance and other formalities in a hassle free manner.  
29.  The Committee is of the view that this is high time  when the ports within the country both major and p rivate 
should be developed in an integrated manner so that  they can unitedly compete with the ports of neight bouring 
countries.  
30.  It was brought to the notice of the Committee that some major countries give exclusive coastal Shippin g rights to 
their vessels. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while considering the demand of the foreign v essels for cargo 
shipping the interests of the Indian vessels and Indian Shipping Industry should be fully protected. 
International Container Trans-shipment Terminal (lCTT) 
31.  The Ministry of Shipping informed that the Gov ernment of India had approved the Capital Dredging for deepening and 
widening of the approach channel and berth basin of  International Container Trans-shipment Terminal (I CTT), at an estimated 
cost of Rs.381.25 crore, with a provision of fundin g through Grants-in-aid to the extent of Rs.297.42 crore and loan assistance 
of Rs.83.83 crore for the capital investment. The following are the advantages of the project: 
(i) A substantial portion of country’s container tr affic can be handled through this trans-shipment te rminal, which is 
presently trans-shipped through Colombo, Salalah, Dubai and Singapore. 
(iii) Saving to the tune of Rs.6000 to Rs.16,000 pe r container to the Indian Exporters. The anticipated traffic that would 
have the benefit on the fully developed stage is to  the tune of 1 million containers reckoning the min imum saving 
of Rs.6000 per container the annual anticipated economic saving is to the tune of Rs.600 crore. As this saving is in 
the freight cost and container handling cost in the  third country foreign port, this saving can also t o be reckoned as 
saving in foreign exchange. 
(iii) With the reduced transportation cost, India’s  produce will become more competitive in the intern ational market 
which consequently increases the foreign trade volume. 
(iv) Economic utilization of the cargo carrying cap acity of Indian Railways and Konkan Railways and Na tional 
Highways since a substantial volume of containers will be transported between hinterland and Port by land mode. 
(v) Additional employment opportunities to the tune  of 25,000 to 50,000.  
(vi)  Development of Port based industries. 

32.  As per the contract conditions of the capital dredging project, during the progress of work, inte rim payments are to be 
released on monthly basis for the actual quantity of work done at half the base rate and the balance amount will be released after 
the completion of the capital dredging work. Accordingly, for theactual quantity of 13.42 million m3 o f dredging completed up 
to 31/01/2010, Cochin Port has released payments fo r 50% of the value of work done. The balance will b e released on 
completion of capital dredging work. The capital dr edging work is scheduled for completion by May 2010 . Navigational aids 
will also be provided in par with completion of the capital dredging work.

crore in the grant-in-aid and Rs.83.83 crore as loa n component. The amount of Rs. 237.97 crore allocat ed in the BE 2010-11 
will be utilized for meeting the above expenses on completion of the capital dredging work.

35.  On the progress of the project, the Secretary also informed the Committee that the work done was about 70 per cent.

concerned to note the slow pace of work of the Vall arpadam transshipment terminal. The Committee notes  that the

SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA (SCI)  
37.  The Shipping Corporation of India Ltd.(SCI) wa s incorporated on 2nd October, 1961 by amalgamation  of Eastern

crore as on 31st March, 2009. The Company’s 218 bul k carriers cater to the movement of almost all type s of dry bulk cargoes, 
but mainly export of iron-ore to Japan and import of coking coal from Australia. SCl’s fleet of 26 Crude Tankers is deployed in 
the import of crude oil to Indian Refineries, in mo vement/storage of the indigenously produced Bombay High crude and in 
cross trades. The Company’s 10 Product Tankers are engaged in coastal movement of petroleum products a s well as in cross 
trades. SCI’s 5 specialised vessels are engaged in transportation for import/coastal movement of LPG, import of Phosphoric 
acid as also in movement of Ammonia.

Rickmers Linie, Germany for shipment of break-bulk/ general cargo from European ports to India. Joint F eeder Services-The 
SCI also operates Joint Feeder Services with M/s Se a Consortium Limited, Singapore for the India sub-c ontinent plying on the 
East Coast of India and domestic passenger-cum-carg o services between Mainland and Andaman and Nicobar  as well as

of the SCI was reviewed. While reviewing the progress made during the Five Year Plan period, SCI considered the achievement 
made so far, the requirement of SCI in the next few  years, the prevailing down turn in the shipping ma rkets, the financing 

difficulties faced by shipping companies for acquis ition of ships and also the opportunities available  to acquire 
secondhand/resale vessels at lower values.

43.  The Committee was informed that the shipping i ndustry has been going through turmoil due to the o ngoing recession in 
the global economy. This has also resulted in decline in vessel prices from late 2008 onwards in the n ew as well as secondhand 
markets. Due to this market turbulence and in antic ipation of better prices, SCI had taken a decision to wait till the new ship 
building market stabilized and there were benchmark prices available in the market. At the same time S CI was endeavouring to 
acquire secondhafi9lresale tonnage from the secondh and market. Due to the above reasons, SCI had been able to order only 8

INLAND WATERWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA  
64. The Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) is responsible for the development of National Wate rways, responsibility 
for the development of State Waterways rests with t he State Governments. The Central Government has de clared three 
Waterways, viz.  Allahabad - Haldia Stretch (1620 Kms.) Sadiya and Dhubri Stretch (891 kms.) and West Coast Canal from  
Kollam to Kottapuram stretch along with Udyogamanda l Champakara canals (205 kms.) as National Waterway s and are being 
developed by IWAI for shipping and navigation by pr oviding/maintaining basic IWT infrastructure i.e.  fairway, navigational 
aids and terminals. Three more waterways namely the  Kakinada-Puducherry canals along with Godavari and  Krishna rivers 
(1095 km), East Coast Canal along with Brahmani riv er and Mahanadi delta (623 km) and Barak river (121  km) are under 
active consideration of the Government for declaration as new National Waterways. 
65.  On being asked about the inadequate allocation  made for the development of inland water ways, the  Secretary while 
tendering the evidence before the Committee submitted that–  
 “........you had raised the issue of ‘nil’ or ‘ina dequate’ allocation for some of the major programmes. One was about 
waterways. As far as the Inland Waterways are conce rned, as the hon. Committee is aware, we have on-go ing schemes 
NW-I, the Ganga NW-II, the Brahmputra and NW- III, the Kerala, West Coast Canal for which a provision ofRs.115 
crore is there, of which Rs.63 crore, specifically,  is for the North-East. So, it, invariably, will go  to the Brahmputra and 
only Rs.52 crore will be available for the Ganga and for the Kerala West Coast Canal. Certainly, it is inadequate. As far as 
the IW-IV and IW-V are concerned, for IW-IV, the es timated project cost for development is Rs.l,570 cr ore and for IW-
V, it is Rs.4,209 crore. We are doing it in a phased manner. In the first phase IW-IV would need an expenditure of Rs.390 
crore for the development of the river portion and Rs.219 crore for the land acquisition which is for the development of 
Buckingham canal. For IW -V, the immediate requirem ent is Rs.2,230 crore, which is again, for developi ng about 370 
kilometers on the river. It is very, very important  from the traffic point of view because there is tr emendous potential for 
the movement of coal from the Mahanadi coal belt. H ere, the cost is high because there is a need to co nstruct five locks 
which itself would cost Rs.l ,843 crore. Though there is no specific Budget provision for this, what we now propose to do 
is this. One, of course, we have already written to  the Planning Commission based on the observations made by the hon. 
Committee at the last meeting. The hon. Minister ha s written to the Deputy Chairman of the Planning Co mmission and 
we are also taking it up at official levels. Apart from this, we are placing the proposal for Phase-I development before the 
Public Investment Board and we hope to move the pro cess of approval, thereby facilitating the provisio n of budgetary 
allocation.” 
66.  As regards the allocations made for the IWAI, the Ministry, in reply to a written query stated th at for 2010-11, IWAI had 
requested for a provision of Rs 164.70 crore under Grants to IWAI. However, it has been allocated only  Rs 50 crore. From this 
budget head, the projects for development of NW 1 & 3 and some other projects like National Inland Navigation Institute, IWT 
promotion, IT activities etc are met. In 2009-10, t he provision against Grants to IWAI (Plan) was Rs. 48 crore which was 
enhanced to Rs 67.85 crore at RE stage, since IWAI was in a position to absorb funds in excess of appr oved BE. IWAI shall 
utilize the entire enhanced RE under this head. 
67.  Planning Commission has provided reduced alloc ation (Rs. 115 crore at BE 2010-11) depending upon the availability of 
funds.  
68.  The important schemes/projects which were prop osed to be implemented from Grants to IWAI (Plan) in 2010-11 are : ( a) 
construction of high level jetty at Patna terminal, (b) setting up of DGPS stations at Katwa, Patna and Varanasi, (c) maintenance 
of night navigation facilities between Tribeni and Varanasi, (d) construction of permanent terminal at  G.R. Jetty, Kolkata, (e) 

up-gradation/development of floating jetties at various locations, (f) acquisition of CSD units for NW 1 & 3, (g) construction of 
terminal at Varanasi, (h) up-gradation of NINI, (i)  capital dredging in NW-3, (j) maintenance of night  navigation facilities in 
NW-3, (k) completion of terminals at Kollam and IWT jetties at Bolghatty and Willingdon island (l) operation and maintenance 
of existing terminals (m) expenditure towards demonstrative cargo transportation voyages being undertaken by IWAI on NW -1 
& 2 (n) up-gradation of IT hardware and software in IWAI offices etc. 
69.  The Working Group on Shipping and IWT for Elev enth Plan, constituted by Planning Commission under  the 
chairmanship of Secretary (Shipping) had recommende d a total budgetary support of Rs. 5580 cr. for IWT  sector during 
Eleventh Plan which included Rs 575 cr. for NW-4 an d 755 cr. for NW-5 (total of Rs. 1330 cr. for these  two waterways). 
However, the actual approved outlay during Eleventh  Plan for IWT sector was only Rs. 615 cr. Since thi s allocation was not 
sufficient even for ongoing projects of National Wa terways 1, 2 & 3, effectively no fund is available for new National 
Waterways therein except token provision of Rs. 1 cr. each fro NW 4 & 5. 
70.   However, instead of giving more money, alloca tion for IWT sector was drastically reduced during 2009-10 to Rs. 110 cr. 
(as against Rs. 180 cr. in 2008-09) and again to Rs. 115 cr. for 2010-11 by the Planning Commission. 
71.  In NW 4 & 5, on which developmental works have  not started, substantial quantity of dredging is i nvolved, EIA/EMP 
studies are already underway through M/s. Consultin g Engineering Services and it is envisaged that bef ore taking up the 
dredging work, the environmental clearance of MoEF shall be obtained as was done in NW-3. 
72.  The Committee notes that an allocation of mere Rs.1 15 crore has been made for the IWAI for the year 20 10-11. 
The Committee is of the view that the amount is ina dequate even to meet the maintenance of the existin g operational 
waterways. Since this allocation was not sufficient even for ongoing projects of National Waterways 1,  2 & 3, effectively 
no fund will be available for the new National Waterways, except token provision of Rs. 1 crore each for NW 4 & 5. The 
Committee also notes the facts presented by the Ministry that the total cost of development of National Waterway 4 is of 
the order of Rs. 1500 crore and that of National Waterway 5 is of the order of Rs. 4200 crore. If both these projects were 
to be completed in a period of 5-8 years, it is est imated that Rs.5700 crore would be required for taking up development 
of these two waterways. The Committee, therefore, r ecommends the Planning Commission to provide this a mount 
during remaining two years of the Eleventh Plan and  the Twelfth Plan. It need to give required priorit y/importance to 
the development of National Waterways. Demands and proposals made by the Ministry of Shipping for deve lopment of 
waterways need to be taken more seriously and makin g a drastic cut on the fund projected by the Minist ry should be 
avoided. The Committee recommends that the Ministry  of shipping should take up the matter with the Min istry of 
Finance and the Planning Commission for increased allocation for the development of National Waterways.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS –– AT A GLANCE  
ELEVENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN (2007-2012) OF THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING 
  The Committee notes that the shipping sector play s an important role in India’s economy. Almost 90% of the 
country’s trade by volume is conducted via  sea and the country boasts of having the largest m erchant shipping fleet 
among the developing nations. The Indian shipping i ndustry not only transports national and internatio nal cargos, but 
also provides various other facilities such as ship building, ship-repairing, lighthouse facilities, fr eight forwarding, etc. 
However, certain core problems such as Port congest ion and lack of depth in channels are plaguing the shipping 
industry.     (Para 7)  
  The Committee notes that the working group consti tuted for Eleventh Plan had recommended an outlay o f 
Rs.7689 crore as GBS for Shipping and IWT Sector, b ut the Planning Commission restricted it to Rs.1301  crore only. 
The Committee, in view of the increasing share of S hipping Sector in Indian trade, feels that the curr ent level of 
allocations is highly inadequate and it will curtai l the growth of shipping and IWT. The Committee, th erefore, 
recommends that the Government of India should increase the allocation for both shipping as well as port sectors for the 
remaining Plan period. The Ministry of Shipping, th erefore, should also come forward with proposals fo r development 
and the Planning Commission should allocate the funds for the purpose.  (Para 8)  
  The Committee emphasises the need for strengtheni ng the shipping sector to take up with the demands granted by 
the globalisation and liberalisation. The Indian sh ipping industry must acquire new heights in terms o f demand and 
infrastructural development. (Para 9)  
ANALYSIS OF ANNUAL PLAN 2010-11 
  The Committee notes that one of the reasons for t he under utilization of the allocation during 2009-10 is a general 
cut in expenditure introduced as a result of fiscal restrictions. The Committee strongly disapproves the across the board 
imposition of fiscal restrictions without taking in to account the relative merit and importance of the  schemes/projects 
for our economy. The Committee recommends that Mini stry of Shipping may take up the matter with Planni ng 
Commission for a review and not apply such general restrictions on Shipping & Port Sectors that play m ajor role in 
Indian trade.    (Para 15)  
  The Committee notes the that Ministry of Shipping  could not utilize even the reduced allocation made at RE stage. 
Out of Rs.1566.33 crore, only an amount of Rs. 110 crore is likely to be utilized during 2009-10. The Committee finds no 
justifiable reason for this. In such a situation, t he Ministry of Shipping may not justify any demand for higher 
allocation. The Committee recommends the Ministry s hould be proactive and take steps in advance to ens ure that 
allocated amount is utilized evenly and optimally.           (Para 16)  
  The Committee expresses dismay over non-utilisati on of funds under Ship Building Subsidy Scheme till  date, 
though the Scheme was discontinued in August, 2007.  The reason given to the Committee was that it bein g a ‘well 
defined’ Scheme with ‘fairly rigid and detailed requirement’, none of the applications pertaining to pre-2007 cases were 
found complete, where ‘in principle’ approval was g iven. It appears to the Committee that the Scheme h ad not been 
structured properly and was full of inherent compli cations. It sounds very strange that the requiremen t under the 
scheme were so unrealistic that these could not be met so far since 2007. The Committee recommends the  Government 
to revisit this scheme by taking a practical and ho listic view. And if it wishes to utilize the amount  kept for the Subsidy 
Scheme, the applicants be helped to meet the requirement to avail the benefit of the Scheme.        (Para 17)  
PORT SECTOR 
  The Committee finds that the total allocation for  ports sector during 2009-10 under both plan and no n-plan was 
Rs.700.03 crore. Out of this amount Rs. 279.11 cror e only the Ministry was able to utilize up to Febru ary, 2010 which is 
close to 40 % of the total allocation. This slow pa ce of programme implementation is a matter of serio us concern. 
Already our port carriage is negligible compared to  the global capacity. Time bound completion of proj ects not only 
controls cost escalations but also the revenue earn ings directly and indirectly as a result of increas ed imports and 

exports. The Committee therefore recommends that th e Ministry should have a clear picture of the progr ammes to be 
implemented during the financial year with the allocated grants. (Para 22)  
PORTS-MAJOR AND MINOR 
  The Committee is of the view that the ports play a major role in the economic development of the cou ntry. The 
Committee, however, notes that the major ports of t he country are already facing stiff competition fro m the ports of 
neighbouring countries particularly from Sri Lanka and Singapore.Now, development of private and minor  ports are 
taking away the business of Major Ports. This according to the Committee is clear reflection on the manner in which the 
Government are handling the affairs of the Major Po rts, wherein the crore of rupees of tax payers have  been invested. 
The Committee recommends that the Government should ensure level playing field for the Major Ports so that they can 
perform and compete with private and minor ports. I n this connection the Committee would like to reite rate its earlier 
recommendations contained in its 134th report which is reproduced as below : 
“The Committee notes that the Department of Shippin g is in the process of formulating a Maritime Polic y for the 
maritime sector which seeks to ensure a coordinated  development of Ports, Shipping, Inland Water Trans port, 
Ship building and Ship repairing with the objective  to upgrade and modernize the port infrastructure i n India to 
benchmark its performance against global standards.  The Committee also gathered from the replies that the 
regulatory authority will be set up at an appropria te time. The Committee observes that since much of the 
activities in the port sector are taking place with  private participation, there is need to establish regulatory 
authority well in time and that too before coming a cross any problem for better control, coordination and 
monitoring for achieving excellence in the port and  shipping sector besides addressing serious securit y 
implications. The Committee, therefore, recommends,  the Department to take steps for setting up of a r egulatory 
authority, on the pattern of Telecom Regulatory Aut hority of India (TRAI) and Insurance Regulatory and  
Development Authority (IRDA) for creating a level p laying field and foster healthy competition and to encourage 
investments for the shipping and port sector beside s monitoring performance standards and adjudication  of 
disputes and disposal of appeal thereof.” (Para 27)  
  The Committee appreciates the performance of mino r ports, whose cargo handling has grown up from mere 5 per 
cent in 1999 to 35 per cent of total cargo handling  in 2009. This only that implies that Government’s policy has not 
allowed major ports to grow and therefore, is losing business.The Government themselves admitted that minor ports 
offer better facilities, cargo clearance and other formalities in a hassle free manner.       (Para 28)  
  The Committee is of the view that this is high ti me when the ports within the country both major & private should 
be developed in an integrated manner so that they can unitedly compete with the ports of neightbouring countries. 
         (Para 29)  
  It was brought to the notice of the Committee tha t some major countries give exclusive coastal Shipp ing rights to 
their vessels. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while considering the demand of the foreign v essels for cargo 
shipping the interests of the Indian vessels and Indian Shipping Industry should be fully protected.                (Para 30)  
INTERNATIONAL CONTAINER TRANSHIPMENT TERMINAL (LCTT) 
  The Committee is of the view that the Internation al Container Transhipment Terminal (ICTT) project is one of its 
kind in the world and it would not only boost the m aritime position of India, the cargo handling capacity of the country 
will also increase considerably, once the project was fully operationalised. The Committee is, however, concerned to note 
the slow pace of work of the Vallarpadam transshipm ent terminal. The Committee notes that the commissi oning of the 
ICTT has been delayed due to one reason or other. T he Committee recommends that the Ministry of Shippi ng should 
prevail upon their own contractors and coordinate w ith concerned Government agencies like NHAI to ensu re that all 
the necessary facilities are constructed in time for the operationalization of the ICTT, with utmost priority.  
        (Para 36)  
 
 

SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA (SCI) 
  The Committee is happy to know that the impact of  global recession has started diminishing and the g lobal 
economy is on revival path. The Committee recommends that SCI should review its planned activities and fix the targets 
accordingly to ensure that its profit is increased.  The Committee notes that for the year 2010-2011, a n amount of Rs.

REQUIREMENT OF CARGO SHIPS AND OIL TANKERS 
  The Committee observes that there is a shortfall of 96.3% and 83.6% in the carriage of cargo capacit y and 
carriage of POL/Liquid cargo capacity respectively.  Presently, the foreign vessels are enjoying almost  90% of Indian 
Cargo business. The Committee observes that quite a large number of cargo vessels are more than 25 years old and that 
dry cargo like iron ore which is a major component of the Indian export could not be carried by these old vessels. The 
Committee is of the view that if the steps are not taken to augment the fleet capacity in general cargo/container segment 
and tanker tonnage, the carriage capacity of India may further diminish in the coming years. The Committee, therefore 
recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should pre pare concrete plans and arrange for resources to bu ild/procure 
more vessels. The Committee notes that an amount of Rs.3985.37 crore has been provided in the budget estimates during 
2010-11 for acquisition of vessels by SCI. The Comm ittee hopes that with the acquisition of above ship s by the SCI, 
carriage capacity of Indian shipping sector will get a major boost.  (Para 54)  
DIRECTORATE GENERAL OF LIGHTHOUSES & LIGHTSHIPS (DGLL) 
  The Committee noted the activities carried out by  DGLL. The Committee observes that the pattern of s pending 
during the previous years are not up to the mark. T he Committee hopes Ministry of Shipping will keep c heck to ensure 
timely implementation of the plans by the Directorate General of Lighthouses & Lightships (DGLL).  (Para 56)

  The Committee notes that the Indian Maritime Univ ersity was set up on 14th November, 2008 in Chennai . IMU is 
the first and only Maritime University in the count ry. The Committee, however, notes an apparent lack of sincerity on 
the part of the Government in expediting the establishment of the University. It is evident from the f act that for want of 
approval and clearances from the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) and Cabinet Committee on Economic  Affairs 
(CCEA), an amount of Rs.53.80 crore allocated in BE  2009-10 was reduced to Rs.5.53 crore at the RE sta ge. The 
Committee hopes that the Government will accept the  demand of a sum of Rs. 282 crore required for over  a period of 
time for the development of infrastructure. The uni versity has the Headquarters in Chennai and the hea dquarters 
building and the campus have to be developed. Another new campus is coming up in Cochin apart from other campuses 
in Kolkata, Mumbai and Visakhapatnam. Additional cl assrooms and hostel facilities also need to be deve loped for 
implementing the OBC reservation in these campuses.  Apart from that, the new courses are also being in troduced and 
so, the allocation demanded is for capital expendit ure. The Committee is also aware of the fact that t here is a great 
shortage of trained and skilled manpower in maritim e sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that  the 
Government should make all possible efforts to star t new courses and augment the number of students in take in the 
premier marine institutes. The Committee strongly r ecommends that adequate additional grants may be gi ven for the 
above programmes.    (Para 63)  
INLAND WATERWAYS AUTHORITY OF INDIA 
  The Committee notes that an allocation of mere Rs .115 crore has been made for the IWAI for the year 2010-11. 
The Committee is of the view that the amount is ina dequate even to meet the maintenance of the existin g operational 
waterways. Since this allocation was not sufficient even for ongoing projects of National Waterways 1,  2 & 3, effectively 
no fund will be available for the new National Waterways, except token provision of Rs. 1 crore each for NW 4 & 5. The 
Committee also notes the facts presented by the Ministry that the total cost of development of National Waterway 4 is of 
the order of Rs. 1500 crore and that of National Waterway 5 is of the order of Rs. 4200 crore. If both these projects were 
to be completed in a period of 5-8 years, it is est imated that Rs.5700 crore would be required for taking up development 

of these two waterways. The Committee, therefore, r ecommends the Planning Commission to provide this a mount 
during remaining two years of the Eleventh Plan and  the Twelfth Plan. It need to give required priorit y/importance to 
the development of National Waterways. Demands and proposals made by the Ministry of Shipping for deve lopment of 
waterways need to be taken more seriously and makin g a drastic cut on the fund projected by the Minist ry should be 
avoided. The Committee recommends that the Ministry  of shipping should take up the matter with the Min istry of 
Finance and the Planning Commission for increased allocation for the development of National Waterways.  
        (Para 72)

  The Committee would like to reiterate its earlier  recommendation contained in its 134th Report on De mands for 
Grants (2008-09) of the Ministry of Shipping which is reproduced below: 
The Committee is pained to note that the Government  has decided neither to consider revival of CIWTC n or to 
amalgamate this Corporation with various Organizati ons, such as Inland Waterways Authority of India (I WAI), 
Kolkata Port Trust (KoPT) or Shipping Corporation o f India (SCI) that too, without getting conducted a ny 
scientific study by an expert agency. The Committee  is of the view that the matter of revival and amal gamation of 
CIWTC should be got examined by some high powered expert committee.  (Para 79)  
  The Committee recommends that in a democratic wel fare State, interest of employees and their livelih ood must 
find uppermost consideration, while taking a decisi on which is adversely affecting them. Before taking  final decision 
with regard to the viability of CIWTC the Committee again recommends that the matter may be got examined by a high 
power expert Committee and job security and livelihood of the employees must be ensured.  (Para 80)  
TAXATION AND TAX RELIEFS 
  The Committee feels that the port and shipping se ctor of the country had not received the attention in the Union 
Budget 2010-11 that it surely deserves. No incentiv es, concessions, tax relief etc. to the Ports and D redging Sectors or to 
the Shipping Industry has been announced. The Committee is of the view that extending the infrastructu re status to the 
shipping sector will make them also accessible to s ome of the tax exemptions and subsidies as enjoyed by other agencies 
which will give a boost to the shipping industry. T he other demands raised by the Ministry are also ho ld ground and 
accepting them is necessary to attract investment in the shipping sector. Cruise shipping is a long pending demand in the 
tourism sector and tax exemptions really will be a welcome step. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the above 
demands may further be pursued with the Finance Ministry to get positive results.  (Para 83)  
SAFETY MEASURES FOR SHIPS 
  The Committee feels that safety and security of t he seafaring vessels need to be given paramount imp ortance, 
especially in view of the increasing piracy and the ft of cargo. This also has relevance in view of the  increased threat 
from, terrorists who are active in our neighbouring seas. The Committee, is however constrained to note that an amount 
of Rs.48.96 crore which had to be reduced to Rs.12 crore at RE stage for want of utilization of funds by the Ministry of 

Defence. The Committee also notes that no justifica tion has been given for not accepting the demand of  Ministry of 
Defence for Rs.100 crore for the survey vessels. Th e Committee would like to have an explanation in th e matter. The 
Committee is of the view that the action of the Gov ernment to reduce allocation to Rs.15 crore for safety and security of 
the vessels is a retrograde step. The Committee rec ommends that the Ministry of Shipping may be provid ed with 
adequate fund at the RE stage to meet the actual threat and challenges in this regard.  (Para 87)  
  The Committee also opines that in the recent time s, the shipping industry is facing an increased cha llenge from 
piracy and sea robbery. This is great threat to maritime navigation resulting in cargo loss, man power loss and increased 
operational costs. There should be some strong meas ures to save the cargo ships and sea men from such anti pirates. 
Keeping in view of the above facts the Committee st rongly is of the views that lack of funds should no t be a problem in 
this regard the allocation may be kept with an open  mind because the safety and security of the ships and the persons 
who are working in it are of utmost importance.  (Para 88)  
DREDGING OF THE HOOGHLY RIVER SYSTEM 
  The Committee notes that the Kolkata Port was inc urring revenue losses mainly due to drop in depth o f the 
navigation channel that prevents large ships from v enturing into the Haldia dock. Due to decline in tr affic movement, 
the earnings of the dock have reduced significantly . Considering that the Kolkata Port is one of the m ajor ports of the 
country, the situation prevailing is not at all healthy for the sector.  (Para 89)  
  The Committee notes that dredging of the Hooghly river system is very essential for the survival of the Kolkata 
port system. The Committee also notes that the poli cy of reimbursement of 100% of the cost of dredging  by the Central 
Government has been referred to the Cabinet for a f resh mandate. The Committee recommends that the Cen tral 
Government should continue to reimburse the entire cost of the dredging at Haldia River system and the  related 
Channels as the Kolkata Port is not in a position to bear the cost.  (Para 91)  
  The Committee notes that the warehousing infrastr ucture in respect of Kolkata and Kandla ports is no t able to 
meet the current requirements. Even though other po rts have sufficient capacity as on date, keeping in  view the 
Ministry’s plan to enhance the carriage capacity of  ports and other measures of port development, once  fully 
operationalised, the required capacity may be increased. Therefore, the warehousing infrastructure is also an important 
field where the Ministry should concentrate along with the other capacity augmentation methods.  (Para 94)  
  The Committee also noted that 25 PPP projects und er the National Maritime development Programme are going 
to be started during 2010-11. The Committee would l ike to know the status of 17 such projects sanction ed during 2009-
110 and the progress thereof.  (Para 95)  
 The Committee also feels that Indian ports need to  be modernized at the earliest so that with the arrival of modern 
equipments in the ports, the port capacity will con siderably increase along with increase in cargo mov ements. The 
Committee feels that consequently, the profitability increases and in a phased manner the cargo handling cost factor and 
the capacity factor could be brought at par with th e international levels. Thus the problem of poor in frastructure and 
high levels of manual handling of work could be managed in a better way.    (Para 96)

INTRODUCTION  
  I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary  Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism 
and Culture, having been authorized by the Committe e to present on its behalf, do hereby present this  
One Hundred and Fifty-seventh Report on “Demands for Grants 2010-11 of the Ministry of Culture”. 
2.   The Committee, at its meeting held on the 7th April, 2010, considered the subject and heard the 
Secretary and other officials of the Culture. 
3.   The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Culture for placing 
before the Committee the material and information d esired in connection with the subject and for 
clarifying the points raised by the Members. 
4.   The Committee considered and adopted the Repor t at its meeting held on the 20th. April, 2010. 
 
 
 
  SITARAM  YECHURY 
 
NEW DELHI ; Chairman,

REPORT  
  India, being one of the oldest civilizations occu pies an important place on the cultural map of 
the world. Culture plays an important role in the d evelopment agenda of any nation. Firstly, it 
contributes immensely to economic growth by creatin g vast employment opportunities. Secondly, it 
provides goals in terms of quality of life and mean ingful existence as an end to economic growth 
itself. Culture and creativity manifest themselves in almost all economic, social and cultural activities. 
The role of culture as a vehicle for national integ ration cannot be overemphasized in the context of 
India’s multi ethno-cultural society. Development o f culture in fact, works as a catalyst to the 
economic development. As such, culture cannot be confined to the boundaries of any particular sector. 
However, it could be recognized that there are cert ain sectors wherein presence and contribution of 
culture and creativity are much more dominant and v isible. Elements of culture encompass media, 
,films, music, handicrafts, visual arts, Performing  Arts, literature, heritage management, cultural an d 
creative industries etc. The cultural development inter-alia  includes areas of culture both in tangible 
and intangible fields. The functional spectrum of t he Ministry of Culture is rather wide, ranging from  
generating cultural awareness at the grassroots lev el to promoting cultural exchanges at an 
international level.

ELEVENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN  
3.  Ministry of Culture informed that against the p rojected demand of Rs.4965.99 crore for the XI 
Five Year Plan, Planning Commission allocated an am ount of Rs.3524.11 crore. The Ministry 
informed that they would require additional Plan allocation for the new schemes/programmes initiated 
in the last 2-3 years such as celebration of 150th Birth Anniversary of Guru Rabindranath Tagore, 
setting up of a National Mission on Libraries, sett ing up of National Centre for Performing Art, 
National Archives for Audio Visual Materials, restr ucturing and strengthening of ASI including the 
activities/programmes proposed and deferred by vari ous cultural organizations on account of a 
substantial cut in Plan allocation under XI Plan. 
4.  The Secretary, while appearing before the Commi ttee stated that: 
“This is a small-budget Ministry of Rs.700 crores o r thereabouts. Sir, the entire Budget of the 
Ministry comes to 12 paise per hundred rupees that Bharat Sarkar  spends; not even one rupee. 
Twelve paise per hundred rupees is the figure that we have placed before Parliament — and we 
are representing again and again — out of which the  core concern of India’s cultural heritage 
monuments get four paisa, that is, 0.04 per cent”.  
5.  The Committee was further informed that Archaeo logical Survey of India, which is a flagship 
organization of the Ministry of Culture was engaged in conservation, preservation and maintenance of 

3675 Centrally Protected Monuments. Unless a substa ntial allocation was made to Archaeological 
Survey of India towards undertaking the massive tas k of maintenance and conservation of our 
heritage, ancient monuments and historical sites, t he heritage preservation and promotion of ancient 
cultural heritage could not be achieved in a sustai ned manner. Unfortunately, this aspect of heritage 
preservation/promotion in the country has received very little attention it deserves. This is due to t he 
meager Plan budget of the Ministry of Culture, whic h acts as a constraint to step up its activities 
including that of Archaeological Survey of India. F urther, to aggravate this situation of inadequacy o f 
funds, every year Ministry of Finance apply a cut i n the total budgetary allocation, especially under 
Plan, at the Revised Estimates stage, the effect of which invariably percolates down to Archaeological 
Survey of India also. 
6.  Expenditure during the XIth Plan from 2007-08, 08-09, 09-10 are as follows:

ANNUAL PLAN 2010-11  
7.   Demand No. 19 containing the details of the bu dget allocation of the Ministry of Culture for the 
financial year 2010-2011 was considered by the Depa rtment-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 7th April, 2010. The 
Committee heard the Secretary, Ministry of Culture and other officials of the Ministry and 
organizations during the meeting. 
8.   Ministry of Culture projected a demand of Rs.1 186.62 crore for the Annual Plan 2010-11 on the 
basis of the proposals received from various cultur al Organizations and Divisions under the Ministry. 
The Planning Commission has allocated a sum of Rs.7 35.00 crore for developmental activities of the 
Ministry of Culture for the Annual Plan 2010-11, thereby reducing the proposal by Rs.451.62 crore on 
account of resource constraints. On being asked, th e Ministry informed that this cut would affect 
adversely almost all activities of the Ministry inc luding organizations such as Archaeological Survey 
of India; Zonal Culture Centres; Akademis; Asiatic Society, Kolkata; Indian Museum; Salarjung 
Museum; Victoria Memorial Hall; National Library; R aja Rammohun Roy Library Foundation; and 
Plan Schemes (including Celebration of 150th Birth Anniversary of Guru Rabindranath Tagore and 
Setting up of a National Mission on Libraries) of the Ministry. 
9.   As against Revised Estimates of Rs.630.00 cror e in 2009-10, Plan allocation of Rs.735.00 crore 
have been made in 2010-11, thereby resulting in an increase of Rs.105.00 crore. Ministry of Culture 
informed that this increased allocation would be ut ilized for developmental activities of National 
Museum, Celebration of 150th Birth Anniversary of G uru Rabindranath Tagore, Celebration of 150th 
Birth Anniversary of Swami Vivekananda, Development  of Sardar Vallabbhai Patel Memorials, 
National Gandhi Heritage Site Mission, Setting up o f a National Mission on Libraries, Sahitya 

Akademi, National Council of Science Museums, Indian Museum etc.. The Secretary also emphasized 
on the changes in the budgetary aspect this year:- 
“ .......centenaries and memorials are essential pa rt of the nation’s celebrations. These have 
been dealt with in an ad hoc manner and from the no n-Plan budget. The logic was that 
sometimes these decisions are taken in the beginnin g of the year or in the middle of the year. 
Since these are not predicted in the Plan period, w e spend out of the non-Plan. This as a policy 
decision has been shifted from non-Plan to Plan. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Memorial has a long-
standing demand. They have been demanding some amou nt of corpus or some amount of 
support. This will be under Plan. Because of the un certainty and because of the time-lag that is 
involved and because of the fact that some of these will be starting in the middle of the year, we 
have kept it at Rs.735 crore. The Planning Commission has also recorded it. An assurance given 
to us is that if we manage to spend or if we requir e to spend this amount and proceed at the end 
of the first half, they will take a view of it. 
10.   The Allocation in 2009 was Rs.700.00 crore, b ut the same was reduced at RE to Rs.63000 crore. 
The Committee was informed that reduction was made due to slow pace of expenditure during first six 
months of the financial year. The expenditure upto 31st March, 2010, is Rs.533.40 crore out of the 
allocation of Rs.630.00 crore. 
11.   The Ministry assured the Committee that all C ultural and other Organizations have taken timely 
initiatives and action to achieve at least 60% Plan  expenditure of by the end of September, so that th e 
precious fund allocated to the Ministry for implementation of various programmes and schemes under 
Art and Culture sector were not surrendered at RE s tage. In order to ensure that these targets were 
achieved review meetings are held at regular fortnightly/monthly/quarterly intervals. 
12.   The Committee underlines the need for more allocati on to the Ministry of Culture lest 
many of its important activities should suffer. For the year 2010-11, the Ministry of Culture has 
been allocated an amount of Rs.735 crore, which comes to less than 12 paise per hundred rupees 
being spent under the General Budget. However, the Committee is surprised to find that during 
the first three years of the XI Five Year Plan, the  Ministry as in the past, has not been able to 
utilize even the reduced allocation. Underutilizati on of funds by the Ministry of Culture is a 
recurring phenomena year after year. During the yea r 2009-10, the allocation of Rs.700 crore 
was reduced to Rs.630.00 crore at RE stage, however , the Ministry could utilize only an amount 
of Rs.533.40 crore. The Committee recommends that t he Ministry should identify the 
bottlenecks and make corrective measures to utilize  the allocations as per the norms laid down 
for the purpose.  
13.   Upon recognizing the fact that the Plan expen diture of the Ministry of Culture and its various 
organizations, particularly of Archaeological Surve y of India, picks up only after September of each 
year, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture in 
its 137th report on Demands for Grants, 2008-09 of the Ministry of Culture, recommended that 
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance should reschedule the present budgetary procedure and 
practices as far as Ministry of Culture is concerne d, so that the final Plan allocation were conveyed to 
the Ministry by December every year, as ASI activities were seasonal in nature and started picking up 
only after the end of monsoon. 
14.   On the basis of the above, Culture Ministry h ad taken up the issue of deferment of exercise of 
finalization of RE for the Ministry of Culture to D ecember from the month of September, with the 

Planning Commission and Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance. Further it also requested 
to consider the matter and issue necessary instruct ions, so that the Revised Estimates for the Ministr y 
of Culture was decided, based on expenditure at the end of December, instead of September. 
15.   In response to the recommendation of the Parl iamentary Standing Committee and the 
suggestions given by the Ministry of Culture, the Ministry of Finance stated that the completion of RE

16.   The Committee notes the comments of the Ministry of  Finance. However, the Ministry of

Culture which the Committee still appreciates. The Committee deplores the “one size fits all” 
attitude of the Ministry of Finance and recommends that the non-utilization of funds due to the

ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA  
19.   The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), an attached office of the Ministry of Culture has a 
network of 24 circles throughout the country. ASI p rotects 3675 monuments, which include 21 
properties included in the World Heritage List by U NESCO. The major activities of ASI are: 
maintenance, conservation and preservation of centr ally protected monuments/sites and remains. In 
addition to the above activities, it conducts archa eological exploration and excavation and underwater 
archaeology regularly. ASI is also engaged in developing epigraphical research; setting up of new site 
museums and reorganization of existing site museums , imparting training programmes in 
Archaeology; strengthening of the Chemistry Branch for development of chemicals for preservation. 
20.   Archaeological Survey of India has undertaken  more than 1500 schemes (works) for structural 
conservation, chemical preservation and horticultural operations based on the priorities, commitments, 
available manpower and financial resources. 
21.   Archaeological excavations and explorations i s one of the oldest and most important activities 
of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). The AS I conducts various operations and programmes 
like Village-to-Village Surveys, Problem-Oriented S urveys, Excavations of archaeological sites and 
mounds, documentation of antiquarian remains and sc ulptures, architectural survey of temples and 

colonial buildings throughout the country, through its various field offices, Excavation and Pre-history 
Branches, Temple and Building Survey Projects as well as Circles. 
22.   Ministry of Culture informed that in the pres ervation and conservation of monuments 
participation of universities, other academic insti tutions and research bodies in academic work is 
ensured by extending matching Grants-in-aid and Fin ancial Assistance to eligible institutions. 
Documentation of antiquities and sculptures stored in various field offices and sculpture sheds is als o 
one of the activities identified and the various field offices have been directed to undertake this work. 
23.   Further, it as informed that greater thrust i s being given by ASI to collaborations with the 
corporate sector such as the Taj Group of Hotels, W orld Monuments Fund etc. for formulation of 
Master Plans and for implementation of integrated d evelopment of some important monuments. In 
order to encourage private-public partnerships in t he area of conservation and preservation of 
monuments, ASI functions in association with Nation al Culture Fund (NCF) with regard to projects 
sponsored by private sector organizations. 
24.   The Committee notes various activities undertaken b y ASI in the field of culture and 
appreciates the efforts of ASI.  
25.   Ministry of Culture informed that the six Exc avation Branches undertook large-scale excavation 
and exploration of sites/regions with simultaneous conservation, while some of the circles had 
undertaken the small scale excavation and explorati on for the years 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2009-10. 
During 2010-11 also ASI proposes to undertake these excavation and exploration activities.

CULTURAL  AWARENESS  PROGRAMME

PROTECTION OF MONUMENTS  
42.   The Committee was informed that there are 367 5 monuments/sites declared as of national 
importance across the country by Government of Indi a. The conservation, preservation, maintenance, 
development of environs and creating tourist relate d amenities ( e.g.  drinking water, toilet blocks, 
facilities for physically challenged, pathways, cul tural notice boards/signage, vehicle parking, cloak  
rooms, etc.) at the centrally protected monuments/s ites are the regular activities which the ASI 
undertakes as per needs and availability of resourc es. Besides providing security with limited 
manpower resources, the ASI protects and preserves the monuments, declared as of national 
importance, on the basis of the requirements assess ed by the concerned officers annually. The annual 
plan is drawn for undertaking the required works in  accordance with the feed back received from the 
field level and the recommendation of supervisory a nd executive level officers. Likewise, State 
Governments are responsible for protection and mana gement of the State protected monuments. 

Ministry of Culture informed that the details in re gard to steps taken by the respective State 
Governments for protection of monuments under their control are not known to the ASI. 
43.   The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Culture did not share resources with the 
States. It has no Centrally-sponsored schemes. It h as only central sector schemes. Until the 13th 
Finance Commission, the States were given massive a ssistance by the Finance Commission for 
archaeological preservation. The Secretary, Ministry of Culture said: 
“... the Planning Commission has told us that please go in for Centrally-sponsored schemes. We 
may have to go completely for a different regime of  going in for partnership with the State 
Archaeology Departments, State Archaeology Director ates so that their monuments, which are 
also a part of our national heritage, not because they are listed in the Central List, could be given 
assistance and working models for their preservatio n, both technical and financial. So, this is 
another area. If this comes up this year, there wil l be an expansion of the Budget that would 
have to come in along with it.” 
44.   The Committee also agrees in-principle to such a co nvergence between the Centre and 
States as far as development and protection of our ancient heritage is concerned. Under the 
existing system, due to lack of sharing and close c oordination, there is complete confusion 
between ASI and the States Archaeology Departments.  As a result, hundreds of our heritage 
sites are either not identified and notified and have been demolished or encroached upon. Such a 
sharing would, the Committee feels, go a long way i n protecting, pressing and developing our 
ancient sites.  
45.   The Committee is concerned at the lack of coordinat ion between the Central and State 
Governments. So much so, the ASI was not aware of t he steps taken by the State Governments 
to protect their monuments. The monuments under the  control of State Governments also need 
to be preserved and protected. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture should 
ensure that the monuments under the control of Stat e Governments are also protected and 
maintained. If necessary, the Ministry should also explore the possibility of giving adequate 
finance to the State authorities in this regard. Th e Committee is of the view that Government 
needs to take effective steps to coordinate and fac ilitate the monitoring of protection of 
monuments by State Governments.  
STAFF STRENGTH OF ASI  
46.   The Archaeological Survey of India has deploy ed regular/temporary staff or persons on daily-
wages for attending to these works on regular basis  at the protected monuments and ancient sites 
depending upon the requirement. 
47.   The Committee was informed that the existing staff strength of the ASI is inadequate in view of 
the number of protected monuments, archaeological s ites and remains under its control and other 
functions. Further, the inadequacies of the manpowe r strength vis-a-vis  the duties and responsibilities 
have been highlighted at various forums including t he Parliament. Various Review Committees 
constituted in the past to look into this aspect ha ve also pointed out the constraints of the manpower  
structure of the ASI and had recommended the streng thening at various levels. However, so far, no 
substantial result has come out. As late as March, 2010, Moily Committee, constituted by the 
Government, has strongly recommended for the streng thening of the ASI. The proposal for 
augmenting the manpower structure of the ASI is in formulation stage. 

48.   The Secretary in his presentation deliberated  on the issue of shortage of manpower in ASI and 
stated inter-alia : 
“The ASI’s Bill, the AMASRA Amendment Act, has been  a historic amendment to which all 
political parties across the board agreed. There wi ll be certain sacrifices that we would have to 
make as we move along but it has been the first momentous change 106 years after Lord Curzon 
made his first Act for the preservation of India’s’  monuments. Hundred and six years later, the 
nation makes a choice and what started as a Commonw ealth Games face-saving project became 
a major exercise. For the next hundred meters of an y protected monument, there can be no 
construction, no construction, no construction! We will have to go through it. Beyond 100 
meters, for the next two hundred meters, you cannot  have high rises blocking the view of a 
monument. So, there will be building restrictions; building heritage bye laws will be made. 
These bodies have to be set up. The entire process of administration, of putting up competent 
authorities, legislative groups, the National Monum ents Authority, would be coming but, more 
so, at the ground level, it is the ASI which has pu t it on record, in writing, that it is unable to 
man 2500 of India’s 3675 monuments. We don’t have a ny manpower. Now, 2500, an 
approximate figure, out of the 3675 monuments that we have, is what you have pointed out now. 
Why is the ASI’s capacity being kept at dwarfish le vel? Why is the ASI not being ramped up? 
Now, that is a question I would also like to ask. B ut now we get on to what is practical. Since 
the Parliament has passed this amendment and since the President has assented, it is now 
incumbent on the nation to keep a watch and ward at  every monument. Ten thousand is the 
number of people that we have projected. Some of them could be Ex-Servicemen, some of them 
could be local volunteers; we are yet to find out. India is too complex to be determined across 
the table. This additional expenditure on ASI has been projected at about Rs.300 crores per year. 
ASI’s establishment doubles, thanks to the amendment of Parliament!” 
“It may not double this year; it will ramp up in sl ow degree. Everybody has his problem. They 
have the procedure of selecting, tendering, etc. Let us assume that out of Rs.300 crore projected 
for ASI, Rs.100 crore is spent this year.” 
49.   The Committee is of the view that ASI has spread it self thin and a severe shortage of 
technical personnel has hamstrung the conservation efforts. The Committee will like to invite 
the attention to the recommendation of the R.N. Mir dha Committee that a minimum of 9,000 
monument attendants would be needed to provide secu rity to the existing structures. The 
Government of India needs to rethink its ‘fence and forget’ approach towards the monuments.  
50.   The shortage of staff and monument attendants is a serious problem affecting the safety, 
security and upkeep of various monuments adversely. The monuments need to be protected just 
like any other assets of nation. The Committee, the refore, recommends that the Government 
should make efforts on a war footing to ensure that  staff strength as recommended by various 
Committees may be increased and personnel are posted at the earliest.  
51.  The Committee has come to know that there are hundr eds of attendants who are 
protecting the monuments for 20 years or more, have  not been regularized till date. As a result, 
their basic pay is static and no other allowances a re being paid to them. It is also learnt that 
some of them had gone to Court, but could not get any relief. It is a strange situation when there 
is a huge backlog at different levels including that of monument attendants, yet the existing staff 
are not being adjusted. The Committee, therefore, s trongly recommends that Ministry of 

Culture should adopt humanitarian approach and take steps to increase their wages taking into 
account their length of service and rate of inflation.  
52.   The current framework operates at two levels - Cent ral, that looks after nationally 
important monuments, and the State-level that is re sponsible for State protected monuments. 
There is an urgent need of activating a third level  of institutional and legal arrangement 
involving local bodies and all these levels need to  work with a very close coordination and well 
defined partnership, legal, financial, etc..  
53.   The Committee recommends that for preservation of o ur monuments activities should be 
decentralized. The historical monuments can be bett er protected by the involvement of local 
people. The Ministry should come out with a decentr alized and integrated mechanism that 
would fill the gaps existing today in this regard. The Committee has already expressed its 
serious reservation about the proposed National Heritage Commission that it will not be able to 
address the major issues currently faced in identif ying, developing, protecting, etc. of our rich 
heritage scattered all over the country from Delhi to Talukas and remote villages.

ENCROACHMENTS AND REHABILITATION  
59.   The Committee was informed that in order to c ontain encroachments of the centrally protected 
monuments/sites, the Superintending Archaeologists of the Circles have been vested with the powers 
of Estate Officer to issue eviction notices/orders to the encroachers under Public Premises (Eviction of 
Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. They are also de legated with the powers to issue notices under 
the provisions of Ancient Monuments and Archaeologi cal Sites and Remains Act, 1958 and Rules 
1959 followed by an order to the District Collector/Magistrate by Central Government to remove such 
encroachment under section 19 (2) of the AMASR Act and AMASR Rules 38 (2). Assistance in 
containing and removing encroachments is also sough t from the respective State Government/police. 
In case, such measures do not bring fruitful result s, action is also initiated against the encroachers  by 
even filing cases in the court of law. 
60.   The Committee was informed that various kinds  of formulae were being worked out to take care 
of the encroachment including the resettlement and rehabilitation aspect of the encroachers. In the 
State of Karnataka, the State Government had worked  out a rehabilitation and resettlement plan by 
taking into consideration the concerned local peopl e who have encroached on the monuments etc. 
They agreed to relocate it, the State Government ha d now approached for sharing the expenses by the 
Government of India and the Government of Karnataka on a 50:50 basis. 
61.  The Committee notes that despite there being strict  rules under the Ancient Monuments 
and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act 1958, the problem of encroachment of monuments 
could not be checked. The Committee was informed that the 35 monuments, all managed by the 
Central Government, could not be traced. Delhi, the  headquarters of Archeological Survey of 
India, tops the list with 12 untraceable monuments.  They now exist only in memory and in 
history books. The Committee would like to invite t he attention of the Government to the plight 
of the older Forts in the country. Many of those Fo rts are made up of dry sandstone on 
foundations of clay, sand and rock. These forts are  facing the problem of encroachments also. 
These forts are ill-maintained and in a dilapidated  condition. The growth of tourism and the 
large number of visitors are putting unbearable pre ssure on the structures. One example is the 

Jaisalmer Fort also known as ‘ Sonar Qila’ or ‘Jewel of Desert ’ which is reported to have been 
listed among the most endangered sites of the World  Monuments Fund. It is reported that the 
waste water has seeped through decayed drains and penetrated the walls of the Fort resulting in 
cracks in various structures of the Fort. The Fort is also facing the problem of encroachment.  
62.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Minis try of Culture should take up the 
matter with the concerned State Governments and oth er authorities to ensure that the Forts 
which are part of our cultural heritage are not fur ther damaged due to human action. The 
Committee also recommends that the Ministry should take effective steps to protect the forts 
from neglect and destruction.  
63.   The Committee feels that since in the removal of en croachment, the major role has to be 
played by the State Government, their stake has to be properly recognized. The Ministry should 
initiate consultation with State Government and wor k out a plan for rehabilitation. Financial 
assistance for heritage protection needs to be increased. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
for a separate allocation for dealing with illegal encroachments in ASI monuments and 
rehabilitation to solve this perennial problem. 
NATIONAL MISSION ON MONUMENTS AND ANTIQUITIES  
64.   The National Mission on Monuments and Antiqui ties, which is functioning under the umbrella 
of Archaeological Survey of India, in a full-fledged manner proposes to undertake major activities like 
documentation of antiquities spread over site museu ms of ASI, museums under the control of State 
Governments, Union Territories and Universities; compilation of data on unprotected monuments and 
sites; digitization of archival drawings of various  architectural institutions and organizations; 
arranging training programmes to the State Departments, local bodies, NGOs, Universities, etc. as part 
of the capacity building programmes; and organizing  various outreach programmes in order to 
sensitize the common people about the historical an d cultural aspects of various heritage sites and 
antiquities. During 2010-11, the programmes under the Mission will be strengthened. 
65.   As per the decisions of the III Mission Monit oring Committee, the templates on built heritage, 
sites and antiquities have been prepared. About 50, 000 listing containing information on unprotected 
built heritage, sites and about 1,20,000 antiquities from different sources have been documented as per 
the format of NMMA. 
66.   The Committee was also informed that many Sta tes have already set up Implementations 
Committees and documentation centers and work has b een initiated on a large scale. Training 
programmes for officials working on the project are  being organized and a large work force is being 
engaged for timely completion of the project. 
67.   The final product of the documentation will b e an interactive website which will give a 
comprehensive picture of all protected and unprotec ted heritage structures in the country. A software 
is being developed to enable the public to provide inputs, if there are heritage structures or sites t hat 
have gone unnoticed by the Mission, the general public can point it out through this platform. 
68.   Currently there are 3,675 protected monuments  under the ASI and 3,500 under the state depart-
ments of archaeology, and the NMMA estimates that there are around seven lakh unprotected heritage 
structures. 

69.  Along with the heritage structures, a national  register of antiquities is also being formulated. The 
sources for this will be the ASI, national and stat e museums and the general public will also be 
encouraged to inform if they posses or discover antiquities. 
70.   All heritage structures-ancient, medieval, mo dern and even residential which match the 
definition of an ‘ancient monument’ under the Ancie nt Monuments and Archaeological Sites and 
Remains Act, 1958, will be enlisted. For antiquitie s, the definition under the Antiquities and Art 
Treasures Act, 1972 will be followed. 
71.   The Committee was also informed that National  Mission on Monuments and Antiquities 
(NMMA) has started an initiative to document and li st all heritage structures, protected as well as 
unprotected, across the country. The project has be en sanctioned a budgetary allocation of Rs. 90 
crore and a stipulated time period of five years fr om 2007-12 for completion. Along with the heritage 
structures, a national register of antiquities is also being formulated. 
72.   The Committee appreciates the setting up of Nationa l Mission on Monuments and 
Antiquities which will bring in record all the cult ural and heritage properties and antiquities 
available in the country. The documentation of the heritage sites and antiquities is a gigantic 
task for which the Government of India have sanctio ned a budgetary allocation of Rs.90 crore 
and the project has to be completed within a period  of five years from 2007-12. The Committee, 
in view of urgency of the work, calls up the Minist ry to complete the work in a time bound way 
and make available more funds if required for the p urpose. The Committee is also of the view 
that Mission has to do a huge task which cannot be completed without the involvement of 
general public. The Committee recommends that Gover nment should take steps to sensitize the 
masses and take assistance of the NGO already working in this area.

73.   The seven Zonal Cultural Centres, encompassin g all the States and Union Territories of the

preservation, innovation, promotion and disseminati on of the various art forms covering the broad 
disciplines of music, dance, theatre, visual arts, literary activities and craft traditions with speci al 
focus on folk and dying art forms within the consti tuent states with a view to reinforce the spirit of  
“Unity in Diversity” as a hall mark characteristic of Indian Culture. Plan allocations is also made to  
Zonal Cultural Centres for their ongoing activity a s well as for taking up new activities. “Octave” - a 
North East Festival involving artists from the Nort h East States as well as from other States, are 
organized by ZCCs every year in major cities of the  country. The variation in allocation and 
expenditure during 2008-09 and 2009-10 under the scheme are due to increased expenditure for North 
East activities by ZCCs. 
74.   The Committee noted that an amount of Rs.14.0 0 crore was allocated in BE 2009-10, which was 
reduced to Rs.12.75 crore at RE 2009-10 due to defe rment of Folk Dance Festival, which was to be 
organized from 23rd to 29th January, 2010 in Delhi. This Festival will now be organized in the month 
of October, 2010 to coincide with the holding of Co mmonwealth Games-2010 in Delhi and thus Plan 
allocation of Rs.14.00 crore has been reinstated for the Annual Plan 2010-11. 
75.   The Committee notes the efforts of Zonal Cultural C entres in preserving the Indian 
culture. However, the Committee is not happy that p lan allocation of Rs.14 crore for the year 

2009-10 was reduced to Rs.12.75 crore at RE stage. Such reduction are not unusual but in cash 
starved Department, efforts should be to utilize th e plan outlay for some other similar purpose, 
if organizing folk dance festival in Delhi was not possible. The Committee feels that there need 
to be more publicity of the events being organized by Zonal Cultural Centres. Without reaching 
the masses, the Zonal Cultural Centres cannot achie ve their objectives. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that concerted efforts should  be made for publicity of the events at 
school and college levels also.

82.   The Committee is of the view that Sangeet Natak Akademi has to do much more and reach

reason given for underutilization of funds ambiguous. The Committee notes that new building in 
New Delhi is under construction and hopes that it w ill be completed at the earliest. Further, the

importance. The Committee recommends that necessary  fund may be provided for installing 
latest security gadgets to beef up the security of the Museum.

You asked me why the Asiatic Society’s allocation h as been reduced. Sir, the allocation was

taken up as a result of which the amount of Rs.21 c rore allocated to the Asiatic Society was

NATIONAL  ARCHIVES  OF  INDIA  
93.   The National Archives of India is the Central  Repository of non-current records of enduring 
value belonging to the Ministries ad Departments of  the Government of India. It also acquires and 
preserves private papers of eminent Indians and mic rofilm copies of records of Indian interests from 
abroad. It provides facilities for historical resea rch and promotes archives on scientific lines throu gh 
the School of Archival Studies, which runs many cou rses in this discipline. It has regional office at 
Bhopal and record centers at Jaipur, Puducherry and  Bhubaneswar. The National Archives of India 
carries out the work of the repair and rehabilitati on of records of Government of India from the point  
of view of long term preservation. The School of Ar chival Studies is presently running a One Year 
Diploma Course in Archives Management and Records M anagement apart from short term courses at 
the professional and sub professional level. These include Records management, Archives 
Administration, Conservation, Reprography etc. 
94.   Plan Allocation of Rs.4.50 crore was made in BE 2009-2010 which was reduced to Rs.3.75 
crore in RE level. Further, allocation was raised to Rs.5.00 crore at BE 2010-11. The Plan provision of 
NAI during 2009-10 and 2010-11 are for its continui ng developmental activities. The Secretary in his 
evidence before the Committee stated that : 
“The National Archives has hardly any scheme to hel p the State Archives. I headed the State 
Archives at Kolkata. I know the situation there. Th ere are no funds. There is no attention. If, at 
least, there is a national body, it will be helpful . I got an amount of Rs. five lakhs there. Now, 
five lakh rupees pay for nothing. The Central Gover nment should come up with larger 
programmes of intervention because, as I said, the Archives lying in Kolkata and Delhi makes 
no difference. They are the treasure of the nation.  The only difference is who is doing the 

chowkidari. So, if I take this advisory and proceed , then, perhaps another six months later, we 
could gave a round-up on what are the ramp-ups that are possible and then make it as a mandate, 
as a pressure point for the next year, that is, the last year of the Plan and whatever can’t be done 
for the Twelfth Plan, something like that.” 
95.   The Committee notes that National Archives of India  has highly competent professionals 
in the field of Archives record management, conserv ation, reprography and other related fields 
of Archival Science. The National Archives has grea t task before if of managing records. The 
Committee is also of the view that the National Arc hives should conduct regular courses for the 
employees of Government offices and if possible dep ute staff from its organization to assist 
various offices to maintain record in a better way.  However, the Committee notes that the plan 
outlay of Rs.4.50 crore made in BE. 2009-10 was reduced to Rs.3.75 crore at RE stage. Again an 
amount of Rs.5.00 crore has been provided in BE 201 0-11. The Committee feels that there is 
some sort of inconsistency in the planning which has resulted in fluctuation of plan outlay at BE 
and RE stages which can affect the functioning and activities of the National Archives of India.
