terms of recruitment and retention of technical manpower and inability to quickly address ongoing
operational issues due to lack of adequate administrative and financial authority.
82. The proposal for establishment of the CAA is based on the report of the feasibility study
conducted by International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) for the ‘Establishment of a Civil
Aviation Authority (CAA)’ in India by replacing the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA).
A draft CAA Bill outlining the setting up of a Civil Aviation Authority in India has been prepared.
83. During the study conducted by ICAO, the ICAO Experts had meetings with civil aviation
stakeholders including Government agencies like Department of Public Enterprises, Department of
Personnel and Training, Planning Commission, AERA and AAI. The views of the stakeholders and
the ICAO team were kept in mind during preparation of the ICAO report.

20
84. When the Committee raised the issue of instances of over pricing of air tickets reported to
the DGCA it was informed that Air fares are market determined and take into account all relevant
factors including the cost of operation, characteristics of services, etc.  Generally scheduled airlines
offer different fare buckets for each flight, in line with the practice followed in other parts of the
world.  As the lower fare buckets get sold out, the passengers pay progressively higher fare with
the increase in demand for seats. Air fares are not being regulated by the Government and Airlines
are free to charge air fares as per the market forces. Although, filing and approval of tariff is not
required, yet DGCA has the power to intervene in cases where he is satisfied that the operator has
established excessive or predatory tariff or had indulged in oligopolistic practices. Accordingly Rule
135 of Aircraft Rules has been amended.
85. The Committee was further informed that with a view to maintain transparency in tariff
publication, DGCA has taken following steps:-
(i) Scheduled domestic airlines have been directed to display established tariff route-wise
and fare category-wise in their websites, on monthly basis and also to notify any
significant and noticeable changes to DGCA within 24 hours of effecting such a
change.
(ii) A T ariff Analysis Unit has been set up in DGCA to monitor air fares of domestic
airlines on a regular basis at periodic intervals.
86. It was further informed that during the regular random check of airfares, it has been
observed that airfares offered by the airlines are well within the fare band uploaded by them on
their respective websites. However, trend of airfares moving towards higher bucket is observed
during week-ends, holidays, etc. when the demand of seats is comparatively high.
87. When the Committee raised the issue of shortage of manpower in DGCA it was informed
that process has been already started to recruit 427 Group A officials and 48 Group B officials in
a phased manner to strengthen the functioning of DGCA in regulating the much crowded aviation
sector.
88. The Committee notes that a large part of plan allocation of Rs.60 crores for DGCA
will be expended for strengthening/modernization of premier aviation regulatory authority.
The Committee notes that the aviation regulator has taken a number of measures that
have started showing positive results in respect of curbing malpractices in DGCA including
making examination, inspection and certification processes more transparent, increasing
aviation safety, enforcing discipline in airline operators, both domestic and international.
The Committee reiterates its earlier position for strengthening the DGCA for making it
more effective. The Committee hopes that the proposed Civil Aviation Authority will have
sufficient powers to develop/regulate Indian skies far more efficiently and effectively. The
Committee feels that DGCA should play a more pro-active role in fare determination and
routes re-scheduling of private players, as many a times air travellers are taken for a ride
by these players. The Committee also likes to know the status of filling up of vacancies at
various levels in DGCA so that the functioning and performance of this agency is not
adversely affected by the manpower shortage.

CAG’s Audit Observations
101. The Committee noted that Comptroller and Auditor General of India during its audit of the
Ministry of Civil Aviation have made some serious observations. CAG while scrutinizing the
implementation of Operation, management and Development entered into by Airports Authority of
India with Delhi International Airport Limited (DIAL) observed that DIAL was unduly benefitted due
to non-levy of interest on excess annual fee actually received as per the provision of OMDA, AAI
was not in a position to levy penal interest on delayed payment by DIAL due to the absence of
enabling provisions etc. In another observation on the unauthorized withdrawal from the Escrow
Account held in a fiduciary capacity on behalf of the Government of India by MIAL, the CAG has
stated that the orders of the Government regarding expenditure from Passenger Service Fee
(Security Component) Escrow account were violated by the airport operator – Mumbai International
Airport Limited, resulting in loss to Government/Airports Authority of India by Rs.15.22 crores.

are serious in nature which shows that undue benefit has been shown to private airport

about the action taken by the Government on both the observations of CAG.
General Observations
103. The Committee notes that various recommendations and provisions made in the
Budget has raised lot of expectations on the aviation sector.  Direct import of ATF by
Indian carriers, moderate budgetary support for Air India and customs duty exemption for
the MRO industry will send some positive signals to the aviation industry. The Committee
also notes that provision has also been made for setting up of the Air Freight Stations
which may provide much needed fillip for the developing air cargo industry and easy
facilitation of cargo movements. One adverse impact of the Union Budget on aviations
sector is the hike in service tax rates to 12 per cent plus cess which will result in hike
in airfares.

24
104. The Committee feels that Ministry should take up the issue of uniform taxation of
ATF with the Ministry of Finance so that air fares do not see much fluctuation specially
upward, quite often.  The Committee hopes that scheduled infusion of equity into Air India
will give some fresh lease of life to the ‘Maharaja’ and with the structured implementation
of turn around plan, Air India could be in a position to re-establish its position in both the
international and domestic markets.
105. The Committee notes that the air connectivity to major cities of North-Eastern parts
of the country still remain as a distant dream only.  The scheduled operators in the country
had to deploy their services to meet the requirements of Route Dispersal Guidelines but
they resort to what is described as ‘Cherry picking’ or ‘Cream skimming’. In other words,
the private airline operators deploy their services only on the profitable routes in North-
Eastern Region depriving air connectivity to tier-II cities there. The Committee hopes that
the Government should come out with an innovative initiative to expand air connectivity in
North-Eastern Region by strengthening the airport infrastructure to develop the tourism
and trade of that region. Promotion of helicopter services in the North-Eastern Region is
another viable option before the Government to include more cities from that region in the
aviation map of the country.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
ELEVENTH PLAN (2007-12)
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation was able to spend
Rs.40,673.04 crores (anticipated) as against the allocation of Rs.49,267 crores for the
Eleventh Plan period resulting in a huge saving. The Committee finds that except Indira
Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi which spent Rs.41.00 against the budgetary allocation of
Rs.42.00 crore for the plan period, all other organizations under the Ministry could not
spend the allocated money fully. This is a disturbing scenario. The Committee notes that Air
India was able to spend Rs.25,603 crores only against the allocation of Rs.32,730.71 for the
Eleventh Plan period, again saving a sum of Rs.7,127 crores. The Committee is surprised
to note that when the national carrier was knocking the doors of financial institutions to
bail it out, it was unable to spend money it had been allocated during the Eleventh Plan
period. (Para 6)
Another case of under-spending is that of Airports Authority of India, the leading
infrastructure provider for aviation industry in the country. AAI could spend Rs.11,873.41
crores against the allocation of Rs.12,964.21 crores for the plan period. The Committee is
not able to understand the logic behind Airports Authority of India’s inability to spend even
the budgetary support of the Government; they could spend roughly 50% only. The
Committee feels that such under utilization of funds by AAI could have definitely slowed
the pace and process of developing airport infrastructure at various places including
Chennai and Kolkata. A curious case in this respect is that of the Hotel Corporation of
India which was able to spend Rs.43.75 crores against Rs.75.00 crores. The Committee feels
that time has come to assess the performance of this PSU in a broader perspective and it
should not be allowed to become a liability to pave the way for its privatization. Air India
Charters Limited is another example in this respect. They could spend only Rs.2088.16
crores against the plan outlay of Rs.2475.26. Neither the Low Cost Carrier of the
Government is expanding its services nor able to spend the allocated plan outlay. The
Committee would like to be informed about the reasons for such under-utilization of funds
by various organizations of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and the remedial measures taken
to prevent such happenings in future. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will ensure
that the organizations under its control were able to spend their allocations to the maximum
possible extent in the Twelfth Plan. The Committee feels that any laxity on spending of
allocation will have the direct impact on aviation sector of the country. (Para 7)
ANNUAL PLAN 2011-12
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Civil Aviation was not able to spend fund
allocated in respect of DGCA, BCAS and AAI – three main organizations. It is not a
welcome sign since allocation under these heads constituted major share of the allocation
under Plan, excluding Air India. The reasons submitted by the Ministry for under-utilization
of funds such as delay in clearances to various projects, delay in acquisition of land for
airport projects and delays in getting necessary regulatory and statutory approvals may be
understandable but not acceptable, if repeated every year, For example, the project of
construction of office buildings for DGCA and BCAS could not be taken up for last two to
three years. The Committee feels that failure to spend the allocated moneys by these
25

26
organizations shows a lack of proper planning for timely execution of major programmes/
projects. Delay on account of various administrative problems and procedural difficulties
cannot be acceptable as excuse as these could be visualized at initial stages and precautions
taken well in time. The Committee recommends that the long pending construction of
headquarters for DGCA and BCAS be started at the earliest in coordination with agencies
concerned and be completed in a fixed schedule. The Committee further recommends that
the Ministry should impress upon all the organizations under its purview to spend the
allocations cent percent in a planned manner. (Para 9)
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
The Committee after scrutinizing the allocations for 2012-13 finds that apart from
equity infusion to the tune of Rs.4000 crore for Air India under the budgetary support, the
allocation for the Ministry is inadequate. The allocation of Rs.738.80 crores under the Non-
plan for the year 2012-13 is lesser than the allocation at Revised Estimates of Rs.764.86
crores for the year 2011-12. The Committee expresses its concern over the static allocation
to the Ministry which concerns with one of the fastest growing sectors having lot of
potential for further growth. The Committee hopes that the Ministry will take up its case
with Planning Commission for allocations of adequate funds at RE stage so that ongoing
aviation projects are not hampered and new ones are taken up. (Para 14)
AIR INDIA LIMITED
The Committee notes that the national carrier had to undergo a tough period during
the last year mainly on account of merger related issues, ever increasing ATF prices,
employees’ resentment over non-payment of dues, allotment of profitable routes to private
carriers, its over-ambitious aircraft acquisition plan, inability to raise funds from the open
market and the reluctance of financial institutions and Oil Marketing Companies to help
the ailing Air India. The Committee finds that though the company was able to increase its
passenger load factor it witnessed a dip in share in domestic and international aviation
markets. (Para 30)
The Committee notes that a large number of amendments to Air Service Agreements
with foreign countries were signed for expansion of international air services by the
national carrier during the last year. The Committee finds that Air India operates almost
500 departures daily offering more than 78000 seats per day connecting about 150 domestic
city-pairs and 125 international city pairs with a 143 strong fleet but still not in a position
to attain a visible competitive edge vis-à-vis  other airlines. The Committee notes some
serious efforts being made both by Air India management and the Government for taking
the national carrier out of the current mess. There are improvements on some parameters
indicating that things have started moving into required direction, which is why the
Government has decided to support the airlines’ recovery process. But in view of the several
challenges and over all slow down in the Sector, Committee would like to caution the Air
India management and the Government to be very careful while implementing its
restructuring/revival plans. The greatest challenge it must overcome on priority is that
relating to HR issues created due to ill-conceived merger plan. The Committee hopes that
allocation of unutilized bilaterals/traffic rights to Air India will benefit it in regaining its
lost market share in international market. (Para 31)
The Committee feels that infusion of Government equity to the tune of Rs.30,000
crore over a nine-year period, induction of 27 Boeing 787 Dreamers, proposal to hive off

27
Air India’s Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) business and its Engineering Services
as two wholly-owned subsidiaries will yield the much desired results in the long run.
(Para 32)
AIRPORTS AUTHORITY OF INDIA
The Committee notes that allocation of funds under the Plan for the airport
infrastructure provider was reduced to Rs.208.65 crores at RE level from Rs.280.15 crores
at BE level in the year 2011-12. However, Airports Authority of India was able to spend
Rs.120.99 crores only during 2011-12. The Committee feels that a cut in plan outlay for the
Airports Authority of India at RE and spending merely 60% of plan allocation does not
augur well for the development of required airport infrastructure in the country. The
Committee was informed that delay in getting requisite clearances and land acquisition for
airport projects were the reasons for under utilization of funds by the Airports Authority
of India during the year 2011-12. The Committee emphasizes the need for a better
coordination with various Ministries and concerned State Governments by the Airports
Authority of India for speedy clearance of projects. The Committee hopes that AAI will
ensure to utilize the allocated funds to the maximum extent during the current fiscal.
(Para 46)
The Committee finds that much emphasized financial autonomy to Airports Authority
of India to plan and execute its projects has not materialized so far. The Committee is of
the opinion that the Government should lend a helping hand to AAI in recovering its
outstanding dues from various agencies for the services rendered to them so that cash flow
of the agency is maintained at the desired level. The Committee hopes that the Ministry
of Civil Aviation will impress the Ministry of Finance in granting permission to AAI to float
tax-free bonds to raise funds so that the on-going and planned airport projects are not
stalled or delayed for want of funds. (Para 47)
The Committee is happy to note that GPS Aided Geo Augmentation Navigation
(GAGAN) – the Indian Satellite Based Navigation System (SBAS) is progressing as per
schedule and hopes that system for aviation application is commissioned by June, 2013.
(Para 48)
It was brought to the notice of the Committee that the Patna Airport was in
dangerous State where a catastrophe was waiting to happen as the existing runway is not
fit for landing/take-off of long-bodied aircrafts. The Committee finds that the existing
airport can not be developed further in view of land constraints. The Committee hopes that
Airports Authority of India with the help of State Government will come out with a solution
so as to expand the air services from this important airport connecting ancient and
important places of our country. (Para 49)
The Committee was further informed about the problems faced by Airports Authority
of India in getting necessary land for the expansion of Leh airport from Defence
authorities. The Committee desires that issue may be taken up with Defence officials at the
earliest so that the long pending modernization of Leh airport gets priority as the existing
terminal is not a position to accommodate more than 250 passengers at one time. The
Committee recommends that Airports Authority of India may take up the expansion of
Kargil airport in consultation with Defence authorities on priority to bring this important
tourist place on the aviation map. (Para 50)
The Committee may be apprised of the status of construction of new airport at Navi
Mumbai to decongest the Mumbai Airport. (Para 51)

present this One Hundred and Seventy Fifth Report on Demands for Grants 2012-13 of the
Ministry of Culture.

1
REPORT
India being one of the most ancient civilizations has a long, varied and rich cultural heritage
both tangible and intangible. India has had a long tradition of State patronage for promotion and
preservation of art and culture.
2. The Ministry of Culture is mandated to preserve and promote all forms of art and culture.
To this end, the Ministry of Culture undertakes the following activities:
/head2rightThe maintenance and conservation of the country’s heritage, ancient monuments and
historic sites;
/head2rightPromotion of the literary, visual and performing arts;
/head2rightAdministration of libraries, museums and anthropological institutions;
/head2rightMaintenance, preservation and conservation of archival records and archival libraries;
/head2rightResearch and development in the conservation of cultural property;
/head2rightObservation of centenaries and anniversaries of important national personalities and
events;
/head2rightPromotion of institutions and organizations of Buddhist and Tibetan studies;
/head2rightPromotion of institutional and individual initiatives in the field of art and culture;
/head2rightEntering into and implementation of cultural agreements with foreign countries;
3. Thus, the functional spectrum of the Ministry ranges from generating cultural awareness at
the grassroots level, to promoting cultural exchanges at an international level. Along with
programmes for the preservation of India’s ancient heritage, the activities of the Ministry encourage
and disseminate a variety of contemporary creative arts as well. The Ministry’s aim is to develop
ways and means through which the basic cultural and aesthetic sensibilities of the people remain
active and dynamic. These activities are carried out through the two attached offices, i.e. ,
Archaeological Survey of India and National Archives of India; seven subordinate offices and thirty-
three autonomous institutions working under the Ministry.
4. The subordinate offices under the Ministry of Culture are: Anthropological Survey of India,
Kolkata, National Museum, New Delhi, National Gallery of Modern Art, New Delhi, National
Library, Kolkata, Central Reference Library, Kolkata, and National Research Laboratory for
Conservation of Cultural Property, Lucknow
5. The budget allocations of the Ministry of Culture for the financial year 2012-13 contained
in the Demand No 19  was taken up for consideration by the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture in its meeting held on the 16
th April, 2012.

a presentation on various aspects of the budget allocations.

9. The Committee notes that out of Rs.3524.11 crore earmarked for Eleventh Five Year
Plan, an amount of Rs.3104.00 crore was likely to be spent leaving a saving of Rs. 430.00
crores. The Committee notes that the unspent amount was mainly in respect of the
archives, museums, libraries and activities for NE region. The Committee was informed that
due to non-finalization of upgradation and modernization programmes and deferment of
activities of Victoria  Memorial and Salarjung Museums, funds could not be utilised  under
‘Museums’. Similarly, Asiatic Society, Kolkata also could not utilize the grant for
modernization of infrastructural facilities. The Committee views any kind of under-
utilization of allocations as a lapse, specially those due to avoidable reasons. In this case,
most of the reasons given by the Ministry were avoidable ones.
10. For example, the Committee has seen itself how the affairs of the National Museum,
Delhi were being (mis)managed. The Committee in its 167
th Report has conveyed its
impression about all these aspects and the Action Taken Notes furnished by the Ministry
amply reflect that even the Committee’s recommendations do not evoke required response/
action. The Committee, therefore, recommends that being concerned with art and culture,
the Ministry has to be pro-active and utilize the allocations judiciously provided for Twelfth
Plan. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to ensure that the schemes/plans do
not suffer on account of under-utilization of funds and shortcomings/flaws are corrected
during the Twelfth Plan period.

12. The Committee notes with concern that out of Rs.805.00 crore provided at RE 2011-12,
expenditure upto 29 th February, 2012 was Rs.570.72 crore. The Committee has a doubt if the
Ministry of Culture would have been able to utilize the remaining amount of Rs.234.28
crore in just one month i.e. March, 2012. If it is so, the same is against the established
financial norms for spending. The Committee deplores the habit of incurring expenditure at
the fag end of the year. The Committee recommends that proper monitoring of the
schemes/plans should be done with reviewing of progress in every quarter to ensure that
rushing for last minute expenditure at the end of the financial year is avoided. The main
reasons for non-utilization are non-finalization of upgradation/modernization plans of
Museums, and non-finalization of schemes which were started in Eleventh Plan period. The
Committee notes that the expenditure is less in those areas which are critical for
preservation and propagation of culture and invariably require more funds such as ASI,
Museums and archives. The Committee recommends that proper planning should be made
at the time of proposal of the plan/schemes and an effective monitoring mechanism be put
in place and ensure that the expenditure is incurred fully and uniformly.

new schemes and activities. The Committee, however, notes with concern that for the year
2012-13, 30% less has been given than what was proposed by Ministry of Culture. The
Committee is of the view that the Culture sector has not received the priority it deserved.
It strongly recommends to give it adequate funds for the Twelfth Plan. Ministry’s financial
performance was not bad except in Museum, Libraries, Archieves, etc. during the entire
Eleventh plan period. The Committee hopes that the Planning Commission would consider
the importance of culture and art in human development and contribution of culture related
activities and services to GDP, employment generation and above all, instilling a sense of
national pride/identity.  The Committee emphasizes the need for developing proper linkages
not only with the Tourism which is conspicuous by absence today, but also with the
Ministries such as Road and Highways, Transport, Civil Aviation, Railways, etc.  with a view
to having an integrated developmental activities for promoting and show-casing our rich
cultural and art traditions to the world.

ARCHAEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA (ASI)
22. The major activities undertaken by ASI are: maintenance, conservation and preservation of
centrally protected monuments/sites and remains. In addition to the above activities, it conducts
archaeological exploration and excavation and underwater archaeology regularly. Since its inception,
the ASI has grown into a large organization having its network of 24 circles throughout the
country.
23. There are 3667 monuments of National importance in the country which are Centrally
Protected Monuments, which include 21 properties inscribed on the World Heritage List by
UNESCO. ASI is also engaged in developing epigraphically research, setting up and reorganization
of site museums, imparting training programmes in Archaeology, strengthening of the Chemistry
Branch and Horticulture Branch. Publication programme of ASI encompassing the fields such as
academic, informative and awareness generation is one of the important activities of ASI.
24. The Committee was informed that the policy towards the conservation/ restoration of
Monuments is of in situ  stabilization, retaining the maximum original fabric and maintaining
authenticity and integrity of the site/monument.  Conservation work of the monuments is attended
to regularly depending upon the need of repairs and availability of resources. The conservation
work is done mostly by using traditional methods and techniques. However, modern technology is
used if no alternative is available, if it is better and if it does not have any harmful effects on the
monuments.
25. The Plan allocation for ASI in 2011-12 was Rs.144.00 crore  which  was increased to
Rs.161.75 crore at RE stage. The allocation was increased as ASI had proposed to implement the
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act (Amendment and Validation Act

9
2010) for which additional funds for creating NMA & competent authority and for making payment
to CISF, Private agency and  State Armed Police Guard. The expenditure incurred upto 29 th Feb.
was Rs, 133.90 crore. During the Eleventh Plan ASI took up massive programme of conservation
and maintenance. More than 800 monuments were taken up annually for conservation and
structural repairs, chemical preservation and environmental development besides day-to-day
maintenance. Better visitor’s facilities were provided in the various monuments/sites including
World Heritage Monuments/Sites, by undertaking an integrated environmental development of major
ancient monuments.
26. The Committee was informed that  ASI maintains 44 sties museums and carried out
museums reforms in phased manner. It opened sites museums at (i) Harappan Sites, (ii) Dholavira,
(iii) Piprahawa (UP), (iv) Lalitgiri (Orissa), (v) Shivpuri (MP) and Sannati (Karnataka).
Reorganization work of galleries, as per 14 Point Museum Reform was carried out and also
upgraded public amenities.

/head2rightASI being a multi-disciplinary scientific organization needs a strong cadre of its own
and therefore, an Institute of Archaeology which was set up in 1985 and remained
non-functional for want of requisite staff should be suitably strengthened.
/head2rightThe ASI being a declared Scientific Department do not enjoy the benefits which the
other Scientific and Technical Bodies in the Government are entitled to. The grave
problems of stagnation thus leads to frustration and demoralization among the
Scientific and Technical Cadre of the ASI. This can be resolved to a greater extent if
the ASI is also granted the benefits available under the scheme particularly “Flexible
Complementary Scheme” governing the promotions of various categories of employees.
This would be a remedy for all ills of the ASI.
/head2rightDuring the course of on the spot study, it was revealed that the ASI was neither
having any permanent/annual training schedules in-house or in-service nor perspective
plan for its workforce. Further, certain category of personnel especially administration/
accounts have not even been sponsored/exposed to any such training programmes for
years. Besides, Sr. Officers and Technical Staff of the ASI should also be considered
for advance training courses in specific disciplines of the Archaeology to keep them
abreast with pace of development in Archaeological management.
/head2rightThe staff position in Science & Epigraphy Branches, which are highly specialized, is
very critical and has created a vacuum in both the cadres. The need for capacity
building especially under the Epigraphy Branch where the subject matter specialists are
needed need no elaboration.
/head2rightThe organizational development/reforms both in terms of human resources and also for
hardware resources play an important role in increasing/improving the quality of
output. It is observed that the ASI is following short in this sphere.

The Committee is constrained to note that even after a lapse of fifteen years from the date
of issue of the notification in this regard no concrete action was taken by Ministry of
Culture and Archaeological Survey of India for developing Archaeological Survey of India
as a Scientific and Technical Department, which amply indicates the administrative apathy
towards the whole issue. The Committee regrets that no internal exercise was undertaken by
Ministry of Culture and Archaeological Survey of India during the last fifteen years for
availing the benefits and privileges which could be extended to the Archaeological Survey
of India as a Science and Technology department. The Committee observes that there has
been deviation in the working of Archaeological Survey of India and that it has failed in
terms of developing Archaeological Survey of India not merely as an administrative body
but also as a spearhead for consolidating the scientific discipline of archaeology in the
country.  The Committee is of the view that the Archaeological Survey of India needs to
reinvent itself, not merely as an administrative wing of the Government, but as an agency

defeated. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture and Archaeological
Survey of India should, without any further loss of time, take necessary follow-up action
on the recommendations of the Committee chaired by Director General, Archaeological
Survey of India so as to avail the benefits which accrue to a Science and Technology
department. The Committee also recommends that, if required, the Ministry of Culture
should also take necessary legislative action to make Archaeological Survey of India
Science and Technology department in the true sense.
HORTICULTURE BRANCH, ASI
37. The mandate of Horticulture Branch of ASI is environmental development/restoration of
Heritage gardens around all 3677 national protected monuments. The Garden Branch of
Archaeological Survey of India is maintaining gardens of various styles from sacred groves to
orchard, courtyard gardens of Havalies to palaces, Fort and Tomb gardens. Several heritage
gardens have exclusive old plants, which is not found in local area thus showing import of plants
from different parts of world by those who grow those gardens at that time. These are also part
of heritage to be preserved with utmost care along with monument to avoid extinction. The
Committee notes that there were 100 gardens in the year 1987-88 which has increased to more
than 500 in 2011-12.

National Gallery of Modern Art, National Research Laboratory for Conservation of Cultural
Property; Autonomous Organizations like National Council of Science Museums, Victoria Memorial
Hall, Allahabad Museum, National Museum Institute, Salarjung Museum, Indian Museum and also
a few schemes.

take initiative to put the plans in order and take prior approval of the Plans so that

that there are various recruitment rules and the posts in the purview of UPSC that takes
a lot of time. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendations to keep these posts out
of purview of UPSC and the same should be pursued vigorously. The Committee
recommends that the Ministry should make all out efforts to fill the vacant in all the
institutions.

Sir, on the Gandhi heritage site, the Committee had given its recommendations about three

79. National Mission on Monuments and Antiquities (NMMA) was constituted for a period of
5 years i.e. 2007-2012 with the objectives to prepare a National database on Built Heritage and Sites
from secondary sources and prepare a National database on Antiquities from different sources and
museums. The term of the NMMA ended formally in March, 2012. The Committee was informed
that a proposal has been sent for continuation in the next 5 year period 2012-17 with certain
modifications. Of an estimated 4.00 lac built heritage and sites, about 80,000 have been documented
so far. Out of an estimated 8.00 lac antiquities, 5.00 lac antiquities have been documented.
80. During the deliberations the Committee was informed  by the Ministry inter-alia  that:–
When we drafted that programme obviously we envisaged that it will have to go into this
thing and do a primary survey. If we had done it, it would have cost 450 crores. In 11th

22

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
ELEVENTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
The Committee notes that out of Rs.3524.11 crore earmarked for XIth Five Year
Plan, an amount of Rs.3104.00 crore was likely to be spent leaving a saving of Rs. 430.00
crores. The Committee notes that the unspent amount was mainly in respect of the
archives, museums, libraries and activities for NE region. The Committee was informed that
due to non-finalization of upgradation and modernization programmes and deferment of
activities of Victoria  Memorial and Salarjung Museums, funds could not be utilised  under
‘Museums’. Similarly, Asiatic Society, Kolkata also could not utilize the grant for
modernization of infrastructural facilities. The Committee views any kind of under-
utilization of allocations as a lapse, specially those due to avoidable reasons. In this case,
most of the reasons given by the Ministry were avoidable ones. (Para 9)
For example, the Committee has seen itself how the affairs of the National Museum,
Delhi were being (mis)managed. The Committee in its 167
th Report has conveyed its
impression about all these aspects and the Action Taken Notes furnished by the Ministry
amply reflect that even the Committee’s recommendations do not evoke required response/
action. The Committee, therefore, recommends that being concerned with art and culture,
the Ministry has to be pro-active and utilize the allocations judiciously provided for XIIth
Plan. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to ensure that the schemes/plans do
not suffer on account of under-utilization of funds and shortcomings/flaws are corrected
during the XII Plan period. (Para 10)
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee notes with concern that out of Rs.805.00 crore provided at RE
2011-12, expenditure upto 29
th February, 2012 was Rs.570.72 crore. The Committee has a
doubt if the Ministry of Culture would have been able to utilize the remaining amount of
Rs.234.28 crore in just one month i.e. March 2012. If it is so, the same is against the
established financial norms for spending. The Committee deplores the habit of incurring
expenditure at the fag end of the year.  The Committee recommends that proper monitoring
of the schemes/plans should be done with reviewing of progress in every quarter to ensure
that rushing for last minute expenditure at the end of the financial year is avoided. The
main reasons for non-utilization are non-finalization of upgradation/modernization plans  of
Museums, and non-finalization of schemes which were started in XI Plan period. The
Committee notes that the expenditure is less in those areas which are critical for
preservation and propagation of culture and invariably require more funds such as ASI,
Museums and archives. The Committee recommends that proper planning should be made
at the time of proposal of the plan/schemes and an effective monitoring mechanism be put
in place and ensure that the expenditure is incurred fully and uniformly. (Para 12)
TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN (2012-17)
The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Culture had projected a
requirement of Rs. 18353.94 crore for the XII Plan to carry out its on-going as well as new
schemes and activities. The Committee, however, notes with concern that for the year 2012-
23

24
13, 30% less has been given than what was proposed by Ministry of Culture. The
Committee is of the view that the Culture sector has not received the priority it deserved.
It strongly recommends to give it adequate funds for the XII Plan. Ministry’s financial
performance was not bad except in Museum, Libraries, Achieves, etc. during the entire XI
plan period. The Committee hopes that the Planning Commission would consider the
importance of culture and art in human development and contribution of culture related
activities and services to GDP, employment generation and above all, instilling a sense of
national pride/identity. The Committee emphasizes the need for developing proper linkages
not only with the Tourism which is conspicuous by absence today, but also with the
Ministries such as Road & Highways, Transport, Civil Aviation, Railways, etc.  with a view
to having an integrated developmental activities for promoting and show-casing our rich
cultural and art traditions to the world. (Para 17)
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
The Committee notes that against the projected demand of Rs.2916.43 crore.
Ministry of Culture has been allocated only Rs.864.00 crore for 2012-13, less than 1/3 of
what was proposed by the Ministry.  The Ministry had made plans for utilizing the enhanced
allocation for schemes like preservation and conservation of monuments by ASI,
introduction of new schemes for libraries, celebrating centenaries, strengthening and
expansion of ongoing plan schemes implemented by Zonal Cultural Centres for creative
industries, benefit of Tribal/Rural artists at the grass root level, ten new schemes by
National Archives, financial assistance for Professional Groups and Individuals, for specified
performing arts, National Mission for Monuments and antiquities, Sangeet Natak Akademi,
NSD etc. The Committee notes the apathy of the Government towards the cause of
preservation and promotion of our ancient culture and has allocated plan outlay of less than
1/3 of what was proposed by the Ministry of Culture. During the XIth Plan also  Art and
Culture got a share of only 0.16% of the total central plan allocation of the Government
of India.  The Committee recommends that Ministry of Culture certainly deserves a better
treatment in allocation of funds in view of its importance. The Committee recommends that
Ministry should strive to utilize the allocations optimally by September every year so that
while submitting proposal for RE, Ministry can justify its stand for more allocation which
is based on trend of last 6 months’ expenditure. However, the Ministry should also take
extra care/measures to monitor the schemes/plans on regular basis. (Para 20)

Committee feels that either the Ministry’s projections were unrealistically high or the
Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance did not accord the importance this Ministry
deserves. There is a need to sensitize the concerned agencies to appreciate the contribution
of art and culture to our nation’s life. Ministry has proposed some very good schemes that
were overdue and must be taken up on priority. (Para 21)

th

st report on the “Functioning of ASI”.  (Para 36)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having been authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Seventy Sixth Report on Demands for Grants 2012-13 of the
Ministry of Tourism.
2. The Committee, at its meeting held on the 12
th April, 2012 examined the subject and heard
the Secretary and other officials of the Ministry of Tourism.
3. The Committee wishes to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Tourism for
presenting before the Committee and furnishing the material and information desired in connection
with the subject and for clarifying the points raised by the Members.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 3
rd May, 2012.
SITARAM YECHURY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
May 3, 2012 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Vaisakha 13, 1934  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture

1
REPORT
Tourism is basically a people oriented, multi dimensional and labour intensive activity. It
is dependent on varied activities which are separate but interdependent. Such a broad spectrum
of economic activities involved in tourism, therefore, make it very vital for overall economic
growth. Furthermore, tourism is highly dependent upon natural capital such as forest, wildlife
and culture.
2. The Ministry of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and
programmes and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government agencies, State
Governments/Union Territories and the Private Sector for the development and promotion of
tourism in the country.
3. Demand No.93 containing the details of the budgetary provisions of Ministry of Tourism for
the financial year 2012-13, was scrutinized by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture at its meeting held on the 12
th April, 2012. The
Secretary, Ministry of Tourism alongwith the senior officials explained to the Committee on various
aspects of the Demands for Grants.
Analysis of Eleventh Five Year Plan (2007-12)
4. The Ministry of Tourism has informed that a Plan outlay of Rs. 5156 crore was
sanctioned during the Eleventh Five Year Plan and the Ministry has been able to utilize 99.23%
of the allocations during the first four years. Details regarding the allocations and expenditure are
given below:

6. The Committee notes that the total allocation made for the Eleventh Plan was
Rs. 4997 crore and the Ministry was able to spend Rs. 4690.57 crore upto Dec 2011. The
Secretary while deposing before the Committee stated that:
…..Sir, that  we are one of the few Ministries in the Government of India which has  done
nearly 100 per cent. So, Sir, we hope that tourism will now go to a different orbit, if not
a different zone.
7. The Committee also notes that as per year-wise utilization detail (Table-I) submitted
by the Ministry, the total utilization during the Eleventh Plan had been around 98% on an
average. The Committee appreciates that Ministry of Tourism was able to spend the
allocation during the Eleventh Plan and hope that the tourism sector must have got
benefited by the funds that have been put into the sector through various schemes.
8. The detailed analysis of the fund distribution and performance of each scheme during the
Eleventh Plan as per Table I and II and other papers furnished by the Ministry of Tourism and
observations and recommendations of the Committee are given in the succeeding paragraphs.
Product/infrastructure Development for Destinations and Circuits
9. For the Eleventh Plan the total outlay under Product/infrastructure Development for
Destinations and Circuits was Rs.2381 crores. However the expenditure stands at Rs.2621.53 crores
whereas the total sanctions were Rs.2514.12 crores.  During the deliberations, the Committee was
informed that Rs.3872.67 crore was expended till 31 st December, 2011for sanctioning 1163 projects.
The Committee also notes that the Government of Odisha was sanctioned Rs.740.67 lakhs for the
“Integrated Development of Buddhist Circuit at Lalitagiri, Ratnagiri, Udyagiri and Langudi” during
2004-05, in the 10 th Plan Period.
10. It was brought to the notice of the Committee that Jabalpur has been identified in 2010-11
by the State Government of MP as the Mega circuit for development of tourism infrastructure and
has submitted the proposal to the Ministry of Tourism for development. However, the Central
Government is yet to include Jabalpur as a mega tourist destination for development by providing
funds.
11. The Committee is of the opinion that even though the Ministry was able to incur the
surplus expenditure under the scheme, it is equally important to know  reasons for excess
expenditure as the desired targets have not been achieved in terms of creation of
infrastructural facilities  and the resultant tourist arrivals. The Committee also emphasizes
the need for a thorough review of the physical achievements made on the infrastructure
projects of the Ministry during the Eleventh Plan period.
12. The Committee notes that the work of the “Integrated Development of Buddhist
Circuit at Lalitagiri, Ratnagiri, Udyagiri and Langudi”  in Odisha was sanctioned during the
Tenth Plan period and is still going on. In the past also, the Committee has drawn the
attention of the Ministry of Tourism to a number of projects which were taken up and
crores of rupees were invested therein but could not be completed and later on, were
dropped. This results in wastage of taxpayers money and country’s scarce resources. The
Committee also desire that information regarding the status of projects sanctioned before
the Eleventh plan period which are still continuing may be submitted to the Committee. The
Committee also  recommends that the projects involving large amount of investment should
be monitored carefully during the implementation stage itself  to ensure that work is
completed in time and investment made therein do not go waste.

4
13. The Committee recommends that the proposal of the State Government of Madhya
Pradesh for developing Jabalpur as a mega circuit for development of tourist infrastructure
may be taken up by the Ministry of Tourism at the earliest.
Externally Aided Projects
14. The Committee notes that for the externally aided projects out of the total outlay of Rs.37
crore, the total allocations for the entire Plan period was Rs.25.65 crores.
15. The Committee was informed that a loan agreement for an amount equivalent to 7331
million Japanese Yen (Rs. 299 crore approx.) was signed between the Government of India and
Japan International Cooperation Agency on 31
st March, 2003 for Ajanta Ellora Conservation and
Tourism Development Project - Phase II. The loan became effective from 31 st July, 2003. JICA has
extended the validity of loan period from July, 2011 to July, 2013 in September, 2011.
16. The Committee notes that out of the allocation of Rs. 25.65 crores, the Ministry
could spend only Rs. 20.78 crores. The Committee also notes that the Ajanta-Ellora project
has not yet completed as some major work on the part of ADI, MTDC and MJP are pending.
It is expected to be completed by July, 2013. The Committee emphasizes the need for proper
monitoring and coordination be ensured with all agencies concerned to complete the project
on time.
Assistance to IHMs/FCIs/IITM/NIWS
17. The Committee was informed that in XI Plan 17 new IHMs and 17 FCIs were sanctioned.
18. The Committee noted that Assistance to IHMs/FCIs/IITM etc. was Rs. 495.00 crores
as per Planning Commission outlays but the actual allocation was Rs. 387.70 crores only but
actual expenditure being Rs. 393.43 crores. Thus, there is over spending. The Committee,
however, is not convinced with the achievement in ratio of the expenditure. There is need
for more focussed approach and opening of more institutes for this purpose.
Capacity Building for Service Providers
19. Ministry of Tourism informed that skill testing and certification facilities at 14 IHMs were
provided and from 2009 to 2012, 21,483 service providers were certified and under ‘ Hunar se
Rozgar” Yojana 23,540 youths were trained .
20. The Committee notes the cuts made in the outlay for capacity building for service
providers scheme wherein the outlay stands at Rs.95.00 crores and the allocations are
Rs.89.00 crores. The actual expenditure of Rs. 67.79 crores shows that total allocations could
not be utilized by the end of the Plan period. This is disappointing mainly because Ministry
of Tourism is underutilizing the fund meant for skill development at a time when India is
faced with huge shortage of trained and skilled people in the tourism and hospitality
industry. We must have functional linkages with need of the industry and academic
institutions specially IHMS, IITM, CCI, NIWS, etc.
Overseas and Domestic Promotion
21. The Committee notes that extra allocation of Rs.145 crore was made for the
Overseas Promotion and Publicity including Market Development Assistance as the plan
outlay was only Rs.1010 crores but the total allocations stands at Rs.1155 crores. Compared
to other projects, the expenditure pace is also very prompt in this case as Rs.1024.00 crore
has been incurred upto 31
st December 2011, whereas in the case of Domestic Promotion and

5
Publicity including Hospitality there was a cut in allocations amounting to Rs.81 crores as
the allocation of Rs.345 crore was made against an outlay of Rs.426 crore. The expenditure
stands at Rs. 315.85 crore. The Committee notes that the expenditure on Domestic
Promotion has no such momentum in comparison to the expenditure pattern of the
Overseas promotion. The Ministry has admitted that 3/4
th of the economy in the tourism
sector is contributed by the domestic tourists and domestic tourists has witnessed a growth
of more than 10%.
22. The Committee, while appreciating efforts to tap tourism market overseas, the
growing domestic market should not get ignored. The Committee feels that there is a need
for being little careful in utilizing funds for this purpose as on overseas promotion an over
expenditure of Rs.145 crores in 2011-12, has been noticed. The Committee would like to
have a clarification in this regard.
Incentives to Accommodation Infrastructure
23. In the case of Incentives to Accommodation Infrastructure, the Committee noted
that  the total allocations have been considerably reduced, mere Rs.66 crore was allocated
out of Rs.235 crore outlay. The committee feels that during Eleventh Plan period the project
was not properly implemented by the Ministry as per the expenditure pattern and this late
hour wake up for more allocations could have been avoided. The Government has identified
that there is a shortage of 2,26,040 hotel rooms by 2016. In such a scenario underutilizing
the fund meant for creating accommodation infrastructure reflects that there is something
wrong. The Committee, therefore, recommends to revisit this programme during the Twelfth
Plan period so that more funds are allocated in the coming years and utilized it effectively.
Computerization and Information Technology
24. The spending pattern on the computerization and Information technology is also very
poor as the total expenditure stands at Rs.57.30 crores out of outlay of Rs 121.00 crores
and allocation of Rs 83.50 crores. In this case also the Committee noticed a reduction of
about 1/3 on the allocations in comparison to the total outlay. The Committee notes that
lack of fund is not a hindrance to technological advancement. What is lacking is the
required willpower to implement the programmes and utilize the money effectively. The
Committee recommends that the detailed review may be made to ascertain, in the age of
technological advancement where most of the tourist promotion are dependant on websites
why Ministry of Tourism is unable to tap the potential.
Market Research including 20 Years Perspective Plan
25. The Ministry has also informed that a number of research studies and surveys were
conducted as a part to develop more tourist destinations and circuits in various States to develop
tourism during the Eleventh Plan period. During phase-I, Punjab, Delhi, Jharkhand, Maharashtra and
Andhra Pradesh were targeted. Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim and
Chhattisgarh are currently being surveyed.
26. The total spending for Market Research including 20 years Perspective Plan
stands at Rs.14.49 crores, whereas the expenditure is Rs.19.50 crores. The Committee
notes that States like Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, West Bengal, Odisha,
J&K and Rajasthan which are having greater tourism potential were not covered. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the remaining States need to be included in the
next phase.

6
Assistance for Large Revenue Generating Projects
27. The total outlay under this head was Rs.200 crores and allocation was of Rs. 89.20 crores,
whereas the actual spending has been at Rs.26.57 crores only. The Committee noted that
Assistance to Large Revenue Generating Projects received a lukewarm response from private
investors. The Ministry has submitted that now it has  proposed to include projects such as hotels,
amusement parks, theme parks etc. within the ambit of the scheme.  In view of poor response
received for the Assistance to Large Revenue generating Projects as accepted by the
Ministry itself, the Committee recommends that the scheme be reviewed and redesign and
the new guidelines may be framed to attract more entrepreneurs to utilize the scheme.
Creation of Land bank for Hotels
28. The Ministry of Tourism has submitted that Creation of Land bank also could not be
implemented as no land was made available to Ministry of Tourism by various land owning
agencies.
29. The Committee notes that creation of Land Bank for Hotels could not pick up during
the Eleventh Plan period as the amount of Rs.12.02 crores actually allocated for the purpose
remained fully unutilized at the end of the Eleventh Plan. The Committee recommends that
this project may be reviewed so that amount, though symbolic, of Rs.1.00 crore for the year
2012-13 earmarked for the purpose is utilized.
Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism infrastructure development
30. The Ministry has informed that Assistance to central  agencies such as ASI,CPWD, ITDC,
Port Trusts etc. to undertake improvement of tourism infrastructure also has received very few
proposals.
31. The Committee observes that Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism
Infrastructure Development was provided extra allocations of Rs.7.01 crore over and above
the total outlay of Rs.25 crores, i.e. Rs.32.01 crore whereas the spending stands only at
Rs.20.51 crores. The Committee feels that this is the result of poor planning and
implementation of the project. The Committee also recommends that if there is any
bottlenecks at the administrative level for the scheme, it should be properly revisited and
necessary corrective measures need to be taken.
Salient Features of the Twelfth Five Year Plan
32. The Committee was informed that Ministry of Tourism projected requirement of Rs.22,800
crores for the Twelfth Plan period.
33. The Proposed Outlay of Ministry of Tourism for Twelfth Plan is as given below:

“In order to realize the potential of this sector, the Government would need to adopt a ‘pro

there exists tourist infrastructure or not. The Committee further notes that if appropriate
tourist infrastructures are developed at all the pilgrim centres, more and more pilgrim
tourists from  India and abroad can be attracted to those places. The Committee, therefore,

of extinction and such a step is required to rejuvenate the traditional artisans and cottage

concrete action to ensure that the benefits of tourism growth under “pro-poor approach”

Rs.50.00 crore for the training of personnel in the unorganized sector made in the budget
will be sufficient to meet the manpower training facilities as per the projected demand. The
Committee therefore recommends that the Government should take steps to provide
allocation adequate enough to meet the requirement of trained personnel to serve the
increasing tourism potential of the country.
97. The Committee notes that the grants are being utilized by very few universities. The
Committee recommends that the universities all over the country may be roped in to avail
the grant and it may be given in those areas where the major tourism potential exists and
states which promotes tourism with vast intervention. The Committee also is of the view
that wide publicity should be given to the scheme so that more Universities are sanctioned
the grant.
Accommodation Infrastructure
98. Construction of hotels is primarily a private sector activity, however, the Ministry of
Tourism provides Central Financial Assistance for construction of budget accommodation to the
North-Eastern States, Jammu & Kashmir and for eco-tourism projects where private sector
investment is not forthcoming. To encourage the growth of budget hotels in the country the
various steps have been taken by the Government of India.
99. The Ministry of tourism submitted a shortage of 23.40 lakh hotel rooms (classified 1.90
lakh and unclassified 21.50 lakh) by 2016 in the Report of the Working Group on Tourism for the
Twelfth Five Year Plan. The Committee is of the view that to reduce this shortage some incentives
have to be given for construction of new hotel rooms particularly in the Budget Category hotels.
100. The Committee notes the step taken by the Ministry to encourage Budget hotels.
The Committee is of the view that to reduce this shortage some incentives have to be given
for construction of new hotel rooms particularly in the Budget Category hotels.  The
Committee is also of the view that concerted efforts need to be taken to meet the massive
requirement of 22,60,040 hotels rooms by 2016. The Committee emphasizes the need for
putting a scientific methods in place to collect the information regarding the actual
availability of hotel accommodation in the country. In this exercise, the State Governments/
UTs as also the local bodies should be involved.
101. The Committee, also in view of the assessment made by the Ministry on the above
scheme recommends that the Ministry should impress upon the State Governments to offer
new initiatives for the creation of quality accommodation to the visiting tourists. Central
assistance may be extended for achieving this goal and the new criteria may be worked out
for achieving this.
North East Region
102. The availability of diverse tourism products in the North East offers a tremendous scope
for the development of tourism in the area. 10% of the Plan allocation is marked for the

20
development and promotion of Tourism in the North-Eastern Region and Sikkim. The Committee
was informed that the Ministry of Tourism has been spending more than the earmarked 10% of
its total budgetary allocation for the North-East region during the years 2009-10, 2010-11 and
2011-12. Ministry of Tourism further informed that they had released 18.8%, 20.84%, and 14.16%
respectively of the total plan allocation (RE) towards the North-East region.
103. The Committee was further informed that funds are not earmarked for any State beforehand
but are sanctioned to the States upon receipt of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) in respect of the
prioritized projects, depending on the availability of fund, inter se  priority and adherence to scheme
guidelines.
104. The Committee notes that in 2011-12 (as on 30.11.2011) an amount of Rs. 93.77 crore has
been released for development of infrastructure under the scheme of Product/infrastructure
Development for Destinations and Circuits. The total expenditure under the scheme was Rs. 567.23
crore. In 2011-12 an amount of Rs. 2.34 crore has been sanctioned in rural tourism to different
states. Besides this, all other schems are being implemented and focus is on Incredible India
Campaign in which Nort-Eastern states are prominently displayed.
105. The Committee notes that the North-Eastern States are getting adequate funds infact
more than 10% during the last three years. This has helped in creation of infrastructure
and other facilities in the region. However, the Committee feels there remains a lot to be
done in terms of provision of  hotels and connectivity. The facilities are not adequate to
meet the requirements of increased number of tourists. The Committee also notes that with
no five star hotels in the region, it is resulting in loss of revenue as high end tourists are
not turning up. The Committee recommends that it is time to wake up to augment tourist
facilities and for this Ministry of Tourism should review their schemes and seek active
participation from States to get more projects implemented. The Committee also would like
to emphasize that Tourism in North East Region is the main source of livelihood as such
it should be provided all the support from the Ministry of Tourism.
106. The Committee however notes that the response to the capital subsidy  scheme has
not been encouraging although potential (of setting up 2 star category hotel) is there. The
Committee in this regard reiterates its recommendations contained in  its 172
nd Report which
is reproduced below:
….The Committee has observed that most of the states are not geared up for the
conventional tourism in respect of accommodation - affordable hotels and guest houses.
They do not have good and affordable accommodation, both  in terms of numbers as well
as quality. This was also evident from field trips to these States. There is no Five Star Hotel
in NER till date.  The Committee notes that Government of India has launched the scheme
for capital subsidy of 30% for hotels (not below 2-star category) with effect from 1
st April,
2008 for a period of five years. However, this scheme has not been successful in this region
in achieving the desired results…
107. The Committee, therefore, would like the Government to see as to why the funds
for setting up of convention centres are not being utilized. The Committee, also notes that
despite of enough funding in the NE region there is dearth of basic facilities there and even
the projects sanctioned by Ministry of Tourism is not getting good responses.
Tax Structure
108. One of the bottlenecks in achieving the full potential of tourism sector in India is the high
incidence and multiplicity of taxes that has led to tourist packages being out-priced in comparison
to those available for competing destinations. The Ministry of Tourism informed that they had

21
recommended the following incentives, concessions and taxations to the Ministry of Finance to be
incorporated in the budget of 2012-13 for addressing the issues:
/head2rightDeemed Export Status for Foreign Exchange Earnings Inbound Tour Operators.
/head2rightExtension of Income Tax Benefit under section 35 AD of the Income Tax Act 1961
to Govt. approved Service Providers.
/head2rightExtension of Income Tax Benefit under section 35 AD of the Income Tax Act 1961
to classified Heritage Hotels.
/head2rightRollback of Service Tax on Hotels and Air Conditioned Restaurants.
/head2rightExtension of Income Tax Benefit under section 35 AD of the Income Tax Act 1961
for Hotel Projects adding at least 25% more rooms.
109. The following incentives, concessions and taxations have been announced in the Union
Budget of 2012-13 for tourism and hospitality sector:
/head2rightInclusion of hotels in the harmonized master list of infrastructure sub-sector.
/head2rightApplicability of incentives under Section 35 AD of IT Act 1961 for hotel owners and
franchises.
110. The Ministry informed that inclusion of hotels in the harmonized master list of
infrastructure sub sector and applicability of incentives under section 35 AD of IT Act 1961 for
hotel owners and franchises has been announced in the Budget 2012-13.
111. In the Working Group Report pertaining to Ministry of Tourism it was stated  that in
majority of the tourist destinations abroad, the luxury tax is ranging from 5 to 7 percent only,
however, it is 4 to 20 percent in various states of India. The Committee observed that affordable
destinations are major tourism attractions for medium and low income tourists. However it is more
important that the tourists facilities also should not be compromised in the effort of making it
affordable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tax incentives should be as
pragmatic as to generate maximum income. At the same time, there should not be any
compromise on the quality of the services provided.
112. The Committee observes that the investment linked tax incentive for new hotels of
two star category and above anywhere in India need to be reviewed so that tax incentive
for hotels is available for below 2 star accommodation and the domestic tourism mostly
consisting of middle class are also benefitted.
113. In the XII plan working group report it is stated that the tax structure varies from State
to State and ranges from 25-30% for hotel accommodation, 25-60% on food and beverages and
20-25 % on road travel. The present tax structure, in addition to making the packages costly,
obstructs the seamless movement of tourists across the states.
114. The Committee observes that the broad scope of economic activities involved in
tourism enables wider participation of people in its growth including the participation of the
informal sector.  However, one of the major constraints to the tourism growth is multiplicity
of tax with high rates. The Committee therefore recommends that adequate tax exemptions
may be given to the tourism sector to ensure its growth in all the possible areas of the
country. Therefore, the Committee also recommends that both the Central and State
Governments should work out a uniform tax structure in the tourism sector.
115. Ministry of Tourism informed that in collaboration with the Ministry of Road Transport &
Highways and the State Governments of NCT of Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana & Uttar Pradesh has

22
made an arrangement whereby taxes could be collected centrally at each of the four starting nodes
at Delhi, Gurgaon, Jaipur & Agra in such a way that the taxes thus collected are to be apportioned
and the tourist coach/car would be allowed unhindered movement in the Golden Triangle.
116. The Committee notes the steps taken for seamless travel which was initiated during
the Commonwealth Games to facilitate tourists by the NCT of Delhi, Rajasthan, Haryana
and Uttar Pradesh and recommends that similar exercise should be taken to emulate the
model by other States.
117. The Committee was further informed that consequent to the meeting of the Task Force of
the 34
th Transport Development Council on 13.10.2011, a group of representatives from Ministry
of Tourism, State Governments, AIMTC, CII, ITTA and NIC has been formed to study and
recommend measures for ensuring seamless movement of goods and passengers across the
country, among other things.
118. Subsequently, in the meeting of the 34
th Transport Development Council (TDC) held on
07.02.2012, the Ministry of Tourism recommended as follows:
/head2rightMultiple tax structures in various States severely cramp seamless movement causing
discomfort to tourists. A simplified/uniform and rational tax structure cutting across all
the States/Union Territories have to be implemented on top priority.
/head2rightA system of single window payment of taxes through which tax can be collected
centrally and apportioned to states, has to be implemented to overcome the bottlenecks
of multiple inter – state road transport barriers.
/head2rightIt is recommended that an online transaction system be instituted within one year to
facilitate smooth movement of tourist traffic and avoid delays and inconvenience to
tourists.
119. The Committee notes that the above recommendations of the Ministry of Tourism for
rationalised tax structure; introduction of a system of single point payment of taxes and
online transaction system for smooth traffic movement merit due considerations. The
Committee therefore recommends that Ministry of Tourism should further pursue the
matter with all the State Governments and Union Territories to avoid multiple tax
structures and provide single window payment of taxes for tourism and tourist operators.
120. The Committee was informed that the proposal for allocation of a separate “TV” series
registration for tourist vehicles and one time/annual payment of taxes would facilitate smooth
movement of tourist traffic as it would do away with the requirement to stop for payment of taxes
at State borders. Ministry of Tourism recommended the implementation of a separate “TV” series
registration for tourist vehicles in the long run. The Committee also supports the view of the
Ministry to provide “TV” series registration for tourist vehicles and one time/annual
payment of taxes to be implemented by all the concerned agencies without any delay.
Environmental Issues and Eco Tourism
121. The Ministry of Tourism commissioned surveys of Resorts, Hotels, Lodges, Camps and
Guest Houses in and around following National Parks under the initiative “Tigers – Our National
Beauties” to assess the impact of tourism on them:
/head2rightKaziranga National Park,
/head2rightKanha National Park,
/head2rightBandavgarh National Park,

23
/head2rightPench Tiger Reserve
/head2rightMudumalai Wild Life Sanctuary.
122. The findings of these surveys indicated mushrooming of Resorts, Hotels, Lodges, Camps
and Guest Houses in and around these parks in an unplanned manner, blocking of wildlife
corridors, lack of eco-friendly practices in management of many Resorts, Hotels, Lodges, Camps
and Guest Houses. The reports of these surveys have been shared with the Ministry of
Environment and Forests for necessary action. The Ministry of Tourism has constituted a
Committee for finalizing the guidelines relating to eco-tourism in and around Protected Areas.
123. The Committee recommends that the Committee constituted for the purpose should
finalize the report in time bound manner and make stringent laws to protect the wildlife
and protected areas.
124. On the coastal regulations and its impacts the Ministry informed that “the information
pertaining to the applicability of coastal area regulations from State to State has been requested
from the Ministry of Environment and Forests. The beach and backwater tourism is one of the
major areas of growth of tourism products. Our beaches have good potential to attract large
number of domestic & international tourists. Therefore the regulations do have impact on
development of beach tourism in the country.”
125. The Committee also notes that a comprehensive waste management system is lacking in
most of the tourist destinations. This will become a serious problem in the coming years because
of the increase in the number of tourists. The Committee also notes the there is  scarcity of water
in almost all tourist places and specially in Hilly areas. This problem  is very acute in places like
North Eastern Region, Coastal Region and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands. The Committee during
its recent visits also got many complaints. The Committee recommends that the Ministry
should  take up the matter at various levels with State and Municipalities to remove the
problem of  shortage of water and waste management. Eco- friendly toilets are the new
concept which may be explored.
126. The pollution caused by the plastic products need to be taken as a serious threat to
the environment and the locals and tourists should be made aware of the hazards it may
cause in the region. The Committee recommends that for tourists, carry-bags from local
handicrafts should be made available with slogans on environment and tourism.
Isolation of Island Region in Tourism Development
127. The Committee came to know that due to restriction in Island Zones, the tourism potential
is affected as very few projects are sanctioned. The Ministry of Tourism informed that  Andaman
& Nicobar Administration has taken up the matter for making amendments in the  Island Protection
Zone notification and the Administration has been pursuing it vigorously as all tourism projects have
been stuck due to the restriction imposed by it. The accommodation infrastructure in A&N islands
is insufficient as compared to its counterparts in other countries in the same region and the tourists
therefore prefer to go to other countries than visit A& N Islands.
128. Regarding infrastructure in Lakshdweep, the Committee was informed that all
accommodation facilities in the Islands are owned by the Union Territory Administration. There is
no private accommodation in the islands. The total rooms available are 221 in the Lakhshdweep.
Additional 60 tourist cottages are being constructed in the islands. It is proposed to construct 25
more tourist cottages each at Amini, Kiltan Chetlat and Bitra Islands, for which the  land acquisition
process is over. About 9,991 (9424 domestic and 567 foreign) tourists visited the Lakshadweep
Islands from 1
st Jan., 2011 to 31 st Dec., 2011.

24
129. The Committee notes with dismay that the tourism potential in the Islands in India
is, in fact  more than the popular tourist destinations like Thailand, Singapore, Hawai etc.
However, the insufficient facilities have marred the scope of these amazing Islands. So far,
there is no such guide map prepared for benefiting the scenic beauty of these areas as a
major tourist attraction. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a special tourism
focus should be given to the Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Islands for tourism
promotion.
130. The Committee is, however, of the view that tourism activities should not be allowed
to be detrimental to the environmental balance. The Committee is of the view that there
should be strict adherence to the environmental regulations while promoting tourism. Our
environmentally fragile areas could not be blindly opened for access to the tourists; however
the regulations should not be applied uniformly in a country like India where the diversity
of geographical distribution is maximum.
Cruise Tourism Potential
131. The Ministry of tourism informed that  cruise tourism is in its infancy in India. With the
Indian economy developing at a steady pace, middle class growing in number and possessing
increasing disposable incomes, Indians could also take on cruise tourism in a big way. India’s long
coast line and strong port positioning imparts a natural advantage to the country to attract
international cruise liners. As per research conducted by leading cruise industry associations, cruise
passengers are high spenders with the international average working out to $ 94 per cruise tourist
per port.
132. The Steering Committee of Ministry of Shipping, consisting of a representative of Ministry
of Tourism, constituted for addressing various issues pertaining to cruise shipping has identified
five ports to be developed-mormugao-Goa, Cochin, Mumbai Chennai and Mangalore. The need of
the hour is to start with a ‘hub-a home port’. Important considerations for a successful home port
include, suitable geographical location vis-à-vis other ports of visit, accessibility by air, a sizeable
local market and adequate port facilities and services. Mumbai is considered to be most apt for this
purpose as it has all the necessary features.
133. W aterways based tourism is well developed in various States like Kerala, Goa, Assam and
West Bengal. The important river cruises are in the Brahmaputra in Assam and in the Ganges on
the routes Kolkata-Varanasi and Kolkata Sundarbans. India has tourism destinations in its interiors,
many of which are connected by rivers. Developing river cruises that connect these destinations
would not only create the access that is so important for cruise tourism, but would also enable
India to strongly position its tourism destinations and its exotic heritage.
134. Ministry of Tourism provides funds to Major Ports for development of cruise tourism.
However, so far only Mormugao Port Trust has submitted project for financial assistance. The
Committee is of the view that the scheme need to be discussed with all the Ports and
appropriate initiative may be taken to implement the cruise tourism projects in all the Ports.
135. The Committee was also informed of the high taxation rates for Yatch, boats, ships which
are registered in India. This leads to people preferring to go to other countries. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the tax structure should be rationalized to attract more tourists
from abroad.
136. The Committee had the occasion to visit cruise terminals at some of the ports. The
Committee noted the absence of basic facilities and poor maintenance of the terminals. The
Committee recommends that to make cruise tourism success in India there is need to make
the terminals more accessible and attractive.

25
137. The Committee recommends that the well developed water ways in the states like
Kerala, Goa, Maharashtra, Assam , in the Kolkata- Varanasi route and Kolkata Sunderbans
need to be focused for cruise tourism facilities. The Port Trusts of Goa, Cochin, Mumbai,
Chennai and Mangalore may be financially aided for fulfilling the ‘hub- a home port”
concept.
138. The Committee notes that in the Western Coast down through Sindhudurg to Goa
have beautiful virgin beaches which are untapped and are equally attractive as overseas
destinations like Singapore to Caribbean and to Mediterranean. The Committee
recommends that a sea route from Mumbai down to Goa  and Mangalore connecting all
these beaches need to be developed which has tremendous tourism potential.
139. The Committee also recommends that appropriate Rules and Regulations may be
formulated for  regulating  cruise tourism to ensure planned growth of the sector. Further,
there is need to put strict rules for ensuring safety measures such as provision of safety
equipments like life jackets, trained manpower etc.
140. The Committee during its visit also noted that there is lack of well maintained boats
and small cruises in A&N Islands. The Committee recommends that the boats should be
upgraded to attract more tourists in A&N Islands.

Another positive outcome has been the fact that with the Civil Aviation Ministry we have
