Special Accelerated Road Development Programme in the North-Eastern Region
(SARDP-NE)
35. The Committee was informed that appreciating the need for accelerated development of
roads and with a view to developing economy of this region in a big way, the Ministry has
formulated a special programme for accelerated road development in the region covering 10141 km.
length of National Highways, State roads and GS roads which is called as ‘Special Accelerated
Road Development Programme in North-East’ (SARDP-NE).  The programme has been
conceptualized and initiated with the following objectives:
• To connect all State capitals with improved/upgraded National Highways.
• To provide connectivity to all the 
88 District Headquarters of the NE Region. Since 23
District Headquarters are already connected to or located on National Highways, the
remaining 
62 District Headquarters are proposed to be connected to National Highways
through improved State roads under SARDP-NE. (2 DHQ are proposed to be connected
by 2 lane road under NH(O).
• To improve connectivity to the neighbouring countries.

13
• To provide road connectivity to backward and remote area of NE Region to boost
socio-economic development.
• To improve some of the important roads of strategic importance.
36. The programme has been divided into 3 parts, Phase ‘A’, Arunachal Pradesh Package of
Roads and Highways and Phase ‘B’.
/head2rightPhase ‘A’ of the programme, covers 4099 km. out of which 2041 km. length is National
Highways and 2058 km. length is of State roads and GS roads. The target for
completion of roads under this Phase is by the year 2013-14. So far, sub-projects
aggregating to 2389 km. have been sanctioned by the Ministry for Rs. 10,164 crore and
improvement of about 775 km. length has been completed so far.
/head2rightThe Arunachal Pradesh Package of Roads and Highways was approved for
implementation by the Cabinet on 09.01.2009. The Package covers 2319 km., out of
which 1472 km. length is National Highways and 847 km. length is State road, GS
roads and Strategic roads. The target for completion of roads under this Phase is by
the year 2014-15. So far, sub-projects aggregating to 1227 km. have been sanctioned
by the Ministry for an amount of Rs. 7404 crore and are in various stage of progress.
/head2rightPhase ‘B’ comprises 35 roads with an aggregate length of 3723 km. Approval to
undertake DPR preparation has been given by the Cabinet. Implementation of Phase ‘B’
of SARDP-NE would be taken up during the 12
th Five Year Plan as suggested by the
Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance, due to paucity of funds during the 11 th
Five Year Plan.

that the Government in February 2009 has approved a scheme for development of 5477 km.
roads in 34 Districts of 8 States affected by Left Wing Extremism under Road Requirement Plan-
I (RRP-I) at an estimated cost of Rs.7300 crore. So far, the detailed estimates for 197 projects
covering 5339 km. length have been sanctioned at an estimated cost of Rs. 7343 crore. Out of
these, 168 projects covering 4511 km. length costing Rs. 5939 crore have been awarded. Up to
March 2012, development work in 1335 km. length has been completed and expenditure incurred
is Rs. 1891 crore.

was informed that poor response of contractors in Gadchiroli (Maharashtra), Bastar
(Chhatisgarh), Malkangiri (Odisha) and some parts of Jharkhand, delay in project preparation due
to inability to conduct field surveys in some areas in Chhattisgarh State owing to security
reasons, security concerns for man and machinery at work site, frequent call of strike/bandh and
threats by naxals leading to stoppage of work and lack of capabilities to take up the work by
State Public Works Departments are the main issues which delay the implementation of this
scheme.
48. The Committee was further informed on the following initiatives taken by the Ministry to
implement the LWE programme:
(i) The State Governments have been asked to initiate the tendering process in advance
after technical approval of the individual projects. This has resulted in early award of
works and taking up the construction work immediately after sanction of the
projects.
(ii) Keeping in view the poor response during tendering for the works in Gadchiroli
district in Maharashtra, the qualification criteria for eligibility of the contractors have
been relaxed to encourage their participation in tendering. In some projects in
Gadchiroli, where no response was received during tendering, the estimates for
nearby stretches have been clubbed so that the big contractors having manpower
skills, equipments and finance could bid for these projects. These projects have been
awarded.

16
(iii) In some projects in Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand, where response was not received
during tendering, splitting has been allowed to encourage the participation of local
contractors.
(iv) Regular monitoring of LWE works is being done in the Ministry to sort out the issues
in implementation.
49. The Committee was further informed that stretches for Road Requirement Plan-II of
LWE have been finalized by Ministry of Home Affairs based on priority indicated by various
State Governments. The new plan will cover 7,294 kms. for development at a cost of
Rs.10,700 crores.
50. The Committee finds that major portion of roads developed under LWE scheme are
State roads and the development of these roads need a great deal of coordination with State
Governments. Though the project was started with a target of development of 5477 km.
roads in 34 districts of 8 States affected by Left Wing Extremism at an estimated cost of
Rs. 7300 crore in 2009, the development work in 1335 km. length only could be completed
with an expenditure of Rs. 1891 crore, till March, 2012. The Committee feels that with such
speed of execution of projects, the completion of the programme will be delayed with an
increase in the cost of project in the coming years. The Committee feels that an efficient
monitoring mechanism with the involvement of concerned States is the need of the hour to
ensure proper utilization of funds and speedy implementation of projects. The Committee
is of the view that delay in the execution of these projects may defeat the very purpose of
formulating the project. These areas are badly in need of development. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that all out efforts be made to construct the roads in those areas
within the targeted period.

Roads of Inter-state connectivity and economic importance
74. The Committee was informed that 10% of the shares of CRF for State roads are earmarked
for development of roads under Ministry’s scheme for improvement of state roads of inter-state
connectivity and economic importance. With the revamped Central Road Fund coming into force,
it has been decided that the road/bridge projects of inter-state connectivity will be fully funded and
projects of economic importance will be funded to the extent of 50% by the Government of India.
Broadly, the following categories of road/bridge projects are eligible for grant of assistance under
the scheme:
(i) Inter-state roads/bridges necessary for ensuring through communication
(ii) Roads/bridges connecting national highways
(iii) Roads/bridges required for opening up new areas for economic growth where railway
facilities cannot be provided in the near future.
(iv) Roads/bridges which would contribute materially to the rapid development, for
instance in hilly areas and significantly rich areas.
75. Funds under the CRF scheme are allocated by Planning Commission from the cess collected
on High Speed Diesel and Petrol by Ministry of Finance. The funds are distributed by Planning
Commission among three Ministries viz. Ministry of Rural Development for development of Rural
Roads, Ministry of Railways for ROB on railway crossings and to Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways for development of National Highways, State Roads including roads of Economic
Importance and Inter-State Connectivity (EI&ISC).

Rs. 249.75 crore. This was enhanced to Rs. 254.30 crore at R.E. 2011-12. During 2012-13, the

requirement would be assessed and enhanced outlay may be proposed at R.E. stage subject to
outcome of such assessments.

Maintenance and Repairs of National Highways:
79. The maintenance of National Highways is of paramount importance. Under this head, funds
are provided for the preservation and proper upkeep of National Highways all over the country.
Over the past six decades, the volume of traffic on Indian roads has increased exponentially;
between 1950-51 and 2002-03, the freight traffic increased 101 times and passenger traffic 132
times. During this period, the share of the road sector in total freight traffic increased from 13.8%
to 62.9% and passenger traffic from 15.4% to 90.2%. However, notwithstanding the vast network
of roads and of National Highways, there are serious concerns about their quality and capacity. The
rise in labour wages and steep increase in prices of materials, particularly, of petroleum products
in recent years are reflected in the high cost of maintenance and repair of National Highways.  For
the year 2012-13 funds for Maintenance and Repairs have been proposed at Rs.
 1,998.03  crore for
the National Highways.
80. It was noted that an amount of Rs. 1029.31 crores was allocated in B.E. 2011-12 which
was increased to Rs. 1329.56 crores at R.E. stage for maintenance of national highways under
non-plan head. Now Rs. 2000.09 crores has been allocated for the next fiscal. When it was asked
on the reasons for such variations and adequacy of this allocation for this important sector it was
informed that the allocations that are available annually for Maintenance & Repair (M&R) of
National Highways (NHs) are of the order of about 40% of the actual requirements as per the
Ministry’s stipulated norms i.e. available allocations are of the order of about Rs. 1,000 crore as
against the estimated fund requirement of Rs. 2,800 crore as per the Ministry’s Norms for
Maintenance of NHs. Proposal for additional fund requirement may be submitted at R.E. stage
based upon the assessments of the progress of works at that stage, extent of new restoration and
repair works required to be undertaken during the year.
81. The Committee feels that maintenance and repair of national highways is not getting
the attention it deserves. The Committee notes that Rs.1998.03 crore has been allocated for
maintenance and repair of national highways but it is only 66 % of the requirement
projected by the Ministry. The Committee feels that the ceiling of allocation of 40% of the
actual requirements as per the Ministry’s stipulated norms should be revisited and
recommends that it needs to be suitably augmented as per the requirement. The annual
addition to National highways network should also be given due consideration for allocation
of funds for maintenance and repair. Funds should not be a stumbling block in carrying out
the repair work. The Committee is of the view that due importance should be given by the
Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance for the maintenance of national highways
in coming years.
82. The Committee recommends that in future plans should be prepared under which
new roads may be constructed only after ensuring the availability of fund for the
maintenance and repair of existing roads.

V ehicular Pollution, Road safety management, Road Transport Regulation and
Administration, Alternate Fuel, Road Transport Planning etc.

92. The proposed allocation in the Annual Plan 2012-13 under this scheme is Rs. 215.15  crore.
93. The Committee feels that the Ministry will not be in a position to satisfy itself by
merely implementing above mentioned measures for road safety unless it properly
implements the Central Motor Vehicles Rules and Act. The Committee notes that the
mandatory fitment of Auto dipper device – an essential safety device needed to be fitted on
the vehicle for a safer night travel, to enforce Rule 106 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules
1989 and Section 110(1)(j) of Central Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 has not been implemented
strictly in the country so far. The Committee also expresses its disappointment over the
delay in introduction of re-drafted Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act which consists major
recommendations of the Standing Committee on measures to strengthen road safety and
related issues.
Model Driving Training Schools
94. When the Committee raised the issue of the status of revised scheme for setting up of
Model Driving Training schools, it was informed that the Ministry has finalized a revised scheme
for setting up of Institute of Driving Training and Research Centre (IDTRs). Under the new
scheme, ten model Institutes of Driving Training & Research (IDTRs) with an estimated amount
of Rs. 140 crore are being set up on PPP model. Sanction has already been accorded by the
Ministry for setting up IDTRs in Himachal Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra,
Gujarat, Haryana, Tamil Nadu, Bihar and Tripura. A proposal for setting up an IDTR in UP is under
consideration.
95. The Ministry  intends that the IDTR should serve as a “Mother” Institute with a cluster of
small institutes in the surrounding districts/areas. The Central Government will sanction and finance
one Mother/Model Institute for each state & union territory. However, one such Institute cannot
meet the demand/supply gap in each State/UTs. State Governments are expected to sanction/finance
the cluster Institutes by presenting the Model Institute as a business model for replication in the
private sector.
96. The Committee finds that Rs.120 crores was allocated for refresher training to
drivers in unorganized sector and human resource development for the year 2011-12. It was
reduced to Rs.28.50 crores at RE stage of which the Ministry was able to spend Rs.10.90
crores only. This clearly shows a tardy implementation of the scheme by the Ministry of
Road Transport and Highways. The revised scheme for setting up of Institute of Driving
Training and Research Centre (IDTRs) has not seen any progress and the establishment of
such centers are delayed due to one or other reasons. The Committee also feels that the
Ministry should involve the State governments for establishment of more and more such
training centres. The Committee feels that imparting of training to drivers in unorganized
sector is one of the major steps toward road safety in the country, but it depends on the
Ministry’s willingness and planning to materialize it.
97. The Committee notes that the vehicles manufacturers have a role to play in training
the drivers, it is their duty to ensure their safety also. Every manufacturer in the country
should be asked to open training centers for drivers in areas wherever their showrooms
exist. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Government should make it
compulsory for the vehicle manufacturers to open driving training centers. The Committee
hopes that active involvement of major auto manufacturers in this novel programme will
help the Ministry in attaining the objective behind the setting up of Institute of Driving
Training and Research Centre (IDTRs).

National Highway Accident Relief Scheme
98. With a view to provide immediate medical assistance to the victims of road accidents and
removing damaged vehicles from the National Highways, a National Highways Patrolling Scheme
was introduced in 1993-94. Under this scheme, State Government/NGOs were provided financial
assistance for the purchase of cranes and ambulances for removal of vehicles involved in the
accidents from the national highways and providing immediate medical assistance to the road
accident victims. However, keeping in view the delays in the purchase of equipments in some cases
and non-furnishing of utilization certificates thereof, the scope of the scheme was amended in
2000-2001 to provide equipment instead of cash grant. Non-Government Organizations were also
included in the ambit of the scheme. During the year 2011-12, 40 cranes and 36 small/medium
sized cranes have been provided to the States and Union Territories.
99. To a query on the ambulances purchased under the National Highway Accident Relief
Service Scheme during 2011-2012 it was informed that during the year 2011-12, no ambulance
could be purchased by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. After finalizing the
specifications, order for supply of 70 Advanced Life Support ambulances was placed on
M/s. AEON Medical Pvt. Ltd. after following the prescribed procurement procedures. The firm has
already fabricated the prototype and final inspection of the ambulance has been completed by an
expert committee. These ambulances will be supplied to 70 Trauma care centres being developed
by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare along Golden Quadrilateral, North-south and East-west
corridors of National Highway Development Project (NHDP) during the year 2012-13.
100. During the deliberations of the Committee non-availability of cranes and ambulances at toll
collecting plazas to meet emergencies was raised. It was replied that the Ministry operates a
scheme namely, National Highway Accident Relief Service Scheme (NHARSS) under which the
Ministry provides cranes and ambulances to States/ UTs for relief and rescue measures in the
aftermath of accidents by way of evacuating road accident victims to nearest medical aid centre
and for clearing the accident site.
101. NHAI through concessionaire is providing well equipped Ambulance with requisite para-
medical staff and necessary medical equipment at average 50 km. of completed stretch under
Operations and Maintenance contract to provide immediate help to accident victims and to take
them to the nearest Trauma care centre/hospital.
102. The Committee notes that the Ministry was able to spend Rs.21.01crores only out of
the allocation of Rs.31.75 crores at RE level for the year 2011-12. Now Rs.30 crores has
been allocated for the year 2012-13 for the purpose of National Highways Accident Relief
Scheme. The Committee finds that reduction in allocation for the current fiscal and the
inability to spend the allocated money in the last year, shows the lack of seriousness of the
Ministry towards providing medical assistance to victims of road accidents and strengthening
of National Highways Patrolling Scheme. The Ministry’s inability in purchasing ambulances
during the last year citing procedural delays will definitely put lives of users of national
highways at higher risk.
Setting up of Inspection and Certification Centres
103. The Committee was informed that the Central Government has the power to fix the age of
motor vehicles for using different purposes under Section 59 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The
age of some categories of vehicles for the purpose of tourist permit and national permit are being
fixed under Rules 82 and 88 of Central Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Fixation of age of vehicle would
also be not advisable, keeping in view the socio-economic condition of country. A vehicle can ply
on the road as long as it meets the requirements of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and Central

28
Vehicles Rules, 1989 with regard to safety, emission and fitness norms. As per the norms, a
transport vehicle has to undergo fitness test every year after two years of the date of initial
registration. The Ministry has decided to put in place a proper inspection and maintenance system
to identify the vehicles which do not meet the emission and safety norms. These centers are
required to be set up in various states with Public, Private and Partnership. A model of automated
Inspection and Certification (I&C) Centre was designed and a scheme for setting up of one such
centre in ten states on a pilot basis was approved. Nine model Inspection and Certifications centres
have already been sanctioned by this Ministry and some these are at various stages of
implementation. During the year 2012-13, allocation of Rs.90.00 crore has been proposed under the
scheme.
104. The Committee finds that Rs.12.43 crores was spent against an allocation of Rs.84.00
crores at BE stage which was drastically reduced to Rs.14.00 crore at RE stage. Again a sum
of Rs.90.00 crores has been allocated for the current fiscal. The Committee fails to
understand the logic behind such a huge variation in allocation under this head. The
Committee may be furnished the reasons for non-utilization of funds and apprised of the
status of model Inspection and Certification centers sanctioned so far and the probable
dates of commencement of functioning of such centers.
Strengthening of Public Transport System
105. The Committee was informed that decline of public transport has been one of the failures of
our transport planning over the years. The percentage of buses in the total fleet of vehicles has come
down from more than 11% in 1951 to 1.1% in 2006. This leads to increase in the personalized
transport which in turn has number of adverse consequences such as congestion, pollution and
accidents apart from being inequalitarian as the poor get excluded from transport services. In order
to reverse this situation, provisions have been made in the Eleventh Five Year Plan at the central level
to extend financial assistance to help the States to strengthen their public transport system including
application of Information Technology like automatic fare collection system based on Global
Positioning System. However such financial assistance shall be restricted to those States which
undertake measures for reforms in the public transport system. The scheme was approved by the
Government in March, 2010 and the scheme was made effective from 15
th March, 2010. During the
year 2012-13, allocation of Rs.30.00 crore has been proposed under the scheme.
106. When it was asked about the steps taken to strengthen the Public Transport System in the
country during 2011 and also on the financial assistance given to State owned Public transport
undertakings during 2011-12 it was informed that with the objective of putting in place a better
public transport mechanism which could be able to provide world-class passenger bus service
across the country, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways introduced a Scheme during XI
Plan, namely, ‘Central Assistance to States/UTs for strengthening Public Transport System’
effective from 15.03.2010. The basic scope/objective of this Scheme was as under:–
(i) To provide financial assistance for use of latest technologies such as GPS/GSM
based Vehicle Tracking System, Computerized Reservation System, Automatic Fare
Collection System, Electronic Ticket Vending Machines, Inter-modal Fare Integration,
Passenger Information System etc. for services covering inter-city and mofussil
areas.
(ii)  To provide financial assistance for preparation of total mobility plan for the entire
State.

National Road Safety Board
109. The Committee was informed that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways had earlier
introduced a bill in Rajya Sabha on 04.05.2010 to establish a National Road Safety and Traffic
Management Board. However, the Parliamentary Standing Committee returned the Bill with the
observation that the present Bill may be withdrawn and the Government should come out with a
comprehensive legislation with a holistic perspective that addresses the entire gamut of road safety.
In view of the observations of the Standing Committee, it is proposed to set up a Directorate of
Road Safety at the centre to attain these objectives. The Directorate will have powers to order
recall of vehicles which expose the driver or rider to unreasonable risk. Also, similar mechanisms
are needed at the State level through the Task Forces of the State Road Councils and District Road
Safety Councils.
110. The Committee finds that the proposed National Road Safety Board is being delayed
by the Ministry due to its inability to take a major policy decision. The Committee feels
that appointing committees and task force one after other, to study the issue or sort out
the shortcomings is not going to address the issues involving road safety. The Committee
hopes that the Ministry will set up the mechanism at the earliest in consultation with the
state governments to minimize road accidents. The Committee urges the Ministry to give
importance road safety as it is being given to development of national highways.
General Observations
111. The Committee after examining the demands of the Ministry of Road Transport and
Highways finds that the allocation for the Ministry needs a relook at the time of RE stage.
The Ministry was not able to convince the Planning Commission in getting the required
funds for various projects mainly due to the underutilization of funds for the year 2011-12
and also reduction of funds for various schemes at RE level during 2011-12. The Committee
feels that the Ministry should improve its record in fund utilization and advise its project
executing agencies accordingly.
112. The Committee feels that the Ministry should do its homework to identify the
projects under various heads before going for Budget Estimates. During the last year Rs.400
crores was estimated for Road Transport sector but was reduced to Rs.150 crores at RE
level. Such drastic cut in funds will not benefit the Ministry in the long run for carrying
out major programmes under research and development, road safety and other related
issues concerning road transport.
113. The Committee hopes that an effective coordination mechanism at the central level
will ensure hassle free clearances for road projects and achievement of targets within the
prescribed time. The Committee feels that the Ministry will impress the State Governments
to give necessary clearances for the road projects in time so that projects are completed
without cost over run.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS — AT A GLANCE
Eleventh Plan (2007-12)
The Committee finds that the Ministry of Road Transport was able to get
Rs.78,158.00 crores at BE as against the approved Eleventh Plan outlay was Rs.71,830.00
crores.  The major component for the enhanced plan outlay was the introduction of special
programme for development of roads in LWE affected areas in 2009 for which Rs.2,325.00
crores was allocated. The Ministry was able to spend Rs.74,607.36 crores against the total
budgetary support of Rs.78,158.00 crores (BE) for the whole plan period. The Committee,
thus, notes a saving of around Rs. 3500.00 crores. Such savings in infrastructure projects
as development and maintenance of national highways should have been avoided. The
Committee feels that the Ministry’s performance in spending allocation for certain projects
needs lot of improvement. The Ministry was able to get Rs.400.00 crores (BE) for
development of Vijayawada-Ranchi Road but they could spend Rs.67.25 crores only for the
whole plan period. Another case is the development of Mughal road in Jammu and Kashmir
for which the total plan outlay Rs.127.50 crore was reduced to Rs.50.00 crores (BE) for the
plan period. But the Ministry was not able to spend any money on the project for the period.
The Ministry’s ability to spend allocations under non-plan heads for the Eleventh Plan
period was also not very good. Their spending on the development of information
technology, machinery equipments, R&D planning studies, training and other charges are
not very encouraging though their allocations were small only.  The Committee hopes that
the Ministry will take corrective measures to improve its performance in Twelfth Plan
period. (Para 9)
Annual Plan 2011-12
The Committee finds that performance of the Ministry in spending the allocated
funds under both plan and non-plan was not satisfactory during the year 2011-12. The
reasons submitted by the Ministry for savings of fund under various heads at the end of
last fiscal are of routine nature and repetitive. The Committee finds that Rs.400.00 crores
(BE), allocated as plan outlay to Road Transport sector, was reduced to Rs.150.00 crore at
RE stage, of which the Ministry was able to spend Rs.123.41 crores only. The Committee
feels that such a reduction in RE stage for a plan outlay should have been avoided. Road
transport sector consists of major programmes relating to road safety, trauma care, human
resources development, training, etc. The Ministry could have ensured that the allocation
was spent to the maximum extent. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons
submitted by the Ministry for under utilization of funds. Savings on the allocation shows the
failure on part of the Ministry in proper planning and execution of various road projects.
(Para 14)
Annual Plan 2012-13
The Committee finds that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has been

32
allocated Rs.33,000 crores (BE) as annual plan for 2012-13 as against Rs.37,500 crores (BE)
plan outlay for the year 2011-12. It means a reduction in fund allocation for various
programmes under the Ministry. The Committee feels that substantial deduction in the
outlay projected by the Ministry under the component of NH (O) and under NHAI
(Investment) will slow the pace of the development of national highways under NHDP and

repair and maintenance is a callous wastage of national resources. (Para 25)

The Committee would like to be informed about the progress of all the Externally
Aided projects, the scheduled date of completion and the Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of
these projects. (Para 28)

The Committee is of the view that development of Non-NHDP national highways are
as important as of national highways covered under various programmes of NHDP. The
Committee was informed that 21% of the existing national highways network is single lane
or intermediate lane. Developments of these national highways to minimum two-lane
standards need huge investments. The Committee notes that against a projected
requirement of Rs.8,848.25 crores for this head, the Ministry was able to get Rs.6,042.80
crores for the year 2012-13. As a result thereof the NHAI may be forced to divert cess
earmarked for NHDP to development of national highways under NH(O). This diversion will
delay the development of both NHDP and non-NHDP national highways. The Committee
hopes that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways must impress the Planning
Commission to allocate more funds for the development of non-NHDP national highways at
RE stage. The Committee feels that the development of non-NHDP national highways will
get due attention from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Planning
Commission in the coming years. The Committee may be apprised of the status of
construction of rail-cum-road Bridge at Ganga, Munger for which the construction works
were started way back in 2002. (Para 33)
Development of National Highways in North-Eastern Region
The Committee notes that the Ministry has a special programme for the development
of national highways in North-Eastern parts of the country.  The Committee hopes that the
Ministry will take up the funding of Phase ‘B’ of SARDP-NE comprising 35 roads with an
aggregate length of 3723 km. during the 12
th Plan with Planning Commission aggressively.
The Committee also hopes that the Ministry will improve its performance in spending the
allocated funds as also in achieving the targets set for development of national highways in
NE region in coming years so that economic growth, trade and tourism are not affected due

33
to non-availability of motorable road in this part of the country. Many of the reasons for
delay in execution of projects at various places of North-East need individualized attention
and local solutions. The Committee recommends that to remove the bottlenecks, authorities
and agencies concerned may be approached and activated. (Para 44)
Special Programme for Development of Roads in the Left Wing Extremism (LWE) Affected
Areas
The Committee finds that major portion of roads developed under LWE scheme are
State roads and the development of these roads need a great deal of coordination with State
Governments. Though the project was started with a target of development of 5477 km.
roads in 34 districts of 8 States affected by Left Wing Extremism at an estimated cost of
Rs. 7300 crore in 2009, the development work in 1335 km. length only could be  completed
with an expenditure of Rs. 1891 crore, till March, 2012. The Committee feels that with such
speed of execution of projects, the completion of the programme will be delayed with an
increase in the cost of project in the coming years. The Committee feels that an efficient
monitoring mechanism with the involvement of concerned States is the need of the hour to
ensure proper utilization of funds and speedy implementation of projects. The Committee
is of the view that delay in the execution of these projects may defeat the very purpose of
formulating the project. These areas are badly in need of development. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that all out efforts be made to construct the roads in those areas
within the targeted period. (Para 50)
National Highways Authority of India
The Committee finds that NHAI is not in a position to complete any project whether
it is NHDP or non-NHDP within the scheduled period, although financing has not been an
issue for them. NHAI is adding projects after projects without achieving the targets in the
older ones. The much publicized GQ and NS and EW corridors under NHDP have not been
completed till date. The much talked about construction of 20 kms. per day has been a
distant dream so far. The Committee notes that as against 13.72 km. constructed in the
year 2009-10, it has dwindled to 10.15 km. in 2011-12. Such a slide in achieving this target
by NHAI shows their deficiency either in planning of programmes or proper execution of the
same. (Para 69)

Chairman for the last two years. It must be telling upon the implementation/award of our
road projects. (Para 70)

with four-lane Bridge. The Committee notes that one of the objectives of GQ project was
to connect all the capitals of the States through which the project passes. However, Patna
was not included in the project. The Committee may be apprised on the reasons for non-

national highways into four-lane without widening or developing bridges on those national
highways is not going to yield the desired result. (Para 71)

connectivity with national highways of the major ports in the country. The Committee
notes that delay in providing road connectivity to Kandla Port for a small stretch of 8 kms.

Report on the revised strategy for implementation of National Highways Development

NHAI will chalk out a workable solution to complete all the pending projects in time,
irrespective of its size, to minimize the cost over run. (Para 73)

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred Seventy Ninth Report  on Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its One Hundred Sixty Seventh Report
on ‘Functioning of National Museum’.
2. One Hundred Sixty Seventh Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented to the Parliament on the 10
th March,
2011 in Rajya Sabha and on 11 th March, 2011 in Lok Sabha.
3. The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its One
Hundred Sixty Seventh Report  were received from the Ministry of Culture on 24 th January, 2012.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report as its meeting held on the 17 th May 2012.
SITARAM YECHURY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
May 17, 2012 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Vaisakha 27, 1934  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One-Hundred Sixty Seventh Report on The
Functioning of National Museum of the Ministry of Culture which was presented on 10 th March,
2011 in Rajya Sabha and on 11 th March, 2011 in Lok Sabha.
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on the 24 th January, 2012
in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report, which have been
categorized as follows:–
(i) Recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry:
Para Nos. 16, 42, 62, 64, 67, 68, 70, 75 and 76 Total—9
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Ministry replies:
Para Nos. 5, 6, 23, 24, 30, 33 and 41 Total—7
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Ministry have not
been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos. 22, 31, 32, 36, 37, 46, 55, 56 and 57 Total—9
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry are
still awaited:
Para Nos. 58, 59, 63, 78 and 79 Total—5
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of those recommendations/observations
which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be furnished to it at the
earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken. The recommendations of the Committee contained in
the One Hundred and Seventy Seventh Report, action taken thereon by the Ministry and
recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has been given in the
succeeding paragraphs.
Closure of Galleries
5. The Committee is at loss to note that out of 26 galleries in the National Museum,
7 remained closed for 3 to 4 years, Manuscripts Gallery being closed for 8 years from 2003. The
Committee found that the reasons given were not convincing at all. For example, ‘Central Asian
Antiquities – II’ gallery after repairing of roof leakages, remained closed as the space of the gallery
was being used for storing the exhibition material. Some of the galleries were sealed by the
investigation agencies pending vigilance inquiries into theft cases. Decorative Arts–I gallery
remained closed due to storage of display materials. Another gallery – ‘Tanjavur Paintings’ could
not be opened because of shortage of synthetic moulding and other wooden material. Two
galleries–Musical Instruments and Wooden Carving – were remained closed due to roof leakage and

2
shortage of display material. Another gallery could not be opened after the demise of the Curator
in-charge of the gallery in 2008.
6. The Committee finds such excuses as shortage of display and other material, posts being
vacant, leakage, etc. for keeping the large number of galleries closed for long time, unacceptable.
It, in fact, reflects an utterly casual attitude as well as lack of proper planning. Problems mentioned
above, if taken up promptly and consistently, should have been undoubtedly sorted out within
reasonable time to complete the work. The Committee is of the view that if this is the state of
affairs in the National Museum situated in New Delhi, condition of museums in other cities cannot
be expected to be any better. The Committee emphasizes the need to sensitize the concerned
authorities to ensure that the problems enumerated above which led to the closure of almost 1/4
th
of the galleries of the National Museum, are addressed in time.
(Para 13 and 14 of the 167 th Report)
Reply of the Government
7. The Galleries were initially closed for various reasons viz. to undertake renovation, works,
to mount exhibition in the gallery, water seepage from roof, etc. Re-opening of the Galleries were
delayed because of reasons beyond the control of the National Museum such as water leakage from
roofs, delegated financial power of DGNM were very limited, i.e. only Rs. 1.00 lakh, etc. Beyond
this amount every file had to be moved seeking approval of the Integrated Finance Division of the
M/o Culture, which took more time. In April, 2011, the DGNM has been given enhanced financial
powers of Rs. 10.00 lakhs. Materials for renovation works have therefore been procured. In view
of this, most galleries are in the advanced stages of renovation and re-opening. Action for filling
up the vacant posts, is in progress.
8. Status of Action Taken to reopen the seven galleries, which have remained closed for
various reasons is as under:–
(i)
Musical Gallery:- This has been reopened in December, 2010.
(ii) Tanjavur Gallery:-  Over 70% renovation work has been completed. Action for
installation of improved lighting system and one large LCD TV is in progress. The
Gallery is expected to be reopened in the first quarter of 2012.
(iii) Wood Carving Gallery:- This gallery was closed for renovation of adjacent gallery i.e.
Musical instruments gallery (Musical Instruments were shifted to this Gallery).
Musical Instruments gallery was reopened in December, 2010. Thereafter, renovation
of Wood Carving Gallery was initiated. Dr. Chhaya Bhattacharya Haesner, Tagore
Fellow at National Museum and Dr. Charu S. Gupta, Dy. Director Crafts Museum,
New Delhi, who are the experts for this gallery were also consulted for renovation
works. Action for reopening of the Gallery is in progress. Lighting and layout has
been approved. Gallery is expected to be reopened in the second quarter of 2012.
(iv)
Central Asian Antiquties-II:- Technical Plan for the Gallery has been prepared with
inputs from Dr. Chhaya Bhattacharya-Haesner, Tagore Fellow working in the Central
Asian Antiquities. A concept note has also been submitted by her. Action for reopening
the gallery is in progress.
(v)
Tribal Art and North East Gallery:- Objects/Collections are on display in the Gallery.
Modern lighting system will be put in place besides some civil works. Gallery is
expected to be reopened in the second quarter of 2012.

3
(vi) Decorative Art Gallery:- Requisite civil and electrical works for building of 10-12 new
show cases, modern lighting system, etc. have been taken up and work is in progress.
For decipherment of inscriptions and informative labels, assistance of some Persian
scholars will be taken. Thereafter, a firm date for reopening the gallery will be fixed.
(vii) Manuscripts:- Gallery Renovation and reopening of Manuscripts gallery with the
existing one officer has been initiated.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
9. The Committee notes the status of work undergoing in various galleries. The
Committee hopes that the steps taken to open the closed Galleries will be completed in a
fixed time schedule. As regards need for obtaining financial sanction beyond Rs. 1 lakh
from IFD, the Committee finds it very low. The Committee is happy to know that this limit
has since been enhanced upto Rs. 10 lakhs and hopes that now the works should get
expedited faster. The Committee does not consider the water seepage from the roof to be
beyond the Ministry’s control; it was perhaps due to lack of required monitoring and
coordination with the CPWD authorities.
10. The Committee finds that the National Museum despite having a large building and a huge
collection in its possession, several of its galleries are closed mainly due to lack of adequate manpower,
essential logistics and proper maintenance. The Committee is also surprised to note that there are no
laid down guidelines with regard to the taking up of renovation of galleries of museums and the work
is taken up only when the problem has reached to an alarming stage which finally results in closure
of galleries. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Culture to explore the techniques and practices
available world-over for renovation of galleries and museums. The Committee recommends the
Government should frame guidelines for renovation of museums in the country in a fixed time schedule.
The guidelines may consist of details as to when and how the galleries will be taken for renovation
with a view to ensure that display of the collections continues without interruption. (Para 15, ibid)
Reply of the Government
11. Necessary action for re-opening of closed galleries and filling of vacant posts have been
taken. At present, there are no laid down guidelines with regard to taking up of renovation of
galleries of National Museum. However, renovation of galleries is taken up periodically. Government
has taken initiative on museum reform and a 14 Point agenda has been formulated to carry forward
the desired reforms in phases. National Museum is taking appropriate action in this regard.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12. The Committee would like to know if it is possible to have guidelines for renovation
of Galleries laid down and if yes, the reason for not having it done so far may be given.
The Ministry should share the 14 point Agenda formulated to carry forward the museum
reforms as well as the actions taken so far in this regard, with the Committee.
13. The Committee feels that every Museum should have some extra space so that in case any
gallery has to be closed due to renovation, etc., the collection from those galleries could be safely
shifted to unutilized space. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the idea of creating
additional space/galleries to display more number of collections in its possession, may be
considered and acted upon. (Para 16, ibid)

4
Reply of the Government
14. At present in the National Museum no additional space is available.  Out of the three phases,
two phases viz. Phase I and Phase II are complete. Phase-III of the National Museum will be taken
up as soon as the space occupied by ASI is vacated for which necessary action is in progress.
Suggestions of the committee has been noted for compliance when additional space is available.
Thereafter more number of collections will be displayed .
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
15. The Committee would like to know the progress regarding shifting of ASI as well as
roadmap for phase III project, if any.  However, the Committee notes that the work is still
to be started and depends on several ifs and buts and does not know how much space would
be generated after phase III.
MAINTENANCE OF THE NATIONAL MUSEUM
16. The Committee notes the problems faced in maintaining the building of the National
Museum as CPWD, it appears has not been able to do the job to the satisfaction of museum
authorities. Despite their consistent efforts, the problems of water logging, seepage, etc. continue
to persist. The Committee is of the view that the National Museum is not like any other building;
it houses lakhs of invaluable collections and precious items which need to be preserved and
maintained under perfect conditions. The CPWD has been engaged in building section since 1854
including handling of maintenance of building of hundreds of cultural institutions in the country.
By this time, CPWD must have acquired expertise in handling the maintenance works of the
Museum or similar institutions. The Committee recommends that a dedicated wing may be created
in the CPWD which can handle the work of maintenance of buildings of cultural institutions like
the National Museum. The Committee also recommends that the performance of the CPWD maybe
closely monitored and in case things do not improve the maintenance of the building of National
Museum and its various civil and electrical works may be taken away from CPWD and handed
over to some specialized and competent agencies preferably under the Government for better
maintenance and upkeep of the Museum building. (Para 22, ibid)
Reply of the Government
17. CPWD has been requested to create a dedicated wing for the maintenance of the National
Museum. Also, the National Museum is considering for entrusting Maintenance work to some
specialized agency as recommended. National Building Construction Corporation (NBCC) was
consulted. They stated that since the main constructions were not done by them, they showed certain
reservations in taking up maintenance work alone. However, when the major work for construction
of Phase-III would be taken-up/awarded to an agency (other than CPWD), maintenance works of the
entire Museum would also be awarded to such agency. In the meantime, the works of electrical and
civil divisions of CPWD have been closely monitored. Even though, both the electrical and civil
divisions of CPWD have improved their maintenance part, their performances are not completely
satisfactory since there have been some isolated seepage/leakage in two galleries.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
18. The Committee is of the view that since CPWD will remain the agency for

5
maintenance works of phase I and phase II, there is need for close liaison with them to
attend the work promptly. National Museum should also be able to alert CPWD in advance
before the monsoon period starts. All the staff should also be sensitized to bring even the
small seepage problem to CPWD’s notice before they become unmanageable. The
Committee hopes that with the construction of building at 3 rd phase, the things will
improve.
SECURITY
19. Another disturbing feature that came to the notice of the Committee was the closure of
galleries in the museum due to theft and vigilance cases. The Secretary, Department of Culture
informed the Committee that he was writing to the CBI about this. The Committee hopes that while
the investigative/enforcement agencies must do their work, the Ministry also needs to be seriously
looking into this aspect and ensuring that the acts of pilferage, theft, etc. do not recur at all.
Needless to say that such things do happen mainly because of lax of security and supervision by
the persons on the higher positions in the Museum administration. (Para 23, ibid)
20. The Committee has been expressing concerns about the security of museums from time to
time in its earlier reports. The Museums have highly valuable and precious collections which form
part of our rich and diverse heritage. The Committee, therefore, recommends to make use of the
best technology available to safeguard the museum to prevent theft or unwanted incidents. The
Committee hopes that the matter should be taken up with the investigative agencies to get things
expedited and to ensure that the gallery closed due to pending inquiry into theft be opened at the
earliest. (Para 24, ibid)
Reply of the Government
21. There has been no closure of any gallery due to theft. A vigilance case against three officers
of the National Museum was reported to Vigilance Section of the Ministry of Culture in 2005. The
case involved scrutiny and examination of lot of documents. Three officers of the National
Museum were charge sheeted and the case has been referred by Central Vigilance Section to the
CBI for preliminary investigation. As requested by CBI, files and documents were provided to them.
However, the disciplinary proceedings could not progress further, since the proceedings have been
stayed by the Central Administrative Tribunal in respect of two officers. The case has therefore,
not been finalized as yet. Further, as suggested by the Committee, the security systems of the
National Museum are being upgraded. In order to ensure a proper security of the National Museum
CCTV coverage in all the galleries, X-ray Scanning/baggage machine and Door Frame Metal
Detector (DFMD), have been proposed and bid were invited through open tender. Technical and
financial evaluation of these bids has been done and bidders/firms have been shortlisted. Since the
work involves expenditure of about 1.5 Crores, the process for obtaining financial concurrence has
been initiated.
Reply of the Government
22. In order to ensure foolproof security to check pilferage/theft of art works, National
Museum has already initiated action for installation of CCTV surveillance in all the galleries/stores,
X-ray scanning of baggage, Door Frame Metal Detector (DFMD) etc. The security systems of the
National Museum are being upgraded. In order to ensure a proper security of the National Museum
CCTV coverage in all the galleries, X-ray Scanning/baggage machine and Door Frame Metal

6
Detector (DFMD), have been proposed and bid were invited through open tender. Technical and
financial evaluation of these bids has been done and bidders/firms have been shortlisted.  Since the
work involves expenditure of about 1.5 Crores, the file has been submitted for obtaining financial
concurrence.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
23. The Committee notes the steps taken by the Ministry to upgrade the security system
and hopes that it would be completed in a fixed timeframe. The financial concurrence
sought in this regard may be expedited.
24. The Committee also recommends that latest security gadgets should be added on
regular basis with a view to improve the security in the Museum.
DISPLAY OF EXHIBITS
25. The Committee notes that out of 206000 collections with the National Museum, only 15681,
constituting 7.61 per cent of total collections, were on display. The Committee is not satisfied with
the number as well as selection of items on display in the National Museum. The Committee does
not agree with the idea of justifying lower display percentage on the basis of this percentage in
other museums. Although the Committee was not informed about this percentage in other world
museums, it however, learnt that display percentage in Louvre in France was about ten. Here also
it is less. The Committee was not informed about the capacity of the National Museum to have
items on display. The Committee feels that our efforts should be to have maximum of them on
display at a time to ensure maximum exposure of our rich and diverse heritage to the people.
Visitors, in fact, can not come to the National Museum again and again. (Para 30, ibid)
Reply of the Government
26. No Museum in the world displays its entire collections because of the fact that all the
collections are not worth to display. Only selected exhibits are displayed for education/propagation
of culture. However, display of objects depends upon the availability of display area and as such,
every Museum displays its collections within the limitations of its space. The details of display of
the collections following museums vis-a-vis their total collections is as under:–
Sl. Name of Museum Total No. of No. of Artefacts Percentage
No. collections of on Display %
Artefacts
  1. National Museum 2,06,000 15,681 7.61
  2. Indian Museum 1,10,000 3500 3.18
  3. Victoria Memorial Hall 28,393 1500 5.28
  4. National Gallery of Modern Art, 17000 1000 5.88
New Delhi
27. The National Museum has noted the suggestion of the committee for compliance. Though
at present only 7.61% of the total collections are on display, when the Phase-III of the National
Museum will be constructed, more number of its collections will be displayed. Phase-III of the

7
National Museum will be taken up as soon as the space occupied by ASI is vacated for which
necessary action is in progress.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28. The Committee would not like to make any comment about the display percentages
in our Museums without knowing this percentage in the famous Museums of the world. It
would like to have those figures.
29. The Committee also observers that the displays in the Museum are not rotated regularly, and
therefore, the visitors lose the charm of visiting the Museum. The Committee recommends that a
year long display-schedule may be drawn up and publicized widely showing which of the artifacts
will be on display when, so that people know this beforehand. It would enable them to plan the
time of visiting the Museum. In the summer vacations, time may be extended in the evening and
the museum should be made more attractive/interesting to the students through creative audio-visual
presentations. (Para 31, ibid)
Reply of the Government
30. Objects on display in different galleries are rotated periodically rotated from time to time,
both to enable visitors to see different objects and also for preventive conservation of the objects.
Besides this, there are arrangements for display of ‘Object of the Month’ and ‘Gallery of the
Month’ where displayed objects are rotated at regular intervals. Special exhibitions are organised
with objects from reserve collections.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
31. The Committee notes the comments and recommends that wide publicity should be
given to the display “of the object of the month” and “Gallery of the Month”.
32. The Committee expresses its concern about the fact that the Art Acquisition Committee of
the National Museum has been defunct for the last 16 years affecting the addition of objects
adversely. No justification for this can convince the Committee about this delay. The Committee
recommends that reasons for this delay must be looked into and steps be initiated immediately to
constitute the Art Acquisition Committee. The Committee would like to be informed about this at
the earliest. (Para 32, ibid)
Reply of the Government
33. Art acquisition Committee became defunct after certain malpractices were reported and
some complaints received. National Museum could not initiate further action for reorganisation of
the Committee due to lack of storage space and since conservation capability stands stretched to
the maximum. At present the existing storage space has fully been utilized and there is no additional
space available to keep any additional art objects. As soon as the space is created after construction
of Phase-III, art acquisition committee would be reconstituted/ revamped. Construction of
phase-III would start, once ASI vacates the premises.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee does not find the reply of the Ministry convincing. Acquisition of

8
Artifacts, an integral function of any Museum should be a continuous process and lack of
space to keep acquired objects should not be an excuse.  Idea of acquiring alternate storage
on temporary basis should have been explored. The Committee recommends that steps
should be taken for creation of Art Acquisition Committee at the earliest.
35. The Committee fails to understand how  909 objects (2269-1360) could be added during
the period when Art Acquisition Committee was not functioning. The Committee would like to be
informed of the procedure adopted for acquisition of collections during that period.
(Para 33, ibid)
Reply of the Government
36. Acquisition of these collections was made through gifts and donations  from PMO, State
Governments, foreign Governments, Institutions, individuals, etc. However, It appears that the
number indicated in the observations of the Committee needs to be rectified. On careful scrutiny,
it was found that total number of acquisitions during 1999-2011 are 928 and details of the same
is as under:–
Gifts – 633; Purchased  - 121 (28 items from National Defence Fund and 93 modern coins from
vendors for new coin gallery.) and Loan – 174
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
37. The Committee notes the addition in collections through gifts and donations and hope
they are kept safely in the existing space.
VERIFICATION OF COLLECTIONS
38. The Committee finds it hard to believe that no verification of artifacts kept in the Museum
had been done since 2003. The Committee expresses its concern about such a casual approach
towards protection and upkeep of the valuable treasures of the nation. The Committee fears that
when the verification process is taken up some of the objects may be reported missing. Lack of
manpower given as reason for not undertaking the verification, is neither convincing nor
acceptable. Help of professional agencies may have been taken for doing this verification. The
Committee feels that the Ministry should have more watchful and National Museum pro-active in
this regard, which they have failed to do so. The proposal of digitization of art objects is a good
effort but physical verification is required to account for the articles. The Committee recommends
that the Government should make all out efforts to take up the process of verification of articles
without further loss of time and to ensure that the process of verification is started soon and be
done regularly in future. (Para 36 , ibid)
Reply of the Government
39. National Museum has initiated process to start the physical verification of the artifacts of
different sections. As a first step, National Museum proposes to utilize the best expertise in the
concerned fields and some have already been identified. Letters to the experts from the field of
Archaeology (Dr. R.D. Trivedi, former Director (ASI)) and Numismatic and Epigraphy (Dr. Munira
Khatun) has been sent for their consent on receipt of which action for physical verification would
start. Collections in the Dr. Zakir Hussein Memoriam Museum will be verified by a Committee of

9
officers of the National Museum in the next quarter. Collections of Paintings Department is being
verified simultaneously as handing/taking over of the collections is in progress.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
40. The Committee is happy to know that verification process has been started.  It would
like to know when the physical verification would be completed and also the status of
consent from the experts. The Committee reiterates that verification should be a continuous
process and all the efforts be made in this regard.
41. The Committee finds that there is a minimal use of IT in the affairs of National Museum.
The Paintings and Manuscripts for major part of the collection in possession of National Museum
are very fragile and some of them are rarest of rare and one of its kinds and their frequent physical
handling can cause irreparable damage in them. The Committee found that the museum is not
equipped to use digital and new media. Today in the digital age of internet, interactive games and
computers, most museum are in need of drastic upgradation of this purpose. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that, as a first step, digitization of objects, both for their conservation and
for giving access to scholars, researchers and general public, through Internet and other means
must be considered for expeditious implementations. (Para 37, ibid)
Reply of the Government
42. Action is in progress for the National Museum to enter into a MOU with M/S Google for
a virtual move-around the Museum’s Gallery. Under the Google art project, to start with, 150
master pieces from the National Museum collections has been identified for digitisation and will be
available on the internet. Primary documentation for this is in progress. The National Museum
intends to cover more art objects in future and make them available for viewing over the internet.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
43. The Committee notes that National Museum has to go a long way in making use of
the latest technology. The Museum has still not finalized the MoU for virtual move around
in the Museum Gallery. Besides this, there is no reply on the recommendation of
the Committee for digitization of objects and for giving access to scholars, researchers
and general public. The Committee may be apprised of the action taken on these
recommendations.
44. The Committee expresses its concern at slow progress of phase III of the building
expansion plan that was started in 2003. Seven years is, in fact, too long to justify the delay for
whatever reasons. Large number of our collections is not being displayed due mainly to the
shortage of display areas. The Committee notes with dismay that despite the fact that EFC for the
phase-III was carried out way back in 2003 and an amount of Rs. 33 crore was also sanctioned,
the project is yet to be taken up. The Committee has learnt that the process of proving alternative
accommodation to the ASI is on and that is taking time. If the non-shifting of ASI was the main
reason of delay in the expansion plan of the museum, the Committee fails to understand why the
allocation of alternative accommodation to the ASI was taking such a long time. The Committee
hastens to add that while earmarking new accommodation to the ASI, its enhanced need for more
space due to its increasing strength should be kept in mind. The Committee recommends that
efforts be made to expedite shifting of the ASI to a suitable space so that its functioning is not

10
adversely affected and the expansion plan of the museum could be taken up without further
delay. (Para 40, ibid)
Reply of the Government
45. National Museum has already initiated necessary steps in this regard.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
46. The Committee notes a studied silence about issues relating to shifting of ASI and
the steps taken by the Ministry in this regard. The Committee would like to have details
about this process started way back in 2003. It hopes that Ministry of Culture, under whose
purview both, ASI and National Museum fall, will take steps to shift ASI in a time-bound
manner so that National Museum can go ahead with the construction of III
rd phase.
47. The Committee further recommends that the cost assessment of the project would need to
be revised/reviewed and adequate allocation made so that the work does not suffer for want of
funds. (Para 41, ibid)
Reply of the Government
48. The cost assessment would be redone  after ASI vacates the premises and Ministry of
Culture will be requested to allocate requisite funds.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
49. The Committee hopes that the project would get sufficient funds once the space is
available for construction and the project will not be delayed due to lack of funding.
SIGNAGE
50. The Committee while visiting the Museum noted that the signage and the labels about the
displays were unattractive and too small in size to see. Certain errors of translation in Hindi and
those of typing were also noticed. The Committee recommends that the immediate steps may be
taken to make the signage and tags more visible and attractive to the visitors. (Para 42, ibid)
Reply of the Government
51. Improved display of Internal and External Signages have already been implemented by
National Museum. Display of labels/tags inside the galleries has also been initiated.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
52. The Committee notes the reply.
53. The Committee is happy to note that based on its earlier recommendations, the Government
has delinked the selection of heads of cultural bodies including that of Director General, National
Museum from the purview of UPSC and adopted that procedure of search – cum – selection
process. However, the Committee is surprised to note that the Govt. could not find suitable
candidates for the post of Director General and the National Museum, as a result, remained

11
headless during the last many years which had a telling impact on all the  activities of the National
Museum. The Committee is afraid that if such a state of affairs continued for a few more years,
the condition of the National Museum may become from bad to worse. (Para 55, ibid)
54. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the appointment of DG of National Museum
should be handled at the highest level and the Government should take urgent steps to appoint a
professional as the Director General from among the museum experts. (Para 56, ibid)
55. The Committee emphasizes the need to make the post of Director General, National
Museum more attractive by providing adequate autonomy, both administrative and financial, to
avoid unnecessary delays in its urgent works. The Committee is of the view that there are many
experts in the country who could have been persuaded to work for the betterment of this institution
in the manner acceptable to them. (Para 57, ibid)
Reply of the Government
56. The Search-cum-Selection Committee in its meeting held on 07.01.2010 decided to re-
advertise the post for inviting more applications to enlarge the scope of selection. Accordingly, the
vacancy for the post was re-advertised in the leading National Dailies on 16.01.2011. But no
suitable candidate has been found for the post of DGNM. However, searching of a suitable
candidate is still going on under Search mode.
57. The Committee is surprised at the maze of recruitment procedure which is not only
extremely complicated about also difficult to follow. In this connection, the Committee takes note
of the evidence tendered by the Secretary on the 30
th September 2010 which is reproduced below:-
“…….. As you rightly pointed out, why do we need so many recruitment rules? It is almost
one recruitment rule for 1.5 posts. If you go through the recruitment rules, you will
amazed, and after putting in 35 years in the bureaucracy, even, I cannot decide much on
all this, Why do we need such complications? And, that is the question which I have been
asking, to which I will retire without an answer…….These were created by our convoluted
systems in deference to what we call inter-Ministerial operating procedures, which go on
ensuring, through checks and balances, that every form of check that is possible is put in
place. It has formed like silt, sedimentation, and over decades has reached such a level that
it would require to be dealt with sternly. My first submission is that the number of
vacancies is mind-boggling……..”                                      (Para 58 , ibid)
58. The Committee feels that this has created all the mess in the National Museum as all the
problems is attributed to shortage of staff. The Committee finds that mainly due to shortage of
manpower, the work of verification of artifacts could not be taken up and some of the galleries
had to be closed for unduly larger period. The Committee finds that in many cases steps to fill
up vacancies were taken years after the posts were fallen vacant, as a result, during the period
of 1994 to 2003, many posts which were lying vacant for more than one year were deemed to
be abolished and as such they could not be filled up.                            (Para 59, ibid)
Reply of the Government
59. The process for filling up of vacant posts has been initiated. Proposal for filling up of 12
Group ‘A’ posts have been taken up with UPSC and necessary action is on to complete
observations raised by them. Requisition for filling up of 26 posts has been made with Staff
Selection Commission. Six posts have been filled up by promotion and requisition for publication

12
of advertisement in respect of 08 posts has been sent to Employment News. Two cases are being
progressed for consideration of Departmental Promotion Committee.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
60. It appears that no efforts were made for searching eminent persons/experts from the
field by the Search-cum-Selection Committee particularly for the higher positions. The
Committee hopes that necessary steps would be taken to fill the vacancies in time bound
manner.
61. The Committee is of the view that the Government’s instruction that a post lying vacant
for more than one year may be deemed abolished, was being followed mechanically with total
disregard to its consequences to the functioning of National Museum. If this instruction is to be
followed in all the Museums, in a few years’ time the Museums will be without any employee and
then the Government would have a strong case to hand them over to private parties for running
them. (Para 60, ibid)
Reply of the Government
62. Out of 41 temporary posts, sanction for 31 posts have been received. Also, 04 permanent
posts which were deemed abolished have also been revived. Action has also been initiated for filling
up the vacant posts as per details given in the reply to Para 58/59.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
63. The Committee notes the reply.
64. The Committee, thus, has a strong reason to believe that the Government has failed to give
attention to the National Museum which it deserved. It recommends that efforts be made to review
all the lapsed posts and they are filled up at the earliest. (Para 61, ibid)
Reply of the Government
65. Four permanent posts which were deemed abolished posts have been revived as mentioned
in reply to Para No. 60. Action in respect of other posts has been initiated for revival. Action has
also been initiated for filling up the vacant posts as per details given in the reply to Para 58/59.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
66. The Committee notes the reply.
67. The Committee welcomes the creations of new posts of Additional Director General and
Joint Director General. The Committee has, however, noted that the selection through UPSC is a
rigid and time consuming procedure. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the posts of
Additional Director General and Joint Director General may be kept outside the purview of UPSC
selection process and instead the search cum selection process may be adopted. It should be
ensured that the posts may be filled up within a period of three months. (Para 62, ibid)

68. Ministry of Culture had proposed in the draft Recruitment Rules to keep the posts of ADG

13
and JDG out of purview of UPSC. However this was not agreed to by both UPSC and DOPT and
hence the proposed RRs have been framed as per extant Govt. rules. The draft RRs have now been
sent to UPSC on 23.11.2011 after the same were cleared by DoPT on 10.10.2011. Their
concurrence from UPSC is awaited.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
69. The Committee would like to know the arguments given by UPSC and DoPT against
Search Committee procedure for not keeping the posts of Additional Director-General and
Joint Director-General out of the purview of the UPSC.
70. The Committee finds that the plethora or recruitment rules and the lack of autonomy in
decision making at the level of the National Museum are greatly affecting the functioning of the
institution. The Committee recommends that National Museum may be made an independent
autonomous body with all the inherent powers to administer its affairs including recruitment and
staffing. The recruitment process of the National Museum may be delinked from UPSC and Staff
Selection Commission. The Museum may be authorized to devise its own procedures for selection
of officers and staff the same way the central universities are recruiting their faculties and
supporting staff. (Para 63, ibid)
Reply of the Government
71.  The Suggestion has been noted for necessary action.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
72. The Committee notes the reply and would like to know what actions were being
proposed in this regard.
73. The Committee notes the lack of commitment in the Ministry not only in filling up of the
posts but also in reassessing the recruitment of staff. The Committee observes that the staff
strength in various categories was assessed many years ago. The Committee recommends that a
reassessment of the vacant positions should be taken up expeditiously and placed before the
Government. (Para 64, ibid)

74. A study was undertaken to reassess the manpower planning for the National Museum.
Report has been submitted. Further necessary action in this regard is in progress.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE

National Museum.

Government and private control and most of them are in a state of neglect and need attention
by specially trained staff. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the matter may be taken
up with the Ministry of Human Resources Development to look into the course details and
revamp it to make it more useful content-wise. The practical aspect of training such as internship

14
in a museum may be added so that the people recruited should be actually handling the objects
and that they know how to handle the objects, collection display etc. The Committee also
recommends that possibility of integration of museology course in the university curricula may
be explored.

appointing agency may be persuaded to keep a separate cadre for museology with transferable options

to work in other museums also and in their place of choice. (Para 67 & 68, ibid)
Reply of the Government
78. A sub-committee of CABC under the Chairmanship of Prof. B.N.Goswami was constituted
which inter-alia was mandated to suggest curriculum on Museum Management. The Committee
has submitted its report to the Govt. Necessary actions are being taken to implement the various
recommendations which includes creation of a separate cadre of Museum Professionals.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
79. The Committee notes the reply.

90. Tender for providing multimedia guides has been finalized and action in this regard is in

lot of activities as suggested by the Board has been initiated for efficient functioning of the National

CONCLUSION
95. The Committee appreciates the frank admission by the Secretary, Ministry of Culture before
it, which has been reproduced in para 12 of this Report. He clearly shares concerns of the
Committee the administration of museum leaves much to be desired in several aspects that have
been described and commented upon by the Committee in this Report. The Ministry of Culture has
been considered so important that it has been put directly under the charge of the Prime Minister
himself. But the Committee is surprised to see that this importance is not reflected by the manner
in which the affairs of the Museum are being managed. The Committee hopes that its observations
and recommendations regarding the functioning of the Museum would be brought to the notice at
the highest level in the Government for taking immediate steps to conduct the affairs of not only
of the National Museum, Delhi but, of all the Museums under the Ministry, in the professional
manner. (Para 79, ibid)

96. The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance and remedial action
being taken, wherever required to improve the functioning of National Museum.

the Committee’s concerns and recommendations.
