INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport,
Tourism and Culture, having authorized by the Committee to present on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Eightieth Report on Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations/observations of the Committee contained in its One Hundred and Seventy Second
Report on Development of Tourism in North-Eastern Region.
2. One Hundred and Seventy Second Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture was presented to the Parliament on the 17
th August,
2011 in Parliament.
3. The Action Taken Replies on the recommendations of the Committee contained in its One
Hundred and Eightieth Report were received from the Ministries of Tourism, Civil Aviation, Road
Transport and Highways, Shipping and North-East Region Development and State Governments on
19
th January, 2012.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report as its meeting held on the 17 th May 2012.
SITARAM YECHURY
NEW D ELHI; Chairman,
May 17, 2012 Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Vaisakha 27, 1934  (Saka) Committee on Transport, Tourism and Culture.

1
REPORT
1. The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the
observations/recommendations as contained in its One-Hundred and Seventy Second Report on
Development of Tourism in the North Eastern Region of the Ministry of Tourism which was
presented to both the Houses of Parliament on 17
th August, 2011.
2. Action Taken Replies have been received from the Government on the 10 th  January, 2012
in respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. Further observations
and recommendations of the Committee on these are  given in the succeeding paragraphs.
3. The Committee desires that final replies in respect of those recommendations/
observations which have been categorized as interim replies by the Committee should be
furnished to it at the earliest.
4. On scrutiny of the Action Taken Replies, the Committee has made observations on each
item of Action taken/proposed to be taken by the concerned Ministries. The recommendations of
the Committee contained in the One Hundred and Seventy Second Report, action taken thereon by
the Ministry and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of action taken has
been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
5. North-Eastern Region consists of 8 States viz.  Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur,
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. This region is full of bewildering cultural
diversity, magical beauty in terms of nature, wild life, biodiversity, etc. Each State is, in fact, a
travellers’ paradise with immense tourism potential which unfortunately remains unutilized. It has
been, therefore, rightly termed as ‘Paradise Unexplored’. The Committee has, however, noted that
NE States are far behind as compared to other States in terms of tourist arrivals, both domestic
and foreign. State of Assam is shade better than other States in this region leaving lot of scope
for improvement in attracting tourists. (Para 100, of the 172
nd Report)
Reply of the Government
6. The number of Domestic Tourist Visits (DTVs) and Foreign Tourist  Visits (FTVs) in the
North-Eastern region have been increasing overall, although the States of Meghalaya, Nagaland have
seen decline in the arrival of foreign tourists in the year 2010, and Manipur has recorded a decline
in domestic tourists in the same year. A Statement showing the domestic and foreign tourists arrival
in the North-Eastern States is given at Annexure-I.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7. The Committee notes with concern that the Ministry’s reply does not reflect the
seriousness required to boost tourism in these States. The Committee is not satisfied as the
Ministry has  thrown no light on the reasons for decreasing the tourist arrivals to certain
North Eastern States. The Committee recommends that steps should be taken to attract
more and more tourists to the North Eastern States so that  ‘the paradise unexplored’ did
not remain unexplored for long.
8. The Committee notes with satisfaction that there was no dearth of funds for this purpose.
Union Ministry of Tourism has released amount ranging  from 15% to 19% of the total budget of
the Ministry which is well above the mandatory provision of 10% for the NE States. The
Committee, however, has noted that funds for Centrally sponsored Schemes/State Plans have not

2
been released uniformally amongst all the NE States. The Committee found that no funds were
released under those schemes for Manipur, Meghalaya and Mizoram during the year 2010-11. For
the State of Tripura an amount of Rs.1.19 crore was released for Centrally sponsored scheme
during this period. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Tourism should ensure that proper
proposals, UCs, etc. are received from the States in time so that funds are released to them without
much delay. (Para 101, ibid)
Reply of the Government
9. The Ministry of Tourism extends Central Financial Assistance to the State Governments/
Union Territory Administrations for tourism projects identified in consultation with them. A
statement showing the number of projects and amount sanctioned to the North-Eastern States
during the Eleventh Five Year Plan up to 30

Reply of the Government
135. Checking FUEL adulteration is a continuous process and the Ministry of Petroleum &
Natural Gas has taken several technological and institutional measures, which are summarized
below:
(i)   
Essential Commodities Act, 1955: As per the Control Orders issued by the
Government to prevent fuel adulteration, under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955,
State Governments are empowered to take action against those indulging in
adulteration. The Central Government has requested the State Governments/Union
Territory Administrations to take steps to control adulteration.
(ii)
Inspections: Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) undertake regular surprise inspections
of Retail Outlets and also take action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG)
and Dealership Agreements against those indulging in adulteration and malpractices.
(iii)
Tamper-proof locking system:  OMCs have introduced new tamper proof tank-truck
locking systems to prevent en-route adulteration by transporters.
(iv) Canalization of import of Superior Kerosene Oil (SKO):  Keeping in view the
misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the import of SKO by private parties has
been canalized through OMCs.
(v)
Creation of separate enfor cement wing:  As advised by the Government, OMCs
have created a separate wing to report to a Director other than Director (Marketing)
to oversee and monitor all activities and operations to curb adulteration.
(vi)
Automation of Retail Outlets:  In order to monitor the activities at retail outlets
through the latest technological means, MOP&NG has directed the oil marketing
companies to complete automation of retail outlets selling more than 200 KL per
month, to begin with.
(vii)   
Monitoring of movement of Tank Trucks thr ough Global Positioning System
(GPS):  In order to prevent adulteration during transportation, OMCs have been
directed to install GPS for complete monitoring of the movement of all the company-
owned/dealer owned/contractor-owned tank trucks.

23
(viii) Third Party Certification of Reta il Outlets:  OMCs have been directed to complete
third party certification of all retail outlets selling more than 100 KL per month.
(ix) Marketing Discipline Guidelines: The Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) under
which the oil marketing companies take penal actions against the erring dealers were
revised during August, 2005 making the penal actions more stringent. As per MDG,
2005, a dealership is liable to be terminated in the first established instance of
adulteration.
(x)
Toll Fr ee Numbers:  The Oil Marketing Companies in the public sector have
introduced toll-free numbers, for both LPG as well as retail outlets, for registration
of complaints by the consumers.
(xi)
Installation of Global Positioning System (GPS) based Vehicle Tracking System
(VTS) on tankers transporting Public Distribution System (PDS) SKO:  Some
State Governments have started responding to the request of this Ministry for
installation of GPS based VTS on tankers transporting PDS Kerosene. OMCs are in
touch with the interested State Governments for implementation of the system.
Further, OMCs have hosted a public portal where information on PDS SKO such as
dispatch time, quantity, and vehicle details are available to general public.

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on
observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred Sixty Eighth Report on ‘Directorate
General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) – Issues and challenges’ of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, which
was presented to the Parliament on the 11
th August, 2011.
2. Action Taken replies were received from the Government on the 2 nd March, 2012 in respect
of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. The recommendations made by
the Committee and the Action Taken Replies submitted by the Ministry have been enumerated in
succeeding paragraphs.
3. DGCA is the watch dog body which, directly and indirectly, regulates almost all the
operations critical to aviation safety in the country. Its functions range from formulation of
standards and procedures, conducting inspection, issuing licenses, granting approvals/certificates to
airlines, airport operators, training institutions, aero clubs, aircraft maintenance engineers, pilots,
crew members, ATCs/ENS and ATM facilities. Besides, it is also responsible for looking after legal/
regulatory matters. Coordination/supervision between different civil aviation organizations, national
and international, civil and military air traffic, and investigation of air accidents are also in DGCA’s
mandate. Needless to say, the dimensions and complexity of these functions have become
enormous today when the aviation sector has grown by 160 per cent. The Committee found the
DGCA did neither have the required powers - legal, administrative and financial, nor it has the
adequate manpower, infrastructure and resources for fulfilling its responsibilities adequately and
effectively.
(Para 56 of the 168
th Report)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
4. The Committee’s finding that the DGCA has neither the required powers-legal, administrative

institutes during the last year and the remedial action taken by those firms. (Para 61)
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee feels that DGCA
should ensure that the airlines operators do not to indulge in unfair trade practices in fixing
air fares during festival and other peak seasons much to the discomfort of the travelling
public. (Para 64)
12

The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. (Para 67)
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee has been informed

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on
observations/recommendations as contained in its One Hundred Sixty Ninth Report on ‘Helicopter
Operations in India’ of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, which was presented to the Parliament on
the 11
th August, 2011.
2. Action Taken replies were received from the Government on the 2 nd March, 2012 in respect
of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. The recommendations made by
the Committee and the Action Taken Replies submitted by the Ministry have been enumerated in
succeeding paragraphs.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
3. The Committee observes that even after a period of almost six decades since its inception,
the helicopter operations in India is still in a rudimentary stage as compared to that in the western
countries in terms of existence of a separate regulatory mechanism, rules and regulations as well
as necessary infrastructure specific to helicopters. The Committee found that currently, the
helicopter operations i.e. rotary wing aircrafts are being governed by the set of rules, regulations
and mechanism under the DGCA which are meant for the fixed wing aircraft. In view of significant
differences between the two, the Committee feels that there is an urgent need to put mechanism,
rules, regulations and the required infrastructure specific to the helicopter sector in place, without
further delay.
(Para 29 of the 169
th Report)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
4. In India, Helicopter market is growing rapidly. Presently India has approx 300
Helicopters, which is expected to increase to 500 in next 5 years. In view to promote the
Helicopters travel in the country Government/State Governments/Ministry of Civil Aviation and
Ministry of Tourism is providing assistance in promoting Helicopters services. Proper
infrastructure may be created at Hilly and remote areas, with no connectivity by other mode
of travel. This would help to connect such places by Air. Presently Helicopters regulations,
which are applicable to the fixed wing Aircrafts. Since the Helicopters has been designed for
ease of travel and require minimum infrastructure to operate, a special focus may be given to
Helicopter Industry. Rules, regulations and mechanism for operations of fixed wing aircraft and
Rotary Wing Aircraft are laid down separately. Helicopter operations are primarily governed by
the following regulations:
Aircraft Rules: Sections B, F, K, N, P and R of Schedule II of Aircraft Rules, 1937
specifically deal with helicopter.
Civil Aviation Requirements (CARs)
5. A number of requirements, specifically for helicopters exist in all the sections of CARs
published by DGCA. These CARs deal with aspects pertains to helicopter pilot licensing and
training, simulators, maintenance and AME licensing, flight operations, heliports/helipads, including
special helicopter operations like off-shore, hill-flying, under-slung, HEMS etc. The latest CAR on

2
“Minimum Safety Requirements for Helicopter Landing Areas used on Regular basis” was issued
on 4 th August, 2011.
Circulars
6. Apart from above Rules and CARs, DGCA regularly issues Circulars inter-alia , dealing with
helicopter operations. The latest Operations Circular on “Weather clearance for helicopter flights”
was issued on 4 th November, 2011.
7. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and would like to have further information
on the assistance provided for promotion of helicopter services to various agencies.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
8. The Committee also found that currently, helicopters are being used mainly for VIP
operations and transporting people to offshore oil operations. The Committee feels that the
Government has not taken enough steps for expansion of helicopter sector in India. The Committee
is of the opinion that helicopter operations have to be expanded to such other areas as tourism,
medical emergencies, disaster management, maintenance of law and order, etc.
(Para 30, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
9. Helicopter Operations in our country has expanded to many areas other than V .I.P.
Operations and Transporting Passengers to offshore locations. Some of these are as follows:-
(a)
Pilgrimage Tourism – Amarnath Yatra, Kedarnath Yatra, Manimahesh yatra and Mata
Vaishno Devi which are some of he important pilgrimage places where Helicopters are
being extensively.
(b) Heli-Skiing – At least 06 Helicopters are used during the season. These Operations take
place from Manali, Himachal Pradesh and Gulmarg in Jammu and Kashmir.
c) Power Lines wash – Helicopters are being used for hot wash of insulators of
Transmission Lines by Helicopters to avoid frequent breakdown of Power Supply.
(d) Passenger Service – Helicopters are also being used to convey Passengers in Inter
Island Helicopter Services in Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep. The same type
of Helicopter Service is also quite popular in North-East India like Nagaland,
Meghalaya, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. These services are being provided by State
Governments on subsidized rates.
(e)
Aerial Survey – Geological Survey of India has also been utilizing helicopters for
mapping the metal/mineral contents in various parts of the country.
10. Being the largest Helicopter operator in India, Pawan Hans helicopters limited (PHHL) has
been providing its services in areas of Offshore, Onshore, VIP Operations, Medivac, Passenger
Transportation etc. In order to promote the tourism PHHL has been providing its regular service
to Mata Vaishno Devi, Sri Kedarnathji, Sri Amarnathji, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep and north
Eastern Part of the country. PHHL has one dedicated Helicopter for Medivac service, deployed with
ONGC, which is fully equipped with necessary life saving equipment.

3
11. For Disaster Management PHHL has submitted a detailed proposal to National Disaster
Management Authority (NDMA) for deploying 5-6 Helicopters at strategic locaions across the
country. During the disaster, PHHL played crucial role in the Orissa Flood (September 2011) and
Sikkim Earthquake (September, 2011). During Orissa Flood, PHHL’s Mi-172 Helicopter was stepped
into emergency services. During this natural calamity at Orissa, PHHL Helicopter (Mi-172) carried
a load of 61 ton, of relief material and other essential items. During the Sikkim earthquake PHHL
deployed 3 Helicopters for rescue Operations and rescued approx 500 people from different
locations, with a total 63 hours of flying during this operation.
12. Under the maintenance of Law and Order, PHHL has deployed one Mi-172 Helicopter with
Government of Orissa for anti-naxalite operations. PHHL is also operating one Dauphin Helicopter
for Government of Maharashtra at Garhchiroli and Dhruv Helicopters for BSF, positioned at Ranchi
and Raipur for maintaining Law and Order.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
13. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
14. In this connection, the Committee would like to make special mention about the use of
helicopters in medical emergency, a strong case for which was made out by the representatives
of the Rotary Wing Society of India before the Committee. The Committee is also convinced that
this country holds a huge potential for using helicopters in this area. Many lives can be saved by
bringing the accident victims from remote and inaccessible areas for providing immediate medical
help during golden hour. The Committee would like that a Feasibility Study may be got conducted
by involving all the stakeholders, government as well as private, to promote the use of helicopters
in those areas.
(Para 31, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
15. CAR on helicopter Emergency Medical Services (HEMS) already exists and one helicopter
susbidised by Lakshadweep Administration is actively involved in ferrying patients from Islands to
Main Land. However, utilization of helicopter services for HEMS will be cost effective and popular
only if adequate subsidy is provided and insurance agencies are also actively involved in the
process. PHHL has submitted a detailed proposal to National Disaster Management Authority
(NDMA) for long term Strategy in disaster management including Medical emergencies. PHHL has
proposed to tie-up with National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) and identifying hospital and
Trauma Centers near Highways. These Hospital and Trauma Centers could be used during medical
emergencies and by providing the immediate medical support during the crucial Golden hour of the
patient, many lives can be saved.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
16. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee may be apprised on
the action taken by National Disaster Management Authority over the proposal submitted
by Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited on the disaster management.

4
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee also feels that promotion of tourism to remote and inaccessible areas can
be done by making helicopters services available for the tourists to such places. The Committee
recommends that the Government should take steps to make heli-tourism more attractive and
affordable by reducing cost of operation through fiscal incentives, lowering taxes on ATF,
waiving off RNFC, rationalizing landing and parking charges after consultation with the State
Governments.
(Para 32, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
18. PHHL has taken various initiatives in the area of promoting tourism and providing
connectivity to inaccessible areas. In additional PHHL has been exploring the possibilities of
deploying Helicopter services in the various new areas (subject to commercial viability) to promote
the tourism in the country e.g. Machail Yatra, Hemkunt Sahib, Karnataka-Hampi Circuit, Tourist
attractions in Himachal Pradesh, Golden Triangle (Delhi-Agra-Jaipur), Religious Circuits in the State
of Kerala, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Bihar, West Bengal, Goa, Madhya Pradesh etc.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
19. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee would like to have
information on the introduction of helicopter services in the above mentioned new areas and
the impact of such services on promotion of tourism on these areas.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
20. Presently, we are having 250 odd helicopters in operation, which are likely to be increased
significantly in the coming areas. In view of the great potential for helicopter travel in the country,
urgent need for dedicated helicopter training organizations can hardly be over-emphasized. The
Committee is not aware about the future requirement of the trained manpower for the helicopter
sector. One gliding centre at Pune and one training academy at Gondia have been proposed.
Currently, we have one fixed simulator in private sector in Delhi and one full motion simulator is
being established by HAL at Bangalore. The existing training facilities, thus, are inadequate to meet
the future requirements of the industry. The Committee does not know about the status of those
centres that were being set up. It would like to have a status report in respect of the proposed
centres.
(Para 33, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
21. Helicopter market in India is growing rapidly, which will require trained manpower in
future. At present there is only one helicopter training Institute with Hindustan Aeronautics
Limited (HAL), based in Bangalore. IGRUA and Gondia Flying Institutes are likely to be
functional in near future. In addition, regular induction of helicopter pilots from Defence Forces
also takes place. Besides these, some pilots get training abroad and convert foreign Licences to
Indian Commercial Helicopter Pilot Licences (CHPL). In view of providing helicopter Pilots,
PHHL is also in the process of setting up a Pilot Training Institute at Hadapsar, Pune. This Pilot
Training Institute will have all modern facilities required for training of Pilots as per international
Standards.

5
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
22. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and feels that merely setting up two
or three flying training institutes is not going to address the issue of shortage of pilots in
helicopter industry totally. The Committee is of the opinion that setting up more flying
training institutes or pilot training institute is the need of the hour.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
23. The Committee recommends that the Government should address the issue of shortage of
helicopter pilots on priority since the industry is gaining momentum rapidly. The Committee feels
that the Government should appoint a Committee of experts to review the present system of
examination and procedures for award of licenses to pilots. It may consider creating of national
pool of independent examiners, standardize the syllabi, increase the frequency of examinations and
rationalize the charges for skill tests.
(Para 34, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
24. As recommended by the Expert Committee Examination System at DGCA’s Central
Examination Office has been revamped. Most the examinations are now conducted online and
frequency of the examination is being increased.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
25. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and hopes that revamped examination
system at DGCA will yield fruitful results in addressing the issue of shortage of helicopter
pilots.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
26. The Committee further notes that for monitoring proficiency of pilots operating over 250
helicopters, DGCA is having four helicopter Inspectors on secondment basis from the industry. The
Committee feels that efforts should be made to have more Inspectors who are type qualified and
in current flying. In the longer term, the Committee feels that there is a need to have adequate
number of Flight Inspectors with long experience to handle proficiency monitoring of pilots. While
doing so, our future requirements should be kept in mind.
(Para 35, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
27. Number of helicopter Inspectors in DGCA has increased from 4 to 7. All these inspectors
are seconded from the industry and are type rated on more than one type of helicopter.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
28. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and feels that the Government will
give serious consideration on the appointment of sufficient number of helicopter inspectors
for safety of pilots and passengers.

6
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
29. The Committee notes that a number of agencies such as PSUs, corporate houses and the
State governments are operating helicopters in India. The Committee, therefore, feels that their
involvement will play a major role in providing requisite infrastructure for helicopter operations in
the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that wider consultations needs to be done with
all the stakeholders while creating a regulatory mechanism for this purpose.
(Para 36, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
30. A system of involvement of all stake holders while framing regulations already exists. Draft
of new regulations is always placed on the website and the same is finalized after incorporating
comments and suggestions received from the stake holders.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
31. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
32. The Committee notes with concern the instances of forceful landing/take off of helicopters
in low visibility, bad weather and even during nights, which are serious breaches of aviation
security norms. It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that at times technical
clearances are given to the helicopters with minor defects to take off. The technical personnel
including pilots are put under pressure not to oppose these deficiencies due to commercial or other
reasons. It happens mainly in the case of chartered helicopters and those under the State
governments flying VIPs. Such violations of rules have led to fatal accidents losing several precious
lives. Lack of proper maintenance and non-observance of operating manuals, mechanical failures
and lack of required instruments have been found as the causes of these accidents. It points out
towards the ineffectiveness of safety audit and mandatory inspections of the helicopters and other
facilities for testing their airworthiness. The Committee recommends that technical personnel/pilots
be provided adequate legal/administrative protection to decline to fly in the absence of mandatory
technical, weather and other clearances. Some kind of penal provision may be considered against
those putting such pressure on the pilots to fly without proper clearances. Conversely, the strictest
actions be taken against those pilots/technicians who violate these requirements even under some
kind of duress. Their licences may be immediately cancelled if prime facie  they appear to have
done so.
(Para 37, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
33. DGCA regularly carries out surveillance/audits of all the helicopter operators and suitable
action against personnel/pilots/organization for any violation, is taken as per the enforcement system
in place.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
34. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.

7
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
35. In order to ensure independent and impartial enquiry into accidents, the Committee would
like to reiterate its earlier recommendation made in its 168 th Report which is reproduced below:
“The Committee is of the view that creation of an independent authority for accident
investigation on an urgent basis will instill confidence in the minds of travelling public.”
(Para 38, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
36. An Independent Accident Investigation Bureau has been set up in the Ministry of Civil
Aviation. The relevant rules are under process.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
37. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee may be apprised on
the status of framing and implementing of relevant rules.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
38. The Committee recommends that the entire gamut of helicopter operations in India may be
reviewed and adequate/appropriate steps may be taken to ensure safer helicopter travel. The
Committee recommends that guidelines/regulations for take off/landing of helicopters during low
visibility should not only be strengthened but enforced strictly.
(Para 39, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
39. Enforcement of Guidelines/Regulations for Take-off/Landing during Low Visibility is ensured
through regular surveillance/audits of all the helicopter operators and suitable action against
personnel/pilots/organization for any violation is taken as per the enforcement system in place.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
40. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
41. The Committee notes that Helicopter Cell has been set up in the DGCA. It, however, is
surprised to find that the Helicopter Cell within the DGCA does not have representation of AAI that
provides ATC services. Though there is a provision of coordination with AAI, the Committee is of
the view that for better coordination between AAI and DGCA in this matter, it would only be
appropriate, if AAI is permanently represented in the Helicopter Cell of the DGCA. The Committee
would also like to be informed of the details of the major observations/decisions made by the
Helicopter Cell and the Action Taken for implementation thereof.
 (Para 40, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
42. The recommendation of the Committee has been noted.

8
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
43. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
44. For expanding the helicopter operations to the newer areas as has been suggested by the
Committee elsewhere, India will have to have a number of heliports, vertiports and heli-routes in
the country. The Committee also emphasizes the need for developing a network of helipads and
heliports in and around metros as well as in the hilly and remote parts of the country. The
Committee is of the opinion that a dedicated heliport wing may be established in the Airports
Authority of India to oversee the development of heliports and vertiports and heli-routes in the
country.
(Para 41, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
45. PHLL has been exploring the possibilities of providing Helicopter services in the various new
areas to promote the tourism in the country and to provide better Air-connectivity to inaccessible
areas. To support this, it is required to have proper Infrastructure in place. PHHL has taken
initiatives in this regard and submitted detailed proposal to ministry of Civil Aviation for
development of Helipads, heliports and other supporting Infrastructure e.g. Passenger Lounge,
Terminal building etc. in the country.
46. In order to provide Air-Connectivity in Inaccessible areas of North East, PHHL has
submitted a detailed 5 year plan (2012-17) to Ministry of Civil Aviation covering projected
requirements of all North Eastern States during next 5 years, which is under consideration in the
Ministry.
47. A general Manager along with supporting staff in ATM directorate of Airports Authority of
India (AAI) is handling helicopter matters pertaining to Standard Operating Procedures and
helicopter routing etc. These procedures and routings are framed after the Heliport operator has
obtained necessary permission for establishment of Heliport from DGCA.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
48. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
49. The Committee feels that a concerted coordination mechanism involving Union and State
governments, meteorological department and other agencies should be evolved to make helicopter
operations safer one. The existing Air Traffic Rules may be reviewed to eliminate delays in
helicopter departures/arrivals from major airports. Flight routing may be made as direct as possible
independent of fixed wing traffic to ease the congestion at the airports.
(Para 42, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
50. In order to avoid delays to helicopters, AAI has promulgated separate helicopter corridors
for Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore Airport without interfering operation of fixed wing aircraft.

9
51. A dedicated Helicopter Routing for Juhu Airport at Mumbai and IGI Airport at New Delhi
has already been published.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
52. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
53. Since the LTC travellers now constitute a significant number, the Committee is surprised to
find that under CCS (LTC) Rules, they are not allowed to travel by Helicopters. The Committee
is of the view that LTC travellers should also be allowed to travel by helicopters and the matter
may be taken up with the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions for amendment
of the LTC rules accordingly.
(Para 43, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
54. In view of promoting Helicopter services in the country, PHHL had earlier proposed that
Helicopter services may be considered to avail the LTC from Government employees. The proposal
has been submitted to Ministry of Finance for consideration.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
55. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and likes to have the information on the
action taken by the Ministry of Finance on the proposal of PHHL on including helicopter service
in LTC for Government employees.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
56. The Committee is surprised to note that around 120 aircrafts which might include
helicopters were not capable of operating in hilly terrains and the operators of such aircrafts have
been advised not to operate in such areas till the necessary instruments (ELTs conforming to 406
MHz) were fitted. Deadline given for this was 31-3-2010. In such a situation, the Committee feels
that the possibility of such aircrafts operating in hilly areas cannot be ruled out, particularly in view
of the lax and inadequate monitoring in the sector. The Committee only hopes that these
instruments would have been placed by the given date, and if not, all such aircrafts should be
grounded and not allowed to fly until they have compiled with this.
(Para 44, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
57. Presently all operating helicopters are fitted with ELT operating on 406 MHz frequency.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
58. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
59. The Committee has been informed by the Ministry that the main obstacle for the proper
planning of the helicopter operations has been the lack of proper infrastructure with the State

10
governments and they have been advised to build proper infrastructure with meteorological briefing
and to follow the civil aviation requirements issued from the Union Ministry of Civil Aviation from
time to time. The Committee is constrained to note that the Ministry of Civil Aviation has failed
to ensure the cooperation and compliance from the State governments for helicopter operations. It,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry may take up these issues with the concerned State
governments proactively to get the needful done.
(Para 45, ibid)
REPLY OF THE GOVERNMENT
60. The recommendation of the Committee has been noted.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
61. The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry. The Committee feels that in the
absence of proper infrastructure and adequate support from the state governments, the
helicopter industry in the country could not see much growth in coming years.

REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on
observations/recommendation as contained in its One Hundred and Seventy Seventh Report on
Demands for Grants (2012-13) of the Ministry of Shipping, which was presented to the Parliament
on 7
th May, 2012.
2. Action Taken replies were received from the Government on 24 th September, 2012, in
respect of all the observations/recommendations contained in the Report. The Replies have been
categorized as follows:–
(i) Recommendations/observations that have been accepted by the Government: Para Nos.
6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15, 21, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 47, 48, 49, 55, 56, 62, 64, 73,
75, 83, 84, 93, 94, 95, 97, 103, 105, 110, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120 and 121.
(ii) Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in
view of the Government replies:
Para Nos. 7, 14, 15, 21, 36, 62, 73, 84, 103, 105, 110, 114, 115, 116, 119, 120 and
121.
(iii) Recommendations/observations in respect of which replies of the Government have
not been accepted by the Committee:
Para Nos. 39.
(iv) Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Government are
still awaited:
Para Nos. Nil
The Recommendations of the Committee contained in the one hundred and Seventy Seventh
Report, Action Taken thereon by the Ministry and recommendations/Observations of the Committee
on each item of action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
PERFORMANCE DURING XI PLAN
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
3. The Committee notes that in the absence of consolidated data for the Eleventh Plan period
with outlay, actual allocation and expenditure for both the Port and Shipping sector, and there being
no physical targets shown, comment on the performance cannot be made. However, as admitted
by Secretary, Ministry of Shipping, underutilizing the Budgetary support, due to any reason, in
Committee’s view, is acceptable only to a limited extent.
(Para No. 6 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
4. In the Eleventh Plan, an outlay of Rs. 1301.00 crores and Rs. 13,725.00 crores as Gross
Budgetary Support (GBS) and IEBR were provided for shipping sector out of which Rs. 923.63
crores and Rs. 8864.76 crores have been utilized which works out to 71% of GBS and 64.58%
of IEBR respectively. Primarily, the shortfall of expenditure has been in two cases namely (i) Indian
Maritime University and (ii) Ship building and Ship repair Sector.

2
5. Insofar as Indian Maritime University (IMU) is concerned, it may be stated that for
implementation of OBC reservations, additional classrooms and hostel facilities were needed but
tender for construction of building in Mumbai campus could not be issued as necessary approval
of plan/design were not forthcoming from local bodies and as a result entire outlay could not be
utilized. Similarly, an outlay of Rs.224.56 crores were provided for carrying out new development
works but the Patta and land of Vizag campus has not been transferred and as a result construction
work could not started.
6. Shipbuilding and Ship Repair sector consist of (i) Hindustan Shipyard Limited (HSL)
(ii) Hooghly Dock and Port Engineers Limited (HDPE) and (iii) Ship Building and Repair (SBR).
The Government has transferred Hindustan Shipyard to Ministry of Defence in December, 2009
resulting the fund left unutilized. Owing to lack of Ship building orders, the activity of HDPEL was
restricted to Ship repair work resulting considerable erosion of working capital of the Company.
The Ministry started providing assistance to pay salary, wages and statutory benefit to its
employees. The Cabinet in its meeting held on 13.10.2011 has approved the Rehabilitation-cum-
Restructuring of HDPEL. In the case of SBR, the budgetary projections were made on the basis
of projections provided by IMU, Vizag which is executing a number of R&D projects in
shipbuilding. IMU had projected on the basis of ongoing projects as well as the new R&D Projects.
In the IMU there was shortage of technical staff hence, efforts were made for recruitment of
experienced staff but considerable time was lost in this process resulting R&D scheme could not
be taken up and fund left unutilized.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
7. The Committee is not satisfied with the reasons given for under-utilisation of funds
of IMU as that is due to non clearance of plan/design from local bodies and the Patta and
land of Vizag campus has not been transferred. The Committee observes that this delay in
construction work have deprived a number of eligible students from getting admission to
IMU.
8. The Committee notes with concern the delay in the recruitment of technical staff,
research and development activities in IMU could not be carried out and finally the funds
left unutilized.
9. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Shipping to expedite Rehabilitation-cum-
Restructuring of HDPEL which has already been delayed. This is a need to sensitize the
concerned agencies to ensure that necessary approved plan for execution of schemes is
obtained in time so that funds allotted for those schemes do not remain un-utilized.
Recommendation of the Committee
10. The Committee was also informed (in the working) group report) that only 1/3
rd of the Total
outlay of Rs.30305.16 crores during the Eleventh plans outlay, i.e. Rs. 10388.87 crores was
allocated to the Ministry of Shipping under the port sector. However, it is equally surprising that
the utilization stands at 59.62% (or Rs.7684.61 crores) only. The Committee finds that this under-
utilization was mainly due to reasons such as delay in clearances, approvals etc. These are, no
doubt, time-taking exercises but if taken up with proper procedure and formalities as prescribed,
it could be expedited easily and quickly. In view of urgent need to modernize and expand our port
facilities and stiff competition with Private Ports staring at them, we cannot afford to delay
projects at our Ports. The Committee recommends that thorough home work needs to be done
before approaching each plan year projects for optimum utilization of scarce fund allocation.
(Para No. 7 of 177
th Report)

3
Reply of the Government
11. The recommendation has been noted for compliance in future.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
12. The Committee notes the reply.
ANNUAL PLAN 2011-2012
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
13. The Committee notes that the funds at BE 2011-12 was reduced to almost half at RE 2011-12
and the utilization was only 50% of BE. The reason submitted by Ministry of Shipping such as
delay in approval, non-submission of extension of dredging subsidy, non-receipt of proposal/
incomplete proposals from shipyards are of routine nature and not convincing.
(Para No. 12 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
14. In the Annual Plan 2011-12 an outlay of Rs. 273.60 crores and Rs.812.92 crores under Plan
and Non-Plan head were provided at BE stage for the Shipping Sector which was reduced to
Rs.207.61 crores and Rs.414.86 crores respectively at RE stage. Against these allocations, the
expenditure were Rs.187.51 crores (68.53% of BE) and Rs.386.12 crores (47.50% of BE)
15. In the plan side, the major shortfall of expenditure has been under the following heads:
(a) Inland Water Transport (IWT)- North Eastern Area: In the North East Region, there
is only one National Waterways i.e. NW-2 hence, there was not much scope for
utilization of fund in the North East Region.
(b) R&D Grant: The budgetary projections were made on the basis of projections provided
by IMU, Vizag which is executing a number of R&D projects in shipbuilding. IMU had
projected on the basis of ongoing projects as well as the new R&D projects. In the
IMU there was shortage of technical staff hence, efforts were made for recruitment
of experienced staff but considerable time was lost in this process resulting R&D
scheme could not be taken up.
(c) Indian Maritime University: An outlay of Rs. 40.00 crores was provided in the BE but
seeing to the pace of expenditure, the requirement of fund were reduced to Rs.30.00
crores at RE stage which was fully utilized.
(d) Directorate General of Lighthouse and Lightships (DGLL): An outlay of Rs.78.60
crores for construction and development of Lighthouses was kept which was reduced
to Rs.45.00 crores at RE stage. But DGLL could utilize Rs. 31.86 crores only because
a few prime projects such as (i) Establishment of VTS-GoK (ii) Estt. of National AIS
net work (iii) Automation of Port Blair LH Distt and (iv) Automation of remaining
Lighthouses could not commissioned resulting there is saving in the outlay provided for
these schemes.
16. In the Non-Plan side, an outlay of Rs.542.11 crores as subsidy for private shipyard was
provided which was reduced to Rs.129.78 crores at RE stage out of which the utilization was
Rs.122.42 crores only. The entire amount could not be utilized because the shipyards had not
submitted complete documents as required by DG (Shipping) for issuing PRCs and Technical
Certificate. Further, the Shipyards could not deliver vessels as per contractual delivery schedule.

4
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
17. The Committee notes the reply and observes that the reasons for under utilization
of funds given are same as those given during submission of Demands for Grants’ detailed
note. The Committee notes with concern that provision for subsidy to private ship-yard was
being made continuously for many years but the same remains under utilized every year.
The Committee may be informed of the steps taken for utilization of non-plan outlay for
the subsidy for private shipyards.
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
18. The Port Sector present really a gloomy picture in case of utilization of outlay for the year
2011-12 where only 55.16% of total allocation could be utilized upto December, 2011. It is just
0.58% in the case of R&D, 47.40% in IT. The post Tsunami works are still going and only
35.31% could be utilized during 2011-12 (upto December 2011). ALHW could utilize only Rs.9.87
crores out of Rs. 17.77 (upto December, 2011) which is just 55.54% of total allocation. A perusal
of the statement of expenditure incurred by ports reveals that there had been shortfall in utilization
of funds against the BE/RE during the plan.
(Para No. 13 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
19. During 2011-12, a BE provision of Rs.96.00 crores was made for post Tsunami restoration
projects. At the RE stage, the allocation was reduced to Rs.43.75 crores. The entire 2011-12 RE
allocation for post Tsunami restoration projects was utilized.
20. It can therefore be seen that shortfall in expenditure for the post Tsunami restoration
projects has been with respect to BE allocation and not the RE allocation for the year 2011-12.
The reasons for shortfall in expenditure with respect to BE provision has been on account of
stoppage of all quarries in A&N Islands, re-tendering due to poor response of agencies in marine
works, downsizing of projects, non sanction of schemes due to non clearance from tribal council
etc.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/BSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
21. The Committee notes the reply with concern that all expects the Ministry to try to
obtain required sanctions/clearance in time for post Tsunami restoration projects.
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
22. The Committee is perturbed to note that the spending pattern of the Ministry of shipping
is resulting is cuts in allocations by the Finance Ministry. The Committee recommends that the
Ministry should look into the reasons for low utilization and take remedial measure by way of
proper planning and implementation.
(Para No. 14 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
23. In order to ensure optimum utilization of fund, a periodical monitoring and review of plan
and non plan expenditure is conducted at the highest level and hurdles, if any, are found in smooth
execution of any scheme/project, remedial measures are taken in consultation with the concerned
agencies so that pace of the expenditure is accelerated.

5
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
24. The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee
25. The Committee in its earlier reports had also recommended that there is need to formulate
plan and policies in a realistic manner. Besides, all the schemes/plans should be reviewed to see
as to why these are not picking up, particularly subsidy to Ship Yards for which no proposal
completed in all respects with proper documentation were received. The growth of shipping sector
is closely linked with the overall development of the country and therefore, deserves top priority
in implementation of plan/schemes by the Ministry of Shipping.
(Para No. 15 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
26. The observation of the committee has been noted. This Ministry is impressing upon the
shipyards applying for subsidy to submit proposals with complete documentation so as to facilitate
expeditious processing of the proposals for release of shipbuilding subsidy. During the current
financial year i.e.  2012-13, there is a budget provision of Rs.400.00 crores for grant of
shipbuilding subsidy to shipyards. This Ministry has received 13 proposals from shipyards for
Rs. 160 cr approx as yet for release. We have already released Rs.28.90 crores and it is expected
that by the second quarter, all the proposals received so far, shall be finalised for release.  Complete
proposals as and when received from shipyards shall be dealt with urgently so that funds could
be released as per the parameters of the scheme during the current financial year.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
27. The Committee notes the reply.
ANNUAL PLAN 2012-13
Recommendation of the Committee
28. Committee notes that the Ministry of Shipping has got without any cut from the Finance
Ministry their projected demand for Rs.812 crores has been made. The Committee recommends
that the allocated funds should be utilized fully as many important projects, especially in the port
sector are to be completed within the scheduled time in order to cope up with the growing demand
and the competition posed by the private players of the country . The Committee also recommends
that periodic monitoring and review should be made for better utilization of funds as in the year
2011-12 the expenditure was only 50% of the BE allocation”.
(Para No. 21 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
29. Mechanism for monthly review and monitoring of expenditure of all entities on both port
and shipping sectors has been set up in the Ministry and is being monitored regularly.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
30. The Committee notes the reply.

6
PORTS
Recommendation of the Committee
31. The Committee considers the ports as the back-bone of the trade and commerce thereby
is strongly linked to the economic growth of a country. The Committee observed the enhancement
of provisions to the port sector under Plan Head to Rs.380.98 crores in the 2012-13 compared to
Rs.246.59 crores in 2011-12. The expenditure during 2011-12 (upto December, 2011) is Rs.75.08
crores only. The Committee, however is of the opinion that already the port sector was far behind
from the projected targets of its capacity additions, modernization of equipments, deepening of
drafts and ship channels etc. And even then they were not able to utilize the allocation. The
Committee is not satisfied with the reasons for low utilization and expresses its concerns that on
the delayed projects, resulting in tow-fold loss-more spending due to cost overruns and loss of
revenue which otherwise would have been generated after completion of the extra capacity. The
Committee strongly recommends for prioritized action on the above.
(Para No. 32 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
32. Regular Review mechanism has been put in place to ensure maximum utilization of allotted
funds.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
33. The Committee notes the reply. It however, emphasizes that the Government should
strictly monitor the efficacy of regular review mechanism.
Recommendation of the Committee
34. The Committee notes the targets of 675.25 MCM in the capital dredging and 429.99 MCM
in maintenance dredging activities during the XI Plan period wherein only 278.93 MCM and 291.63
MCM respectively could be achieved which constituted 41.31% and 67.82% of the targets. The
Committee would like to reiterate its recommendations contained in the para 142 of its 170
th Report
on the “Modernization of Major Ports”. The Committee recommended:–
“Both capital and maintenance is an important component for cargo handling capacity and
to increase the efficiency of the Indian Major Ports. The Committee recommends that
projects taken up/proposed to be taken up are executed in a time bound manner. ...The
Committee, therefore recommend that in view of the increase in the expenditure on
dredging, the Government of India should take their responsibility and prepare a long-term
plan for financing the dredging operations in all the Major Ports.”
(Para No. 34 of 177
th Report)
Reply of the Government
35. The observations of the Committee are noted. The Planning Commission has constituted an
Inter-Ministerial Committee on Capital dredging for Major Ports to suggest measure to improve
capital dredging in all Ports. Based on the recommendations of the Committee a long-term Plan to
undertake capital dredging and financing will be formulated for Major Ports. The Ministry of
Finance and Planning Commission have agreed in-principle that capital dredging projects are eligible
for Viability Gap Funding (VGF) support. Accordingly, Ministry of Finance has conveyed that as
a concept, PPP projects for Capital dredging in Ports is admissible for VGF support, subject to
the other conditions of the Scheme and guidelines being satisfied.

7
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
36. The Committee notes the reply. It would hasten to add that DCI needs to be
empowered/supported in a big way and its pending payments etc. should be settled. In the
face of PPP in capital dredging, it should not be allowed to be closed eventually.

104. The international shipping market is facing problem of oversupply of tonnage and Indian

SCI’s revenue generation has been severely affected at present and the primary reason is the

to ensure capturing business opportunities from PSUs:
Dry Bulk carrier and Tanker Division
113. SCI by and large participates and endeavors to pitch in with the vessels as and when
vessels are available in dates for any PSU cargo/Contract of Affreightments (COA) etc. SCI’s dry
bulk vessels are predominantly tramping, however any Transchart released PSU cargoes are always

114. These PSU cargoes are mostly opened on voyage basis in the market and a vessels revenue
return or the economic viability for a particular business also hinges on its proximity to the cargo

offer at much below market level rates with the ultimate motive to capture the business, whereas
SCI with her brand new fleet with much higher opex and capex cost may not be able to sustain

115. The container services department has a service from Indian Sub Continent to Europe,

18
North West Continent, Far East, Gulf, Mediterranean and East Africa. SCI also has slot
arrangements for carriage of containers, from USA. SCI has a Coastal Service which currently
operates between Mundra and Pipavav to Cochin and Tuticorin.

referred to them by the PSU’s through Transchart. Then SCI carries this cargo by quoting
competitive rates and in some cases where the PSU’s have a rate limit, then by matching the rates
that the PSU has received. In case, SCI do not have a service to a particular location then it tries
to arrange the shipment by purchasing slots with other liners. SCI have also entered into Annual
Rate Agreements with some of the major PSU’s like IOC, BRBNML, BPCL/KRL etc. These
agreements are entered into between the SCI, the PSU and the Transchart.
117. Further, SCI is trying to garner more PSU’s to enter into Annual Rate Agreement so that
there is seamless movement of cargoes.
Joint Ventures
118. In addition to the above efforts taken by the respective Operating Divisions, efforts have
been taken by SCI by way of entering into JVs with PSUs to capitalize on opportunities emerging
from them. Some of the steps taken by SCI include formation of Joint Venture with SAIL and that
proposed with Coal India Ltd. These JV companies would cater to the cargo transportation
requirements of SAIL and Coal India Ltd. by building on SCI’s expertise in this field and in-turn
ensure that emerging opportunities from these PSUs are covered by us and not by Foreign players.

has highlighted some important tax related issues which were required to be addressed in the Union

138. The Committee is of the view that even though the Indian tonnage is growing as per the
projections, the India fleet are not gaining the momentum. Even the fleet acquisition plans of SCI
has been passing through a very difficult phase. At the same time Indian ship building industry and
ship repair sector are equally struggling to get enough business. This is happening at a time when
Ship Building Orders are given to foreign shipyard and Indian Ships and dredgers are looking

overseas destinations for the repair works. The Committee recommends that, the Ministry of

(Para No. 117 of 177 th Report)
Reply of the Government
139. Absence of the significant domestic market and intense competition from foreign shipyards
have adversely affected the Indian shipbuilding industry. The Indian shipbuilding market is exposed
to threat of imports due to no protection of tariff barriers. In contrast, foreign markets are
projected by policy measures of their respective countries.
140. Governement of India introduced a shipbuilding subsidy scheme during 2002-07 which led
to unprecedented growth in Indian shipbuilding activity. Withdrawal of the scheme in August, 2007,
let to an immediate downturn in the shipbuilding industry.
141. A proposal was placed before the COS (Committee of Secretaries) in February, 2012 for
the following Policy measures for Indian shipbuilding industry:
(i) Provision of subsidy to Indian shipyards for construction of five years from 2012-13
to 2017-18.
(ii) Gr ant infrastructure status to shipbuilding industry.
(iii) Indian built-Indian flag vessels to be accorded first preference for movement of all
types of Government cargo, coastal cargo and cargo playing on Inland Waterways
Network.
(iv) Import duty exemption on import of capital equipment for ship building
(v) Service tax exemption to ship building and ship repair industry
(vi) Steel supplied by domestic steel companies to Indian shipyards to be treated as deemed
export for the purpose of duty concessions.
142. COS considered the above proposals on 17.2.2012 and inter alia directed that Ministry of
Shipping may take up the proposal for grant of infrastructure status for shipbuilding with Ministry
of Finance. A revised proposal may be submitted before the COS after carrying out a detailed study
on the policy support measures provided by the other countries like China, Japan and Korea, and
also data on investment likely to be generated by the shipbuilding industry. The Ministry is taking
necessary action as recommended by the COS and shortly shall again approach COS for policy
support measures to boost Indian shipbuilding industry.

26. The underutilization of funds under the CBSP Scheme has been only during the year 2007-08

229. The recommendations of the working group for improving regional air connectivity in India
to promote tourism in lesser known destinations are as under:-
CENTRAL GOVERNMENT
OPERATIONAL REFORMS
(i) Currently agencies like Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) and Bureau of
Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) do not distinguish between large scheduled Airlines and
small operators. Regulatory and compliance requirements for Small/Non Scheduled
operators have to be modified keeping in view the size of Aircraft, fleet and workload
of small operators.
(ii) Create a separate Feeder Scheduled Airlines Category to meet the requirements of
feeder sector. This category should be exclusively reserved for Aircraft/Helicopters

34
below 50 seats with sector length not exceeding beyond 500 kilometres. The Aircraft/
Helicopters below 5700 kilogram with minimum 6 seat capacity irrespective of number
of engines should be permitted to operate in this category. Non scheduled operators
desirous of operating at least one regular commercial flight with thrice weekly
frequency on new sectors (virgin or non operational since preceding 2 years) for
partial aircraft utilisation should be treated as ‘Deemed Operator’ in this category.
(iii) The existing guidelines for code share operations may be amended to promote regional
connectivity as a part of a long – haul itinerary by way of code share between the
long haul operator and the regional operator.
(iv) Non scheduled operators desirous of regular passenger flights with minimum thrice
weekly frequency should be allowed to file their flight schedule for approval of regular
operations for sectors which are not serviced at present. For such regular operations,
the operator should be permitted to advertise their schedules and undertake advance
booking through reservation network and search engines.
(v) Additional administrative/technical posts even in categories which are out sourced to
third party substantially adds to overhead of the operator and makes the small
aircraft operations unviable. In case of small operators flexibility of deployment and
multitasking by staff and crew should be permitted. DGCA should not insist on
minimum sets of flight crew etc. which should be based on level of operations and
flying hours while meeting Flight and Duty Time Limitations. Duality of functions
like quality control by operator and contracted Maintenance, Repair and Operations
(MRO) results in duplication of manpower and conflict in accountability. In technical
departments like engineering and operations one coordinator should be able to
perform all the departmental work and deal with multiple departments in DGCA and
BCAS etc.
(vi) In case of Non scheduled operators, DGCA headquarters should delegate more powers
to Regional Controllers so that they are not required to approach Headquarters for
every small approval.
(vii) In terms of regulatory approvals starting with NOC issuance, import permission,
Aircraft Type Rating and Endorsement, Air Operator’s Certificate (AOC) issuance etc.,
strict time limits should be specified for approval mechanism. Similar committee
mechanism to the present system of Empowered Committee in Ministry of Civil
Aviation should be established in DGCA with monthly frequency wherein all pending
matters requiring approval by Non Scheduled operators can be decided in timely
manner.
(viii) The current policy of Scheduled Airlines (Regional) restricts the operator to operate
from only one Metro Airport whereas the traffic affinity from many important cities
requires connectivity to at least two Metro Cities i.e. Jodhpur needs connectivity to
both Delhi and Mumbai, similarly Ranchi requires connectivity to Delhi and Kolkata.
Permission to connect two metros from any intermediate point will result in better
point to point servicing and provide higher Aircraft utilization of small operators .In
order to safeguard the interest of Scheduled Airlines, policy may forbid Scheduled
Airlines(Regional) to operate point to point nonstop services between two Metro
Airports.
(ix) The current policy of Scheduled Airlines (Regional) permits the operation of flights to
Metro Airport of the Region based on geographical base of operator i.e. Kanpur or
Jaipur based operator can operate to Delhi but not Mumbai. In many cases the traffic

35
requirement of some important cities may require flight operations to Metro Stations
of other Regions i.e., Surat or Pune based operator would find greater traffic flow
towards Delhi or Bangalore compared to Mumbai. Scheduled Airlines policy should
permit the Operator to connect any one Metro Airport instead of such geographical
stratification.
(x) Metro Airports like Delhi and Mumbai have classified the flight operations of Aircraft
less than 40000 kg as non revenue flights and discourage such operations. Small
operators are not given time slots and parking permissions. Ministry may issue strict
guidelines to Airport operators to facilitate Regional Operations.
(xi) Foreign Pilots of Non Scheduled Operators’ Permit (NSOP) Operators face serious
problems in operating flights to Defence Airfields since they have to obtain security
clearance from Ministry of Defence before operating every single flight. Such
clearance has to be filed at least 2 days in advance and during weekends such time
limit becomes even longer. Many times such stipulation results in cancellation of
flights and prohibits last minute substitution of operating crew in case of non
availability of rostered pilot due to any exigency. DGCA should obtain security
clearance of all Foreign Pilots from Ministry of Home Affairs before permitting
Foreign Pilots to fly in India and once they are endorsed, such requirement should
be dispensed with.
(xii) Extension of watch hours becomes a major constraint at airports having single shift
operations. In case the operators wish to operate minimum thrice weekly frequencies
on regular basis, Airports Authority of India (AAI) should provide an extension of
watch hours at such airports without additional overtime charges. This facility should
be extended only in case of regular passenger operations.
(xiii) DGCA should permit bush operations at unmanned Airports with limited Non-
Directional (Radio) Beacon (NDB) and Very High Frequency (VHF) facilities.
INCENTIVES
(i) In order to encourage investment in regional aviation category, Banks and Financial
institution like Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) should create a
special fund in the form of equity and loans including working capital loans against the
securitization of Aircraft Assets. Debt funding up to 50% of Aircraft value subject to
valuation of Aircraft should be provided by banks without seeking additional security
from promoters. Small operators should be entitled to benefits applicable to other Small
and Medium Enterprises (SMEs).
(ii) New sites should be given incentives. Special incentives should be provided for
regional connectivity at airports which are non operational. Allocation of cost of
operation should be done in a manner which makes regional connectivity viable. Start
– up aid or subsidies in the form of waiver of landing/navigational charges, wherever
applicable, should be considered in the initial few years or till such time the economies
of scale are achieved, whichever is earlier.
(iii) S ervice Tax should be rationalized from 10.3% and non scheduled operators should be
charged on per seat basis as the scheduled airlines are charged. Service tax on
Medivac (Medical Evacuation) flights should be abolished.
(iv) Fixed Base Operator (FBO) charges which account for more than half of the flying
charges at airports should be rationalized and make operations viable.

36
STATE GOVERNMENT
OPERATIONAL REFORMS
(i) State Governments should devise long term Aviation policy of the State enlisting the
priority routes for Intra-State connectivity.
(ii) State Governments can provide security and fire tenders during the time of flight if
operators undertake minimum thrice weekly frequency.
INCENTIVES
(i) State Governments may consider introducing scheme of providing limited seed capital
in the form of Equity and nominate one or two officers on the Board of the proposed
airlines. This would help small operators in professionalising their management and
Nominee Directors can assist the company in obtaining timely approval from various
banks and government agencies. This would ensure better market confidence amongst
Aircraft sellers, leasing companies and travelling public. Nominee directors will also
ensure judicious utilisation of funds and focus on well defined business plan including
State priorities. Nominee directors would be also be able to ensure fair cost and
subsidy assessment in cases where State Governments/Government of India are keen
to operate few sectors due to strategic reasons and are willing to subsidize such
flights.
(ii) Subsidies should be available to any operator on ‘first come first serve’ basis to attract
multiple operators within the State, who could become multi aircraft operator in due
course. Duration of subsidy can be limited to 18 to 36 months. Quantum of subsidy
may be up to 25% of seat revenue in case of aircraft below 20 seats and 15% of seat
revenue for aircraft between 20 to 50 seats in the form of seats guarantee or
operational subsidy. Such subsidy should be reimbursed to operator on monthly basis
since delay in providing payment to operator results in cash crunch defeating the very
purpose of such subsidy.
(iii) Reduction in sales tax on Air Turbine Fuel (ATF) should be offered based on the
Maharashtra Model, under which there is no taxation on fuel for flights operated out
of non metro cities for destinations within Maharashtra.
